Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verse 1:

﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ain, Sad﴾

These are letters of enunciation (huruf hija'), written according to what they denote and read according to their names, so it is as though they were written for one who spells them out. The discussion of their collective counterparts (naza'ir) has already been presented, as has the preferred view among the opinions concerning them in Surat al-Baqarah, and likewise their placement within speech.

The basic principle in pronouncing these letters is that each letter should be pronounced with a pause after it, because the fundamental nature of these letters is that they enumerate independent letters or letters abbreviated from words.

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) recited the names of all five of these letters with the vowels sounded clearly and the final letters of their names pronounced with sukun (silent).

Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, and Ya'qub recited the name of the second letter, which is (ha), with imalah (vowel inclination). In a narration from Nafi' and Ibn Kathir, they recited (ha) with a vowel between kasrah and fathah.

Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited (ya) with imalah.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far recited the dal of (sad) with idhhar (clear pronunciation). The rest recited it with idgham (assimilation) into the dhal of ﴿Dhikru rahmati rabbika﴾ [Maryam: 2]. The reason (ha) and (ya) were not elongated, even though the reciter pronounces the names of these letters that occur at the beginnings of the surahs and not their written forms, is that the names of these two letters end with a hamzah that is softened (mukhaffafah), for the reason we mentioned in the opening of Surat Yunus, namely softening by removal for the sake of pausing (al-sakt).

Know that if you follow other than the preferred view regarding the meanings of the openings of the surahs: as for the views that make all the openings share one meaning, the matter is evident. As for the views that assign particular meanings to some of them, it was said regarding the meaning of ﴿Kaf Ha Ya 'Ain Sad﴾ that its letters are abbreviated from the names of God the Exalted: al-Kafi (the Sufficient), or al-Karim (the Generous), or al-Kabir (the Great); the Ha from Hadi (the Guide); the Ya from Hakim (the Wise) or Rahim (the Merciful); the 'Ain from al-'Alim (the All-Knowing) or al-'Azim (the Mighty); and the Sad from al-Sadiq (the Truthful). It was also said that their collection is a name of God the Exalted, to the extent that it was said to be the Greatest Name (al-Ism al-A'zam), which when called upon, responds. And it was said that it is a name of the Qur'an, that is, by a new designation. There is no hadith on this that can be relied upon.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verses 2–3:

﴿This is a mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zakariyya﴾ ﴿when he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾

This is the opening of a discourse, so "dhikr" (mention) must be the predicate of an omitted subject. Its like is commonly omitted in such headings. The estimated reading is: "This is a mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant." It carries the sense of "remember" (imperative). It is also permissible that "dhikr" originally be an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) standing in place of its verb, in the sense of a command: "remember a remembrance." It was then shifted from the accusative to the nominative to indicate permanence, as in His saying ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾ [al-Fatiha: 2]. This was discussed in the commentary on Surat al-Fatiha. What favours this reading is the conjunction in ﴿And mention in the Book Maryam﴾ [Maryam: 16] and its like.

This discourse is composed in a wondrous manner of brevity and of departure from the customary style of narration. The original wording would be: "Mention of Our servant Zakariyya, when he called upon his Lord and said: 'My Lord, etc...' Then the mercy of your Lord." The placing of the report first, that God had shown mercy to him, indicates concern for this virtue of his, and an announcement that God shows mercy to whoever turns to Him, together with the mention, in the addition of "Lord" to the pronoun of the Prophet ﷺ and to the pronoun of Zakariyya, of honouring both of them.

The story of Maryam and 'Isa begins with what is connected to it concerning the circumstances of the family of Maryam and her guardian, because in all those circumstances there is a reminder of God's mercy and His honouring of His friends.

Zakariyya is a prophet from among the prophets of the Children of Israel. He is the second Zakariyya, husband of Maryam's maternal aunt, and he has no book among the books of the Torah. As for the one who has a book, he is Zakariyya ibn Berekhiah, who lived in the sixth century BC. The biography of the second Zakariyya has already passed in Surat Al 'Imran, and the story of his supplication passed there.

The phrase ﴿when he called upon his Lord﴾ is a temporal clause related to "mercy" (i.e., God's mercy to him at that time), or it is a substitute (badal) for "dhikr" (i.e., remember that time).

Nida' (calling) originally means raising the voice to request attention. It has been discussed at His saying ﴿Our Lord, we have heard a caller calling to faith﴾ [Al 'Imran: 193] in Surat Al 'Imran, and at His saying ﴿And they will be called out: this is the Garden you have been made to inherit﴾ [al-A'raf: 43] in Surat al-A'raf. Nida' is often applied to speech that requests the attention of a person to a deed, or the attention of the mind to understand a speech; for this reason the particles with which the request for attention is opened are called "particles of nida'." It is also applied to supplication requesting a need, even if it does not involve calling aloud, because the custom of supplication is generally to be audible, that is, in humble entreaty, since this has a greater effect on the heart of the one called upon. The meaning of the sentence is: Zakariyya said, "O Lord," with a hidden voice. It was hidden because Zakariyya saw that this was more conducive to sincerity, while hoping that God would answer his supplication, so that the answer would not be something people talk about. Therefore he did not supplicate with loud entreaty, although entreaty is generally more helpful for the sincerity of turning to God. Perhaps Zakariyya's certainty sufficed to strengthen his turning, so he chose for his supplication safety from the mixing of showing-off (riya').

There is no contradiction between it being a nida' and its being hidden, because it is the nida' of One who hears what is hidden.

What is meant by mercy is the answering of his supplication, as He will make explicit when He says (﴿O Zakariyya, We give you good news of a boy whose name is Yahya﴾ [Maryam: 7]). The verse only reports the description of Zakariyya's supplication as it occurred, so there is no indication in it of praise for concealing the supplication.

[Page 64]

The clause "My bones have weakened, and my head has flared with white hair" (﴿قالَ رَبِّ إنِّي وهَنَ العَظْمُ مِنِّي واشْتَعَلَ الرَّأْسُ شَيْبًا﴾) explains the phrase "he called upon his Lord" (﴿نادى رَبَّهُ﴾) in verse 3. This clause and what follows it serve as an introduction (tamhid) to the main purpose of the supplication, which is his words "so grant me from Yourself an heir" (﴿فَهَبْ لِي مِن لَدُنْكَ ولِيًّا﴾). This introduction is given because of the state of distress he was in, which compelled him to ask for a child. God answers the one in distress when he calls upon Him. Therefore his request for a child was not a request for mere comfort, enjoyment or pride.

He described the condition that made his need for a child pressing, both in his present state and in his future. The weakening of his bones and the spread of white hair over his head were a present state that required seeking help from a child, together with what such a state usually implies of nearness to the time of death. This is an aim in itself and also a means to another aim, which is inheritance after death.

The two predicates in his words "My bones have weakened, and my head has flared with white hair" are used figuratively to mean their implication, which is a plea for pity for his condition, since the one being informed (the listener, with the verb in the passive form pronounced with a fatha on its final letter) already knows what the two statements contain.

Weakness (al-wahn) means frailty. Attributing it to the bones, rather than to other parts of the body that weakness also affects, is more concise in indicating that weakness has reached his whole body, because the bone is the support of the body and the hardest part of it. Weakness cannot reach it unless it has already reached what is above it.

The definite article in "the bones" (al-'azm) is the generic article, indicating all the bones of his body. The spread of white hair over his head, or its dominance over it, is likened to the blazing of fire in charcoal, by the common feature of a bright thing spreading through a black body. This is a compound figurative comparison (tashbih murakkab tamthili), which admits of being analysed into separate parts within the comparison. It is the most artful type of compound comparison. Thus the black hair is likened to charcoal and the white hair to fire, in the manner of the implicit figurative representation (al-tamthiliyya al-makniyya), and both are alluded to by the verb "flared" (ishta'ala). The flaring is attributed to the head, which is the place of the hair that white hair has spread over, because the head is not overspread by white hair except, usually, after the beard has been overspread.

So the spread of white hair on the head is a sign that he had reached deep old age.

Attributing the flaring to the head is a rational figurative attribution (majaz 'aqli), because flaring is a property of fire, to which the white hair is likened. So the natural thing would have been to attribute it to the white hair. But when the noun "white hair" (al-shayb) is brought as a specification (tamyiz) of the relation of flaring, the particular quality of the figure and its strangeness are achieved, together with the particular quality of preference after possibility. The indefinite form of "white hair" (shayban) conveys magnification, and so a wonderful brevity is achieved. The usual form of the expression would have been: "the white hair flared in the hair of the head."

Because this clause contains such particularities of the sciences of meaning and rhetoric (al-ma'ani wal-bayan), it has the greatest effect upon the people of eloquence. The author of the Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) drew attention to it, and the author of the Miftah (al-Sakkaki) clarified it, so consult them both.

[Page 65]

Abu Bakr ibn Duraid has taken its meaning in his verse:

"The white-haired one flared in his blackness, like the flaring of fire in dry ghada wood."

But it deserves to be the source of the proverb: "Water, but not like Sada" (ma' wa-la ka-sada).

White hair (al-shayb) is the whiteness of the hair. Whiteness comes upon the hair because of a loss of the substance that gives the hair its original colour. This loss is usually due to advancing age, which is why white hair is a sign of old age, though hair may also turn white from illness.

The clause "and I have never been unsuccessful in calling upon You, my Lord" (﴿ولَمْ أكُنْ بِدُعائِكَ رَبِّ شَقِيًّا﴾) is an interjected clause placed between the introductory clauses. The preposition "bi" in his words "bi-du'a'ika" (in calling upon You) denotes accompaniment.

The wretched one (al-shaqiyy) is the one who has been struck by misfortune (al-shiqwa), which is the opposite of happiness (al-sa'ada). That is, misfortune is the deprivation of what is hoped for and the going astray of one's effort. The negation of wretchedness is used, and what is intended is the obtaining of its opposite, which is happiness, by way of metonymy (kinaya), since there is no intermediate state between them in common usage.

A structure like this has, in their speech, become like a proverb for attaining happiness from something. A parallel to it is the words of God Most High in this surah, in the story of Abraham: ﴿It may be that I shall not be unsuccessful in calling upon my Lord﴾ (Maryam 19:48). That is, perhaps I shall be happy, that is, one whose supplication is answered.

In the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Prophet (ﷺ), what he relates from his Lord concerning those who remember God and those who sit with them: "They are the companions; no one who sits with them is made wretched." That is, one who sits with them is made happy. One of the poets, whose name we do not know, and who was from the Islamic period, said:

"I was a companion of Qa'qa' ibn Shawr, and no one who sits with Qa'qa' is made wretched."

That is, his companion becomes happy through him.

[Page 66]

The meaning is: "I was never rejected by You in what I have asked of You before this." That is, it is known that God always responds whenever He is called upon.

This is an introduction to the answer, by a route other than the introduction in the clauses accompanying it. Rather, it is the route of urging the continuation of God's gracious dealings with him, and of seeking nearness to Him through the answers He has already given him.

It is reported that a needy man asked Hatim al-Ta'i, or Ma'n ibn Za'idah, saying: "I am the one you treated well on such-and-such a day." He said: "Welcome to the one who has sought nearness to us through us."

The clause "and I fear my kinsmen after me" (﴿وإنِّي خِفْتُ المَوالِيَ مِن ورائِي﴾) is coordinated with the clause "and my head has flared with white hair" (﴿واشْتَعَلَ الرَّأْسُ شَيْبًا﴾). That is: "I have drawn near to death, and I fear my kinsmen after me."

As for what has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Abu Salih, from the Prophet (ﷺ) in a mursal form (a report whose link to a Companion is missing), that he said: "May God have mercy on Zakariyya; what was it for him, the inheritance of his wealth?" — perhaps he feared the poor understanding of them concerning the religious and scholarly legacies that he would leave behind. Such precious things are hard for a believer to see lost. For this reason he said: ﴿who shall inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾. The souls of the prophets aspire only to lofty matters and the interests of religion, and whatever is other than that is secondary.

So his words "who shall inherit me" mean the inheritance of his property. This is supported by what 'Abd al-Razzaq related from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "May God have mercy on Zakariyya; what was it for him, the inheritance of his wealth?"

The apparent meanings indicate that the prophets were inherited from, as God Most High says: ﴿And Solomon inherited David﴾ (al-Naml 27:16). As for the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from; what we leave behind is charity," it is the Prophet himself that he means, as 'Umar understood it in his report with al-'Abbas and 'Ali in the Sahih of al-Bukhari, when 'Umar said: "The Messenger of God meant by that himself." So that would be one of the particularities of Muhammad (ﷺ).

[Page 67]

If that was a previous ruling, then Zakariyya's intention was the inheritance of the traces of prophethood only, namely the sacred books and the guardianship over them.

Al-mawali means the paternal kinsmen (al-'usba) and the closest relatives, the plural of mawla in the sense of walī (protector, guardian).

The meaning of "from after me" (min wara'i) is "after me," since "wara'" is used to mean what comes after a thing, as al-Nabigha said:

"There is nothing beyond God for a man to seek."

That is, after God. So the meaning of "from after me" is "after the time of my life."

The phrase "min wara'i" is in the position of a qualifier of "al-mawali" or of a circumstantial clause.

The wife of Zakariyya was named Elisabeth (Alisabat), from the descendants of Aaron, brother of Moses, so she was of the tribe of Levi.

The barren one ('aqir) is the woman who does not bear children, so it is a term specific to women. For this reason it is stripped of the feminine marker, since there is no ambiguity. Its verbal noun is al-'aqr, with fatha or damma on the 'ayn and sukun on the qaf. He used the verb "was" (kanat) to indicate that barrenness was firmly established in her and fixed upon her, and therefore she was deprived of children.

The meaning of "from Yourself" (min ladunka) is that it is from God, with a special nearness, because the speaker knows that everything comes from God by His decree and His creation of causes and their effects following their creation. So when he said "from Yourself," it indicates that he asked for an heir not following the usual course of the existence of children, since the usual causes were absent. Thus the granting of it would be a mark of honour for him.

The phrase "to me" (li) and "from Yourself" (min ladunka) are connected to the verb "grant" (hab). "To me" was placed before "from Yourself" because it is more important to the aim of the one calling upon God, and it is a particular aim, which takes precedence over a general aim.

[Page 68]

The reading of "who shall inherit me" (yarithuni) by the majority is with a damma, as a qualifier of "an heir" (waliyyan).

Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it in the jussive mood, as an answer to the supplication in his words "grant me" (hab li), signifying a causal relation, because the basic nature of the eight conditional answers is that they are in the sense of the causal fa'.

The phrase "the family of Ya'qub" (al ya'qub) may mean specifically the Children of Israel, as the word "family" (al), which indicates excellence and nobility, suggests. Then Ya'qub would be Israel, as if he had said: "and inherit from the family of Israel," that is, the bearers of the law and the rabbis of Judaism, as in God's words: ﴿We gave the family of Abraham the Book and wisdom﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:54). A man's family is mentioned in such a context when they follow his way. Of this kind is God's words: ﴿Surely the people most entitled to Abraham are those who followed him﴾ (Al 'Imran 3:68), and His words: ﴿the offspring of those whom We carried with Noah﴾ (al-Isra' 17:3), although all people are the offspring of those who were carried with him.

It is also possible that the intended Ya'qub is another than Israel, namely Ya'qub ibn Matan, as said by Ma'qil and al-Kalbi. He was the paternal uncle of Mary, brother of 'Imran, her father.

It has also been said that he was the brother of Zakariyya, meaning that he had no children, so that Zakariyya's son would be the heir of Ya'qub, since he was Ya'qub's nephew. On this view Ya'qub is among the kinsmen whom Zakariyya feared after him.

[Page 64]

The clause "My bones have weakened, and my head has flared with white hair" (﴿قالَ رَبِّ إنِّي وهَنَ العَظْمُ مِنِّي واشْتَعَلَ الرَّأْسُ شَيْبًا﴾) explains the phrase "he called upon his Lord" (﴿نادى رَبَّهُ﴾) in verse 3. This clause and what follows it serve as an introduction (tamhid) to the main purpose of the supplication, which is his words "so grant me from Yourself an heir" (﴿فَهَبْ لِي مِن لَدُنْكَ ولِيًّا﴾). This introduction is given because of the state of distress he was in, which compelled him to ask for a child. God answers the one in distress when he calls upon Him. Therefore his request for a child was not a request for mere comfort, enjoyment or pride.

He described the condition that made his need for a child pressing, both in his present state and in his future. The weakening of his bones and the spread of white hair over his head were a present state that required seeking help from a child, together with what such a state usually implies of nearness to the time of death. This is an aim in itself and also a means to another aim, which is inheritance after death.

The two predicates in his words "My bones have weakened, and my head has flared with white hair" are used figuratively to mean their implication, which is a plea for pity for his condition, since the one being informed (the listener, with the verb in the passive form pronounced with a fatha on its final letter) already knows what the two statements contain.

Weakness (al-wahn) means frailty. Attributing it to the bones, rather than to other parts of the body that weakness also affects, is more concise in indicating that weakness has reached his whole body, because the bone is the support of the body and the hardest part of it. Weakness cannot reach it unless it has already reached what is above it.

The definite article in "the bones" (al-'azm) is the generic article, indicating all the bones of his body. The spread of white hair over his head, or its dominance over it, is likened to the blazing of fire in charcoal, by the common feature of a bright thing spreading through a black body. This is a compound figurative comparison (tashbih murakkab tamthili), which admits of being analysed into separate parts within the comparison. It is the most artful type of compound comparison. Thus the black hair is likened to charcoal and the white hair to fire, in the manner of the implicit figurative representation (al-tamthiliyya al-makniyya), and both are alluded to by the verb "flared" (ishta'ala). The flaring is attributed to the head, which is the place of the hair that white hair has spread over, because the head is not overspread by white hair except, usually, after the beard has been overspread.

So the spread of white hair on the head is a sign that he had reached deep old age.

Attributing the flaring to the head is a rational figurative attribution (majaz 'aqli), because flaring is a property of fire, to which the white hair is likened. So the natural thing would have been to attribute it to the white hair. But when the noun "white hair" (al-shayb) is brought as a specification (tamyiz) of the relation of flaring, the particular quality of the figure and its strangeness are achieved, together with the particular quality of preference after possibility. The indefinite form of "white hair" (shayban) conveys magnification, and so a wonderful brevity is achieved. The usual form of the expression would have been: "the white hair flared in the hair of the head."

Because this clause contains such particularities of the sciences of meaning and rhetoric (al-ma'ani wal-bayan), it has the greatest effect upon the people of eloquence. The author of the Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) drew attention to it, and the author of the Miftah (al-Sakkaki) clarified it, so consult them both.

[Page 65]

Abu Bakr ibn Duraid has taken its meaning in his verse:

"The white-haired one flared in his blackness, like the flaring of fire in dry ghada wood."

But it deserves to be the source of the proverb: "Water, but not like Sada" (ma' wa-la ka-sada).

White hair (al-shayb) is the whiteness of the hair. Whiteness comes upon the hair because of a loss of the substance that gives the hair its original colour. This loss is usually due to advancing age, which is why white hair is a sign of old age, though hair may also turn white from illness.

The clause "and I have never been unsuccessful in calling upon You, my Lord" (﴿ولَمْ أكُنْ بِدُعائِكَ رَبِّ شَقِيًّا﴾) is an interjected clause placed between the introductory clauses. The preposition "bi" in his words "bi-du'a'ika" (in calling upon You) denotes accompaniment.

The wretched one (al-shaqiyy) is the one who has been struck by misfortune (al-shiqwa), which is the opposite of happiness (al-sa'ada). That is, misfortune is the deprivation of what is hoped for and the going astray of one's effort. The negation of wretchedness is used, and what is intended is the obtaining of its opposite, which is happiness, by way of metonymy (kinaya), since there is no intermediate state between them in common usage.

A structure like this has, in their speech, become like a proverb for attaining happiness from something. A parallel to it is the words of God Most High in this surah, in the story of Abraham: ﴿It may be that I shall not be unsuccessful in calling upon my Lord﴾ (Maryam 19:48). That is, perhaps I shall be happy, that is, one whose supplication is answered.

That is, one who sits with them is made happy. One of the poets, whose name we do not know, and who was from the Islamic period, said:

"I was a companion of Qa'qa' ibn Shawr, and no one who sits with Qa'qa' is made wretched."

That is, his companion becomes happy through him.

The speaker of an omitted saying, indicated by the context after the supplication, for brevity. That is, "We said: O Zakariyya, etc."

*Al-tabshir* means promising a gift. In a hadith (a report from the Prophet ﷺ), he said to the Ansar (the Helpers of Madina): "Then rejoice and be hopeful." In the hadith of the delegation of Banu Tamim: "Accept the good news." They said: "You gave us good news, so give us [a gift]."

The meaning of *ismuhu Yahya* is "name him Yahya," so the statement is in the form of a report but is used as a command.

Regarding *samiyy*, the commentators explained it as "one who shares the same name," meaning that We had not given anyone before his existence a namesake with this name. On this reading, this announcement is a secret from God, entrusted to Zakariyya, so that he would not suppose that anyone might name his son Yahya between this good news and the birth of the child. This is a favour from God and an honour to Zakariyya, since He made his son's name unique. Unique names have the merit of stronger identification of the named person, because few share them, and no one like him exists during his lifetime. They also have the merit that people later follow him, when they name their sons with that name, seeking blessing and good omen.

In my view, *samiyy* here means one who shares the descriptive name, by applying the term "name" to the attribute. The root of *ism* is (w-s-m), and *simah* (mark) originally was *wasmah*, as in His saying, ﴿They name the angels with the naming of females﴾ [al-Najm: 27], meaning they describe them as females. From this is His later saying, ﴿Do you know anyone worthy of His name?﴾ [Maryam: 65], meaning that God has no like among His names. This reading is more evident in praise of Yahya and in the favour shown to his father. The meaning is that no prophet before Yahya had gathered what Yahya gathered. He was given prophethood while still a child, as He said, ﴿And We gave him wisdom while still a child﴾ [Maryam: 12]. He was made *hasur* (one who abstains from women), so that it would not be a hardship for him in his purity from what is forbidden, and so that he would not face difficulty in combining the rights of worship with the rights of a wife. He was born to his father after old age and to his mother after barrenness. He was sent as a bringer of good news of the mission of 'Isa (peace be upon him), though he himself was not a messenger. His proper name was made unique, not preceded by anyone before him. These are merits and virtues bestowed on him and on his father. They do not imply that he was the best of the prophets, because excellence comes from a combination of virtues, not from some of them, however great. For this reason it has been said that a distinction does not entail superiority, and this is a word of truth.

The clause ﴿He said: My Lord﴾ is the response to the good news.

*Anna* is an interrogative used for wonder. The wonder is a figurative way of expressing gratitude, and it is an acknowledgement that this is a rare gift, not customary, since one may not ask God to grant a child and then marvel at God's answering him. It is possible that he thought God would grant him a child from another wife, by permitting him to marry a woman who was not barren. The discussion of a parallel verse has already been given in the Surah of Al 'Imran.

The clause ﴿and my wife has been barren﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the first-person pronoun. This is repeated along with his words in his supplication, ﴿and my wife has been barren﴾. This implies that Zakariyya thought the lack of childbirth was due to his wife's barrenness. People used to reckon this when a man had no impotence, castration or obstruction, because they thought that erection and ejaculation were the cause of pregnancy when the woman did not have the defect of barrenness. This is an error, since failure to give birth is either due to a condition in the woman's womb, or due to a condition in the man's semen, which is not fit for the development of the ova that the woman's womb produces.

The *min* in ﴿from old age, a great decline﴾ indicates the starting point, and it is a metaphor in the sense of causation.

*Al-kibar* means the great number of years of life, because it is accompanied by the appearance of diminished vigour and disorder of the body's system. *'Itiyyan* is the object of *balaghtu*.

[p. 71]

*Al-bulugh* (reaching) is a metaphor for the arrival of a time. Here he made himself the one reaching old age, while in the verse of Al 'Imran he said, ﴿old age has reached me﴾ [Al 'Imran: 40]. Since reaching was a metaphor for the attainment of a quality, it is correct to attribute it both to the quality and to the one who has the quality.

Its pattern is *fu'ul*, and its original form is *'utuww*. Analogically the *waw* should have been kept, since it follows a *damma*. But because they found it heavy to have two *damma*s followed by two *waw*s, which are like two *damma*s, they got rid of this heaviness by changing the *damma* of the 'ayn into a *kasra*. Then they changed the first *waw* into a *ya'*, because it fell as a quiescent letter after a *kasra*. When it was changed into a *ya'*, that *ya'* came together with the *waw* that is the lam. It seems they did not vowel the *ta'* in *'utiyy* with the meaning of dryness except to avoid confusion between it and *'utuww*, which is transgression. So there is no reason to seek lightening one of them without the other. He likened his bones to dry sticks by way of metaphor (*makniyyah*), and attributing the quality of *'utiyy* to them is an imaginative metaphor (*isti'arah takhyiliyyah*).

He likened his bones to dry sticks by way of metaphor (*makniyyah*), and attributing the quality of *'utiyy* to them is an imaginative metaphor (*isti'arah takhyiliyyah*).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verse 9:

﴿He said: "So it is. Your Lord says: 'It is easy for Me, and I created you before, when you were nothing.'"﴾

The clause ﴿He said: "So it is"﴾ is disjoined (fuṣilat) because it follows the manner of conversational dialogue (muḥāwara), and it is an answer to his expression of astonishment. Its purpose is to nullify the astonishment contained in his words ﴿My wife is barren, and I have reached extreme old age﴾ [Maryam: 8]. The pronoun in "he said" refers to the Lord, from His words ﴿He said: "My Lord, how can I have a boy?"﴾ [Maryam: 8]. The demonstrative in "So it is" refers to Zakariyya's words ﴿My wife is barren, and I have reached extreme old age﴾ [Maryam: 8]. The prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa al-majrur) is the object of the verb in ﴿Your Lord said﴾, meaning: the state of your old age and your wife's barrenness is as it is, and your Lord has decreed it. Thus the verb ﴿Your Lord said﴾ is intended as the creative speech (al-qawl al-takwini), that is, the decreeing one, meaning the attachment of His will and power (ta'alluq al-irada wa al-qudra). The purpose of stating it is to prepare for the nullification of the astonishment indicated by his words ﴿It is easy for Me﴾. The clause ﴿It is easy for Me﴾ is therefore a explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), answering a question arising from "So it is," because the statement of the cause of astonishment stirs the listener's expectation to know what nullifies that established astonishment, namely that it is easy in relation to the great power of God Most High.

It is also permissible that what is indicated by "So it is" is the speech derived from ﴿Your Lord said﴾, meaning that the word of your Lord ﴿It is easy for Me﴾ has reached the utmost clarity in its own category, such that it cannot be made clearer than what you have known. In that case it follows the manner of comparison, like His words ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], which has been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah. According to this possibility, the clause ﴿It is easy for Me﴾ is a reason (ta'lil) for the nullification of astonishment, a nullification derived from His words ﴿So it is; your Lord said﴾. The shift from the third person in ﴿Your Lord said﴾ to the first person in ﴿It is easy for Me﴾ [Maryam: 21] is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person). The expected form would be: "It is easy for Him." The word hayyin, with the yā' doubled, means easy to attain.

The clause ﴿I created you before﴾, according to both possibilities, occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (al-hal) relative to the pronoun of the third person in ﴿It is easy for Me﴾. That is, bringing the boy into being for you is easy for Me, in the state where I have created you before this boy and you were not existent, meaning: in the state where it (the boy's creation) resembles My creating you. Just as there is no wonder in the creation of a child in ordinary circumstances, so too there is no wonder in the creation of a child in rare circumstances, since both are bringing into existence after non-existence. The meaning of ﴿and you were not anything﴾ is: you were not existent.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿I created you﴾ with the first-person singular ta'.
Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read (we created you) with the nun of majesty.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verse 10:

﴿He said, "My Lord, appoint for me a sign." He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to the people for three nights, while being sound."﴾

He intended to set up a sign of the conception of the child having occurred, since the glad tidings did not specify a time, and the one promised may be delayed for a wisdom. Zakariyya wished to know the time of what was promised. In this hastening there is an allusion to seeking to have it hastened, and for this reason the complement of "a sign" (āyatan) is omitted. The idafa in "your sign" (āyatuka) is in the sense of the lam: "a sign for you," meaning, "We have made it a sign for you."

The meaning of ﴿that you will not speak to the people﴾ is that you will not be able to speak, because that is what suits its being a sign from God, the Exalted. It does not mean forbidding him from speaking to people, since there is no suitability in that for it being a sign. We have already discussed the verification of this in the surah of Al 'Imran. The period in which he was unable to speak to the people is stated here as three nights, while in the surah of Al 'Imran it is stated as three days. It is thus known that "nights" here means nights together with their days, and that "days" there means days together with their nights. He emphasised this here by describing them as ﴿sound﴾ (sawiyyan), that is, three complete nights, meaning together with their days. Sawiyy is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, and the description with it is the same for the singular, the feminine singular and the plural of either.

It has also been explained that sawiyyan is a state (hal) of the pronoun of the addressee, meaning "while you are sound," that is, without the affliction of muteness and dumbness. Yet it is a sign for you that wisdom required, which we have explained in the surah of Al 'Imran. On this view, mention of the description serves merely to emphasise reassurance; otherwise, its postponement for three nights is sufficient to reassure one that the affliction is absent.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verse 11:

﴿So he came out to his people from the prayer niche, and he signalled to them, "Glorify [God] morning and evening."﴾

The apparent meaning is that he came out to his people in order to pray as was his custom. He was in his niche in a particular worship and hidden supplication, then he came out for the congregational prayer, since he was their chief rabbi (al-hibr al-a'zam).

The verb (kharaja) has been given the sense of (tala'a, to emerge and appear), so it takes (ʿalā), as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So he came out to his people in his adornment﴾ [al-Qasas: 79].

Al-mihrab: a room or enclosure set aside for private worship. Al-Hariri said: "fa-mihrabi ahra bi" (so my prayer niche is more fitting for me).

Al-wahy: signalling with the eye or other means, and gesturing to convey a meaning whose nature is to be conveyed by speech.

(An) is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), and the clause ﴿Glorify [God] morning and evening﴾ is an explanation of (awha), because (awha) contains the sense of speaking without its letters.

He commanded them to glorify so that they would not suppose that Zakariyya, since he had not spoken to them, had vowed silence, and that they would then follow him and remain silent. Silence was among the forms of worship in earlier nations, as will come in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So say: I have vowed a fast to the Most Merciful, so I will not speak today to any human being﴾ [Maryam: 26]. So he gestured to them to begin what they were accustomed to of glorification, or he intended that they glorify God in gratitude for His granting their prophet a son who would inherit his knowledge. Perhaps they had known of his expectation of the answer to his supplication, or he commanded them with this in an ambiguous manner which he would explain when the impediment of his tongue was lifted.

[Page 76]

This is an implied verb of saying (maqul qawl mahdhuf). The context shows it, since this speech is addressed to Yahya, so it must have come from a speaker, and the only fitting speaker is God Most High. This marks a transition from the good news of his birth to his prophethood. It is more apparent that this is the Qur'an informing the community, not a report of what was said to Zakariya. Here begins the mention of Yahya's virtues, and what lies between is omitted because it is not relevant to the purpose. The context indicates this. The estimated wording is: "We said: O Yahya, take the Book." The Book is undoubtedly the Torah, since Yahya had no revealed book of his own. The verb "take" (akhdh) is used metaphorically for understanding and reflection, as one says, "I took knowledge from so-and-so," because the one who cares for a thing resembles one who takes it. "Strength" (quwwah) refers to a moral strength, namely resolve and steadfastness. The preposition "bi" (with) expresses accompaniment, meaning taking it while being steadfast in it, that is, in acting upon it and leading the community to follow it. Weakness had begun to creep into the Jewish community in its practice of its religion.

"And We gave him" (wa-ataynahu) is coordinated with the omitted speech, meaning: We said, "O Yahya, take the Book, and We gave him wisdom." "Hukm" is a term for wisdom (hikmah). Its meaning was discussed earlier in His words, "Whoever is given wisdom has indeed been given much good" [al-Baqarah: 269], in Surat al-Baqarah. Here it refers to prophethood, as was mentioned earlier in His words, "When he reached his full strength, We gave him judgment and knowledge" [Yusuf: 22], in Surat Yusuf. Thus this is a particular distinction of Yahya, that he was given prophethood in his childhood. It has also been said that hukm means hikmah and understanding.

"Sabiyyan" (as a child) is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in "ataynahu." This implies that God granted him soundness of thought and perception of realities in childhood, in an unusual manner, just as He granted His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) soundness and correctness of judgment in his youth. It is unlikely that Yahya was given prophethood while still a child, because prophethood is a great rank and is granted only upon reaching full maturity. The scholars agree that Yahya was given prophethood well before the age of forty. Perhaps God, when He willed that he be a martyr early in his life, honored him with prophethood at the beginning of his life.

"Hanan" means compassion (shafqah). Among the attributes of God Most High is al-Hannan (the Compassionate). In Arabic speech one says "hananayka," meaning compassion from you after compassion. That Yahya's compassion is described as "from Us" indicates that it exceeds what is customary among people. "Zakah" refers to the purification of the soul and its cleansing from impurities, as in His words, "Then say, 'Would you be purified?'" [al-Nazi'at: 18]. Or it may mean blessing (barakah).

"Taqiyy" is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of muf'il, from ittaqa, meaning one who has the quality of taqwa (God-consciousness), which is avoiding what contradicts the religion. The verb "kana" (was) is used in describing him with taqwa, in His words, "he was taqiyy" [Maryam: 13], to indicate that he was firmly established in this quality.

[Page 77]

Likewise, He coordinated his dutifulness to his parents with his being taqiyy, to indicate that he was firmly established in this quality.

"Birr" means honoring and striving in obedience. "Barr," with a fatha on the ba', is a descriptive adjective on the pattern of a verbal noun, so describing someone with it is hyperbole. "Birr," with a kasra on the ba', is a verbal noun (ism masdar), since it does not follow the regular pattern.

"Jabbar" means one who disregards the rights of people. It seems to be derived from "jabr," which means compulsion and usurpation, because he seizes the rights of people.

"Asiyy" is an intensive form on the pattern fa'il, meaning one who is extremely disobedient. The intensity applies to the negation, not to the thing negated, meaning that he was not disobedient at all.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verse 15:

﴿And peace be upon him the day he was born, and the day he dies, and the day he is raised up alive.﴾

The most apparent view is that this is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿And We gave him judgment while still a child﴾ [Maryam: 12], with the Muslims being addressed by it, so that they may know the dignity (karāma) of Yaḥyā (John) with Allah.

As-salām (peace): it is the name of the greeting with which the visitor and the traveller open, containing praise or supplication. It is called salām because it includes a supplication for safety (salāma), and because it indicates that the one who approaches is at peace with the other and does not fear harm from him. Thus what is meant here is peace from Allah upon him, which is Allah's praise of him, like His saying ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 58]. When as-salām is defined with the article (al-), its meaning is like that of the indefinite, or it is meant as the specific (ʿahd), i.e., peace directed to him, as will come in the discussion of peace upon ʿĪsā (Jesus). So the meaning is that Allah's honour is firmly established over him in these three states mentioned.

Page 78

These three states mentioned here are the states at the beginning of stages: the stage of arrival into this world, the stage of departure from it, and the stage of arrival into the Hereafter. This is a kināya (allusion) that he is in the place of divine care during these states.

What is meant by "day" is the unrestricted time in which those states occur.

The present tense verb was used in ﴿the day he dies﴾ to evoke the state in which he died. The account of his being killed is not mentioned in the Qur'an except in summary.

[79]

The clause ﴿And mention in the Book Mary﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause ﴿the mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zechariah﴾ [Maryam: 2], as one story following another. Therefore the good coherence of the two clauses in being both declarative and imperative need not be observed, though that coherence is not obligatory. Moreover, you have learned that it is better for his saying ﴿the mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zechariah﴾ [Maryam: 2] to be a verbal noun (maṣdar) that stands as a substitute (badal) for its verb.

[The meaning of] "mention" (al-dhikr) here is recitation: recite the account of Mary which We relate to you.

Opening the story with this carries added attention to it and a stimulus for the listener to learn it and reflect upon it.

"The Book" means the Qur'an, because this story is part of the Qur'an. This surah is distinctive in adding the phrase ﴿in the Book﴾ after the word "mention" (udhkur). The benefit of this is to draw attention to the fact that the mention of those whom one is commanded to mention is contained in the verses of the Qur'an, and is not merely a mention of their virtue in some other speech of the Prophet (ﷺ), such as his saying: "Had I stayed in prison as long as Joseph stayed, I would have answered the summoner." Such a phrase does not occur in another surah, because the intended meaning has been made clear in this surah, so it is understood that it is intended in the rest of the verses in which the word "mention" (udhkur) occurs. Perhaps Surah Maryam is the first surah in which the word "mention" (udhkur) occurs in the stories of the prophets, for it is the forty-fourth surah in the order of revelation.

[The word] "when" (idh) is an adverbial complement related to "mention" (udhkur) in terms of it containing the meaning of story and narrative, and it is not related to it in its apparent meaning, because that meaning would not be sound. It is also permissible for "when" (idh) to be merely a noun of time, not an adverb, and to be made a substitute (badal) for Mary: that is, "mention the time of her withdrawal to a place toward the east." A similar construction was mentioned earlier in his saying ﴿the mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zechariah when he called upon his Lord﴾ [Maryam: 2].

"Withdrawal" (al-intibādh) means isolation and seclusion, because "nabdh" means to cast away and to throw out. Thus "intibādh" is originally an reflexive form (iftiʿāl, muṭāwiʿ) of "nabadhahu," then it was applied to an action that occurs without a preceding agent for it.

The word "a place" (makānan) is in the accusative as the object of "withdrew" (intabadhat), because it contains the meaning of "descended" (ḥallat). It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative as an adverb of place, because of the vagueness in it. The meaning is: she withdrew from her family to a place in the east.

[80]

"Place" is indefinite to indicate vagueness, because there is no purpose in specifying its type, since that would add nothing of perfection to the aim of the story. As for the attention given to describing it as "eastern," this is to draw attention to the origin of the Christians' taking the east as their qibla for their prayers, since Mary's carrying of Jesus took place in a location to the east, the direction of the sunrise. As Ibn ʿAbbas said: "I know better than anyone of God's creation why the Christians took the east as their qibla" [based on] His saying, exalted is He, ﴿a place to the east﴾; that is, that facing it is not a command from God, exalted is He. Thus the mention of the place being eastern is a wonderful point from the history of the laws, together with its harmony with the rhyme-endings (fawāṣil).

The "taking of a screen" (ittikhādh al-ḥijāb) means placing something that screens one from people. It is said: she screened herself in order to bathe, and it is said: in order to comb her hair.

"The Spirit" (al-rūḥ) is the angel, because the attribution of the sending to Him and its being related to the pronoun of majesty indicate that he is one of the angels. And he appeared to her in the form of a man.

"Appearing" (al-tamaththul) is the forced assumption of likeness, that is, that form was not the angel's original form.

"A man" (basharan) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "appeared" (tamaththala), and it is a circumstantial accusative in the sense of an eloquent comparison. "Bashar" means a human being. God, exalted is He, said ﴿I am creating a human (basharan) from clay﴾ [Ṣād: 71], that is, I am creating Adam, peace be upon him. "Sawiyy" means "made complete," that is, perfect in creation. He appeared to her in that way for the sake of harmony between the perfection of the reality and the perfection of the form, and to indicate the perfection of her chastity, when she said ﴿I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing﴾, since there was nothing in his form that would be disliked for women like her. For she supposed that he was a man who had hidden himself to solicit her

[81]

for herself. So she hastened to seek refuge from him before he spoke to her, a hasty denial of what she imagined of his intention, which is what is most commonly understood from men like him in such a situation. The clause ﴿I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you﴾ is declarative, and for that reason it was emphasized with a particle of emphasis. The meaning is: she informed him that she had made God her refuge from him, that is, she made the side of God a place of shelter for her from what he intended. This is an admonition to him. Her mention of the attribute "the Most Merciful" rather than other attributes of God is because she wanted God to have mercy upon her by repelling one whom she thought to be an aggressor against her. Her saying ﴿if you are God-fearing﴾ is a reminder to him through admonition that he must fear his Lord. The coming of this reminder in the form of a conditional, which implies doubt about his piety, is intended to stir up his fear. Likewise the bringing in of the verb "to be," which indicates that piety is firmly established in him. This is the most eloquent admonition, reminder, and exhortation to act upon his piety.

The restriction (qaṣr) in his saying ﴿I am only a messenger of your Lord﴾ is a restriction relative (qaṣr idāfī), that is, "I am not a human," in reply to her saying ﴿if you are God-fearing﴾, which presupposes her belief that he is a human.

The majority read "li-ahaba" with the hamza of the first person after the lām of purpose. The attribution of the gift to himself is a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī), because he is the cause of this gift. Abū ʿAmr and Warsh from Nāfiʿ read "li-yahaba" with the ya of the third person, that is, "that your Lord may give you," although it is written in the Muṣḥaf with an alif. In my view, the reading of these with the ya after the lām is merely the pronunciation of the softened hamza after the kasra of the lām in the form of the pronunciation of the ya. Her dialogue with the angel was an attempt intended to turn him away from what he had come for, because she knew he was sent from God, so she wished to return to her Lord about a matter she could not bear,

[82]

as Abraham, peace be upon him, returned [to God] concerning the people of Lot, and as Muhammad (ﷺ) returned [to God] concerning the imposition of fifty prayers. The meaning of the dialogue is that this would bring great harm upon her, since she was betrothed to a man and had not yet consummated the marriage, so how would people receive her bearing a child without a known father? Her saying ﴿and I have not been unchaste﴾ is a clearing of herself from unchastity, by what the verb "to be" requires of the permanence of the attribute which is the predicate of the verb "to be," and the aim of it is the emphasis of the negation. So she hastened to seek refuge from him before he spoke to her, a hasty denial of what she imagined of his intention, which is what is most commonly understood from men like him in such a situation. The clause ﴿I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you﴾ is declarative, and for that reason it was emphasized with a particle of emphasis. The meaning is: she informed him that she had made God her refuge from him, that is, she made the side of God a place of shelter for her from what he intended. This is an admonition to him. Her mention of the attribute "the Most Merciful" rather than other attributes of God is because she wanted God to have mercy upon her by repelling one whom she thought to be an aggressor against her. Her saying ﴿if you are God-fearing﴾ is a reminder to him through admonition that he must fear his Lord. The coming of this reminder in the form of a conditional, which implies doubt about his piety, is intended to stir up his fear. Likewise the bringing in of the verb "to be," which indicates that piety is firmly established in him. This is the most eloquent admonition, reminder, and exhortation to act upon his piety.

The restriction (qaṣr) in his saying ﴿I am only a messenger of your Lord﴾ is a restriction relative (qaṣr idāfī), that is, "I am not a human," in reply to her saying ﴿if you are God-fearing﴾, which presupposes her belief that he is a human.

The majority read "li-ahaba" with the hamza of the first person after the lām of purpose. The attribution of the gift to himself is a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī), because he is the cause of this gift. Abū ʿAmr and Warsh from Nāfiʿ read "li-yahaba" with the ya of the third person, that is, "that your Lord may give you," although it is written in the Muṣḥaf with an alif. In my view, the reading of these with the ya after the lām is merely the pronunciation of the softened hamza after the kasra of the lām in the form of the pronunciation of the ya. Her dialogue with the angel was an attempt intended to turn him away from what he had come for, because she knew he was sent from God, so she wished to return to her Lord about a matter she could not bear,

[82]

as Abraham, peace be upon him, returned [to God] concerning the people of Lot, and as Muhammad (ﷺ) returned [to God] concerning the imposition of fifty prayers. The meaning of the dialogue is that this would bring great harm upon her, since she was betrothed to a man and had not yet consummated the marriage, so how would people receive her bearing a child without a known father? Her saying ﴿and I have not been unchaste﴾ is a clearing of herself from unchastity, by what the verb "to be" requires of the permanence of the attribute which is the predicate of the verb "to be," and the aim of it is the emphasis of the negation. Thus the import of her saying ﴿and I have not been unchaste﴾ is different from the import of her saying ﴿no human has touched me﴾, and this is among the things by which this story exceeds its account in Surah Āl ʿImrān, because her story in Surah Āl ʿImrān was revealed after this one, so it was sound to suffice in this story with her saying ﴿no human has touched me﴾. Her saying ﴿no human has touched me﴾ means: no husband has consummated the marriage with me, since she was betrothed and engaged to Joseph the carpenter, but he had not consummated the marriage with her, so when she conceived a child, her betrothed and her family accused her of fornication.

As for her saying ﴿and I have not been unchaste﴾, it is a negation that she had not been unchaste before that hour, so she would not consent to be accused of unchastity after that. So the statement is a metonymy (kināya) for her being above the stain of unchastity, by the principle of presumption of continuity (istiṣḥāb). The meaning is: I was not unchaste in the past, so shall I become unchaste in the future?

There is a perplexity among the exegetes at this point, which al-Fakhr [al-Rāzī] and al-Ṭībī mentioned, and what we have mentioned provides a way out of its difficulty. Mary's speech is not framed in the manner of astonishment like Zechariah's saying ﴿How can I have a son when my wife is barren?﴾ [Maryam: 8], because the two situations differ: Zechariah's situation is that of one desiring offspring, while Mary's situation is that of one who is apprehensive of it and disclaims its occurrence.

"Baghiyy" is a noun for a fornicating woman, and for that reason the feminine ending (tā' al-ta'nīth) is not attached to it. Its pattern is faʿīl or faʿūl in the sense of fāʿil, so its original form would be baghūy, because it is from "al-baghy." When the wāw and the yā' came together and the first of them was vowelled with sukūn, the wāw was changed to yā' and assimilated into the original yā', and a kasra was substituted for the ḍamma of the ghayn for the sake of harmony with the yā', so it became baghiyy.

The angel's reply means: the matter is as I have said, similar to his saying in the story of Zechariah ﴿Thus said your Lord: it is easy for Me﴾. It is a turning away from nullifying her aim of returning to God, to explaining the ease of this creation in terms of divine power, by way of the wise style of discourse (uslūb ḥakīm).

In his saying ﴿it is easy for Me﴾ there is an indication that what she feared of the occurrence of the opposite of her statement, and of their slander of her honour, is not a great matter in comparison with what God wills of guiding people through the mission of Jesus, peace be upon him, since God, exalted is He, is not diverted from carrying out His will by whatever harm may befall some of His servants in that, because the consideration of public interests takes precedence over the consideration of private interests.

So the pronoun in ﴿it is easy for Me﴾ refers to what her dialogue contained of harm befalling her, as we explained with respect to her saying ﴿no human has touched me, nor have I been unchaste﴾. Thus between the angel's reply to her and God's reply to Zechariah there is a difference in meaning.

The speech on both matters was through the tongue of the angel from God. But it was attributed in the story of Zechariah to God, because the angel's speech was a conveyance of revelation from God as a reply from God to Zechariah's private supplication, and in this story it was attributed to the angel because it was a reply to her address to him.

His saying ﴿and that We may make him a sign for people and a mercy from Us﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon ﴿We sent to her Our Spirit﴾, in terms of what is in that of the Spirit's saying to her ﴿that I may give you a pure boy﴾, that is, because the gift of a pure boy is a honour from God to her, and making him a sign for people and a mercy is an honour for the boy. Thus there occurs a shift (iltifāt) from the third-person style to the first-person style.

[84]

The clause ﴿and it was a matter decreed﴾ may be part of the angel's speech, and it may be a new independent sentence (mustaʾnafa). The pronoun in "it was" refers to the gift mentioned in his saying ﴿that I may give you a boy﴾. This is a cutting off of the discussion and an announcement that the creation had already taken place in her womb.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 19, verses 22–23:**

﴿So she conceived him and withdrew with him to a remote place.﴾ ﴿Then the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree. She said, "Oh, I wish I had died before this and had become something forgotten and completely out of mind."﴾

The *fa'* (ف) here indicates sequence and immediacy (*tafri'* and *ta'qib*). That is, she conceived the boy immediately after that exchange.

*Al-haml* (الحمل) means conception. It is said *hamalat al-mar'ah waladan* ("the woman conceived a child"), and this is the basic usage. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿His mother bore him with hardship﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15]. It is also said *hamalat bihi* ("she conceived him"). The *ba'* (ب) appears to emphasise adherence, as in ﴿and wipe over your heads﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6].

Abu Kabir al-Hudhali said:

*She conceived him on a night of darkness, by force, while the knot of her waistband had not been untied.*

*Al-intibadh* (الانتباذ) was mentioned shortly before, and likewise the accusative *makanan* (مكانًا) was already discussed.

*Qasiyyan* (قصيًّا) means far away, that is, distant from the place of her family. It is said that she went out to the land of Egypt, fleeing from her people who would blame her, and that her betrothed, Yusuf the carpenter (Joseph), helped her, and that she gave birth to 'Isa (peace be upon him) in the land of Egypt. This is not authentic.

In the Gospel of Luke it is stated that she gave birth to him in the town of Bethlehem, in the Judean land, when she went up there with her betrothed Yusuf the carpenter, since he was required to appear in the town of his family because the king of the land was conducting a census of its inhabitants. This is the apparent meaning of the Exalted's words ﴿Then she brought him to her people, carrying him﴾ [Maryam: 27].

(p. 85)

The *fa'* in His words ﴿Then the pains of childbirth drove her﴾ indicates customary sequence (*al-ta'qib al-'urfi*), meaning that the labour pains came upon her after the full period of pregnancy was completed. It is said that this was after eight months of her pregnancy. *Ajaha* (أجاءها) means "compelled her" and is originally from *ja'a* (جاء). It was made transitive by the *hamzah*, so one says *aja'ahu*, meaning "he made him come." It was then used figuratively for one thing compelling another to something, as if it brings it to that thing and forces it to come to it. Al-Farra' said: its root is from *ji'tu* (جئت), and the Arabs have made it *ilja'* (إلجاء, compulsion). In the proverb: "The worst thing is what brings you to the marrow of the Achilles tendon." Zuhayr said:

*And a neighbour who walked eagerly towards us, fear and hope had driven him.*

*Al-makhad* (المخاض), with a *fatha* on the *mim*, is the labour pain of the pregnant woman, which is the movement of the foetus towards emergence.

*Al-jidh* (الجذع), with a *kasra* on the *jim* and a sukun on the dhal (ذ), is the original trunk of the palm tree from which the fronds branch out. It is the part between the roots and the branches. That is, she leaned against the base of a palm tree.

The clause *qalat* (قالت, "she said") is an explanatory resumptive sentence (*isti'naf bayani*, a clause that answers an implicit question). This is because the listener wishes to know her state at the time her labour came, after her matter had been hidden and not disclosed among the people, and it was time for it to be revealed. The listener is answered that she had wished for death before that. She was in a state of grief, seeing death as easier for her than falling into that situation.

This indicates her steadfastness and sincerity in facing the trial that Allah, exalted is He, had tested her with. For this reason she was in the station of *al-siddiqiyyah* (truthfulness, sincerity).

What is referred to in her words *qabla hadha* (قبل هذا, "before this") is the pregnancy. She meant that her honour should not be exposed to slander, and that she should not bring shame upon her family. She did not wish that she had died after the pregnancy became visible, because at that point death would not remove the slander against her honour after her death, nor the disgrace upon her family, since her family would see her belly with its pregnancy while she was dead, and then the rumour would fall upon her.

(p. 86)

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read *mittu* (مِتُّ) with a *kasra* on the *mim*, for the reason mentioned earlier in His words ﴿And if you are killed in the way of Allah or die﴾ [Al 'Imran: 157] in Surah Al 'Imran. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Abu Ja'far read it with a *damma* on the *mim* according to the original form. Both are dialectal forms of the verb *mata* (مات, "to die") when it is joined to a connected pronoun of the nominative.

*Al-nisy* (النسي), with a *kasra* on the *nun* and a sukun on the *sin*, is the reading of the majority. It means a worthless thing whose nature is to be forgotten. The pattern *fi'l* (فِعْل) can come with the meaning of *ism al-maf'ul* (the passive participle), with the qualification that it is prepared for the action to attach to it, without the attachment having already occurred. An example is *al-dhibh* (الذبح) in His words ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾ [al-Saffat: 107], meaning a great ram prepared to be slaughtered. So a ram is not called *dhibh* except when it is prepared for slaughter, and a slaughtered animal is not called *dhibh* but *dhabih*. The Arabs call things that are commonly neglected *ansa'* (أنساء, "forgotten things"), and when departing they say: "Look at your *ansa'*," that is, the things that you are likely to forget.

She described the *nisy* with *mansiyy* (منسيّ) for emphasis on its being forgotten, meaning: "Oh, I wish I had been something not remembered, and whose family had forgotten and abandoned it, so that they would not pay attention to what befalls it." Thus she wished for death and for the end of her being remembered among her family, from before that time. Hamzah, Hafs and Khalaf read *nasyan* (نَسْيًا) with a *fatha* on the *nun*, which is a dialectal form of *nisy*, like *al-witr* and *al-watr*, and *al-jisr* and *al-jasr*.
