Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verse 24:

﴿So he (the infant) called to her from beneath her: "Do not grieve; your Lord has placed beneath you a stream."﴾

The implicit subject pronoun in "fanadaha" (he called to her) refers back to what the pronoun in "fahamalathu" (so she carried him) refers to, i.e., "the newborn called to her."

Page 87

Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, Abu Ja'far, Khalaf, and Rawh from Ya'qub read ﴿min tahtiha﴾ with a kasra on the mim of "min," taking it as a preposition (harf ibtida') governing "nadaha" and "tahtiha" in the genitive case.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and Ruways from Ya'qub read "(man)" with a fatha on the mim, taking it as a relative pronoun (ism mawsul), and they read "(tahtaha)" with a fatha, taking it as an adverb of place (zarf) made into the relative clause (silah). The intended referent of the relative pronoun is the boy who was beneath her. This is an irhas (preparatory sign) for 'Isa and a karamah (miraculous favor) for his mother, peace be upon them both.

The qayd (restrictive phrase) "min tahtiha" serves to confirm this, and to convey that he called to her at the moment of his birth, before she lifted him, as a hastening to console and give good news, and to depict that state, which is the state of the child's complete closeness to his mother. The "an" in "alla tahzani" is explanatory (tafsiriyyah) for the verb "nadaha." The clause "qad ja'ala Rabbuki tahtaki sariyyan" is a statement meant as a reason (ta'lil) for the clause "alla tahzani," i.e., your state is one worthy of joy rather than grief because of the divine honor in it. Al-sarriyy: a small stream of water, like a canal, abundant flowing water.

God granted her good food and good drink as an honor to her, which everyone who sees her would witness, and her betrothed Yusuf the carpenter was with her, along with whoever might see her and thus bear witness to her chastity and innocence from what might be suspected of her. As for the water, it is because it was not customary for her to take shelter by a riverbed to give birth there. As for the ripe dates, it is said that the time was winter and it was not the season for ripe dates, and the trunk of the palm was the trunk of a dead palm, so the fall of ripe dates from it is a departure from habit. She was given ripe dates rather than dried dates because ripe dates are more pleasing to the soul, as they are like fruit, whereas dried dates are sustenance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verse 25:

Page 88
﴿And shake towards you the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you ripe, fresh dates﴾ ﴿So eat and drink and be comforted in your eye﴾ [Maryam: 25-26]

The benefit of His saying ﴿And shake towards you the trunk of the palm tree﴾ is that the dry trunk should bear ripe dates through the blessing of her shaking it, and that is another karamah (divine honour) for her. It also lets her witness with her own eyes how a dry trunk bears ripe dates. In this there is a karamah for her as well, owing to the strength of her certainty regarding her station.

The ba' in ﴿bi-jidh'i al-nakhlah﴾ (by the trunk of the palm tree) serves to emphasise the attachment of the verb to its object, like ﴿wamsahu bi-ru'usikum﴾ (and wipe over your heads) [al-Ma'idah: 6] and His saying ﴿wa la tulqu bi-aydikum ila al-tahlukah﴾ (and do not throw yourselves by your own hands into destruction) [al-Baqarah: 195]. The verb hazzi has been construed with the meaning of qarribi or adni (bring near), and so it takes (ila, to). That is: shake the trunk of the palm tree and bring it near, and it will draw near to you, become soft after dryness, and drop upon you ripe dates. The meaning is: bring the trunk of the palm tree near yourself. Thus the doer of the action and its complement are one, and both are a pronoun referring to a single antecedent. There is no harm in this, since the meaning is sound and similar constructions occur in usage, such as ﴿wadmum ilayka janahak﴾ (and draw your arm close to your side) [al-Qasas: 32]. The one who presses and the one pressed to him are one. The grammarians prohibited the doer and the object from being two pronouns referring to one antecedent except in verbs of the heart and in the two verbs 'adima and faqada, only because this is not heard in usage, not because the meaning is corrupt. Therefore the prohibition of other verbs is not to be extended by analogy.

Al-rutab: dates that have not completed their drying.

Al-janiyy: fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, i.e. plucked (mujtana). It is a metonymy for the recency of its falling, that is, for its freshness, and it was not from the dates that had been stored earlier, because when dates are closer in time to their palm tree they are sweeter in taste.

Page 89
As for (tassaqatu), the majority read it with a fatha on the ta' and a shaddah on the sin; its original form is tatasaqatu with two ta's, and the second ta' was assimilated into the sin so that lightening through assimilation would be achieved.
Hamzah read it with a light sin, by omitting one of the two ta's for lightness. And rutaban, in all these readings, is a tamyiz specifying the attribution of the falling to the palm tree.

Hafs read it with a damma on the ta' and a kasrah on the sin, as the imperfect of saqatat al-nakhlatu tamraha (the palm tree dropped its dates), an intensive form of asqatat; and rutaban is the object.

Ya'qub read it with a yā' with a fatha underneath and a fatha on the qaf and a shaddah on the sin, so that the hidden pronoun refers back to ﴿jidh'a al-nakhlah﴾ [Maryam: 23].

The clause ﴿fakuli﴾ and what follows it is a summarising conclusion (fadhlaka) of the clauses before it, from His saying ﴿qad ja'ala rabbuki tahtaki sariyyan﴾ (your Lord has placed a stream beneath you) [Maryam: 24], that is: so you are in the midst of a comfortable life.

Qurrat al-'ayn (comfort of the eye) is a metonymy for joy by way of opposition, based on their saying: "his eye became hot" when he wept much. So a metonymy by the opposite of that for joy is a metonymy of four levels, and it was previously mentioned in His saying ﴿wa qalati imra'atu Fir'awna qurrata 'aynin li wa laka﴾ (and the wife of Pharaoh said: a comfort of the eye for me and for you) [al-Qasas: 9]. Qurrat al-'ayn includes the ease of life and includes the delight in a newborn child. In its being a comfort of the eye there is a metonymy for the assurance of his safety and the distinction of his standing.

The fatha on the qaf in ﴿wa qarri 'aynan﴾ (and be comforted in your eye) [Maryam: 26] is because it is the imperfect of qarirat 'aynuhu, of the pattern radiya; it was assimilated, and the vowel of the second radical of the word was transferred to its first radical in the imperfect, because the first radical is quiescent.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verse 26:

﴿So if you see any human being, say: "Indeed, I have vowed a fast to the Most Merciful, so I will not speak today to any human being."﴾

This is part of what 'Isa added to her [the speech]. It is a revelation from Allah to Maryam, which He caused to be spoken through the tongue of the infant, as an instruction from Allah to Maryam and a guidance to cut off argument

صفحة ٩٠
with anyone who wished to dispute with her. So He taught her to vow a fast accompanied by abstention from speech, so that she would be in worship and would be relieved from the questions of the questioners and the disputes of the ignorant.

Abstention from speech was among the forms of worship in some earlier laws, and the Arabs had borrowed it in the Jahiliyyah, as indicated by the hadith of the woman from Ahmas who performed Hajj while remaining silent (musmitah). It was abrogated in the law of Islam in its application (bi-l-nisbah). In the Muwatta' [it is related] that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw a man standing in the sun, and said: 'What is the matter with this one?' They said: 'He has vowed not to speak, not to seek shade from the sun, not to sit, and to fast.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Tell him to speak, to seek shade, to sit, and to complete his fast.' This man was called Abu Isra'il."

It is related from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he entered upon a woman who had vowed not to speak. He said to her: "Indeed Islam has demolished this, so speak." In the hadith [it is also related] that "a woman from Ahmas performed Hajj musmitah," meaning she did not speak. So silence was a form of worship in the law of those before us, and it is not a law for us, because Islam abrogated it by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Tell him to speak," and by the practice of his companions.

The reports cited here indicate several matters:

First: The Prophet ﷺ did not make the fulfilment of such a vow obligatory, which shows that it is not an act of nearness to Allah.

Second: He did not order an expiation (kaffarah) for it, unlike the vow that cannot be fulfilled or the vow that does not specify a particular act, such as saying "a vow is upon me." In the Muwatta', after mentioning the aforementioned hadith, Malik said: "He did not order him to make expiation

صفحة ٩١
and had there been an expiation in it, he would have ordered him to do it. This indicates that it is an act with no standing whatsoever."

Third: He indicated the reason why the vow is not valid with it, by his saying: "Indeed Allah is not in need of this man's punishing himself."

From this we learn that the meaning of worship is that it be a statement or an act which includes a meaning that brings purification to the soul and leads it to a praiseworthy end, such as fasting and Hajj; the hardship in them is borne for the sake of the lofty end. Worship is not a vengeance by Allah upon His servant, nor a punishment for him, as the people of misguidance used to draw near to Allah by punishing their own souls, and as some religions prescribed slight punishment to subdue their coarseness. On this meaning is His saying, the Exalted: "So eat from it and feed the one who is content and the one who asks. Thus We have subjected them to you that you may be grateful" [al-Hajj: 36], and "Their flesh will never reach Allah, nor their blood, but piety from you will reach Him" [al-Hajj: 37], because they used to think that nearness to Allah through offerings lay in shedding their blood and leaving their flesh cast down for the scavengers.

In al-Bukhari, from Anas: "The Prophet ﷺ saw an old man being supported between his two sons, and said: 'What is the matter with this one?' They said: 'He has vowed to walk.' He said: 'Indeed Allah is not in need of this man's punishing himself.' And he ordered him to ride, and did not regard walking in the circumambulation as an act of nearness."

Also in it, from Ibn 'Abbas: "The Prophet ﷺ passed by a person who was circumambulating the Ka'bah while tied by his hand to another person with a leather strap, or a thread, or something other than that. The Prophet cut it with his own hand, then said: 'Let him loose with his hand.'"

صفحة ٩٢
In the Musnad of Ahmad, from Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As: "The Prophet ﷺ came upon two men who were tied together. He said: 'What is the matter with these two?' They said: 'We have vowed that we shall remain tied until we reach the Ka'bah.' He said: 'Release yourselves; this is not a vow. The vow is only that by which the face of Allah is sought.'" He said: its chain is good (hasan).

Fourth: The narrator of some of these reports related them with the wording: "The Messenger of Allah forbade that." Therefore Malik said in the Muwatta', after the hadith of the man who vowed not to seek shade, not to speak, and not to sit: Malik said: "The Messenger of Allah ordered him to complete what was for Allah an obedience, and to leave what was for Allah a disobedience." The reason it is a disobedience is that it is an audacity against Allah, to worship Him with what He has not legislated, even if there is no hardship upon the self in it, like a vow of silence for an hour. It is also a torment of the soul which Allah has honoured, and torment is not permitted except for an act which Islam regards as a benefit for the person in himself, or for the community, or for warding off a corruption, such as retaliation (qisas) and flogging. For this reason He said: "And do not kill yourselves; indeed Allah is ever Merciful to you" [al-Nisa': 29].

The Prophet ﷺ also said: "Indeed your blood, your property, your souls and your skins are sacred to you," because the law of Islam does not attach its legislation except to the bringing about of benefits and the warding off of corruptions.

What is derived from Malik's statement on this is that it is a disobedience, as he said in the Muwatta'. For this reason Shaykh Abu Muhammad said in al-Risalah: "Whoever vows a disobedience, such as killing a soul, drinking wine, or the like, or what is neither obedience nor disobedience, there is nothing upon him, and let him seek forgiveness from Allah." His saying "and let him seek forgiveness from Allah" is based on the premise that he has done his vow in opposition to the Prophet's prohibition of it.

صفحة ٩٣
If anyone performs silence without a vow or an intention of worship, it is not forbidden, unless it reaches the point of a wearying hardship.

Among the Christians, the regarding of silence as worship has remained, and they make it a mercy towards the dead that they stand silent for a moment.

The meaning of ﴿So say: "Indeed, I have vowed a fast to the Most Merciful"﴾ is: vow a fast, and if you meet any human being, say: "I have vowed a fast," the clause being omitted because of the context. The utterance which includes a report of the vow has been treated as an expression for the act of making the vow, and for the report of it as a metaphor (kinayah) for the act of making the vow, because of their mutual implication, since the basic principle in a report is truthfulness and conformity with reality, as in His saying, the Exalted: "Say: We believe in Allah" [al-Baqarah: 136]. It is not meant that she says this without doing it, because Allah, the Exalted, does not permit lying except in a state of necessity together with the impossibility of truthfulness in that state. For this reason the hadith says: "Indeed in allusions (ma'arid) there is a sufficient alternative to lying." The word "saying" has been applied to what indicates what is in the soul, which is the allusion (ima'), that she has vowed a fast, metaphorically, by the indication of His saying: "So I will not speak today to any human being." The meaning is that she should convey this by a sign indicating that she has vowed a fast, by making a gesture that indicates abstention from eating, and a gesture indicating that she does not speak for that reason. If fasting in their law was conditioned on abstaining from speech, as has been said, then one gesture is sufficient. And the speech of the fast is an independent act of worship which the fasting person may perform together with abstaining from speech; she makes two gestures to indicate that she has vowed both matters. Maryam knew that the infant who had spoken to her was the one who would take up the answer on her behalf when she was asked, by the indication of His saying: "So she pointed to him" [Maryam: 29].

صفحة ٩٤
The nun in His saying tarayinna is the heavy emphatic nun (nun al-tawkid al-thaqilah), joined to the verb whose final letter has become a ya' because the nun of the nominative has been dropped on account of the conditional particle; the ya' is then vocalised with a vowel homogeneous with it, as is the case with the heavy emphatic nun.

Al-insi: the human being. The ya' in it is for the relative (nisbah) to al-ins, which is a collective noun of insan. The ya' of nisbah serves to denote a single individual of the species, like the ya' of harasi for one of the guard (haras). This is an indefinite noun in the context of negation, which conveys generality, meaning: I will not speak to anyone.

He turned from "ahad" to "insiyyan" for the sake of rhyme with the ya' ending. This is not a precaution against her speaking with the angels, since that does not occur to the minds of those addressed, to whom this statement was directed; so to construe it that way is a grotesque absurdity.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verses 27–28:

﴿Then she brought him to her people, carrying him. They said, "O Mary, you have certainly come with a thing unprecedented (fariyyan)."﴾ ﴿"O sister of Harun (Aaron), your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother an unchaste woman."﴾ The fa' (then) indicates that Mary came to her family immediately after the speech of her son, who had spoken to her, ended.

In the Gospel of Luke, she remained in Bethlehem until the completion of forty-one days, which were the days of purification from the blood of postnatal bleeding. Accordingly, the sequence indicated by the fa' is a customary sequence, like the saying: "He married, then a child was born to him."

Her people (qawmuha): the people of her neighbourhood.

The clause "carrying him" (tahmiluhu) is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the ta' in "she brought" (atat). This circumstantial clause serves to show that she came openly with him, not concealing him, because she knew that God would clear her of what she was accused of, like anyone who came in her condition.

Page 95
The clause "They said, 'O Mary'" (qalu ya Maryam) is a resumptive clause of explanation (isti'naf bayani). Her people uttered this statement as a rebuke to her.

Fariyy: a form of fa'il from fara, one of the verbs with yā' as its third radical. This word has several meanings, and the most apparent of its senses here is that it means "grave in wrongness," as said by Mujahid and al-Suddi. It derives from the root iftara, meaning "to be accused of lying," because the woman attributes to her husband falsely the child she conceived through fornication.

From this is His Exalted saying: ﴿nor shall they bring a slander they have invented between their hands and their feet﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 12].

Some of the lexicographers said that fariyy and fiyra derive from ifra' with a hamza, meaning cutting the skin, either to corrupt it or to burn it, distinguishing between afra and fara, and that the unaugmented fara is for setting right.

Ukht (sister): the feminine of akh (brother), a noun that is attached to another noun. It is used literally for the daughter of the same two parents as the one to whom it is attached, or the daughter of one of his parents. It is also used for a woman who is from the descendants of the namesake to whom it is attached when that is the name of a tribe, as in their saying: "O brother of the Arabs." As in the hadith of the guest of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, where he said to his wife: "O sister of Banu Firas, what is this?" If the word banu is not mentioned, attached to the name of the tribe's ancestor, it is understood as implied. Sahl ibn Malik al-Fazari said:

O sister of the best of the Bedouin and the settled, how do you see a young man of Fazarah?
He means: O sister of the most excellent of the Arab tribes, from their Bedouin and their settled folk.

So His Exalted saying ﴿O sister of Harun﴾ may be taken in its literal sense, so that Mary had a brother named Harun who was righteous among his people; they addressed her by attributing her to him as an added rebuke, meaning: it was not fitting for the sister of such a man to do your deed. This is the stronger of the two interpretations. In Sahih Muslim and elsewhere, it is narrated from al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah who said: "The Messenger of God sent me to the people of Najran, and they said: 'Do you see what you recite, "O sister of Harun," and Musa was before Isa by so-and-so many years?' Al-Mughirah said: 'I did not know what to answer. When I came to the Messenger of God, I mentioned that to him. He said: "Did they not know that they used to name themselves after their prophets and the righteous before them?"'" End. In this there is a rebuke of the people of Najran, who criticised the Qur'an on the assumption that there is no one in the people named Harun except Harun the prophet, brother of Musa.

It is also possible that the meaning of "sister of Harun" is that she was one of the women of the descendants of Harun, brother of Musa, like Abu Bakr's saying: "O sister of Banu Firas."

Mary was indeed of the descendants of Harun, brother of Musa, of the tribe of Levi. In the Gospel of Luke, there was a priest named Zechariah of the division of Abijah, and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, named Elizabeth; Elizabeth was the wife of Zechariah and a relative of Mary, that is, her cousin. What occurred to the exegetes regarding Mary's lineage, that she was of the offspring of Sulayman ibn Dawud, is an error.

Perhaps her people spoke with both expressions, so the Qur'an related it in a way that suits both, for conciseness. There is nothing in this possibility that contradicts the hadith of al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah.

As-sau' (with a fatha on the sin and a sukun on the waw): a verbal noun of sa'ahu, when one harms him and corrupts some of his condition. Thus, attaching a noun to it indicates that it is one of his affairs and actions, and that it is its verbal noun. So the meaning of ﴿a man of evil﴾ (imra'a sau') is a man of corrupting conduct.

The meaning of baghiyy was mentioned shortly before. By these words they meant a metonymy for her having brought a matter that is not of the character of her family: that is, she brought an evil that is not of her father's character and a fornication that is not of her mother's character, and she departed from the conduct of her two parents, so she was a woman of evil and was an unchaste woman; "your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother an unchaste woman," so she was an innovator of abominations among her family. They intended to blame her, yet they used words whose explicit meaning is praise of her parents, implying that it was proper for her to be like her parents.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verse 29:

Page 97

﴿So she pointed to him. They said, "How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a young child?"﴾ That is, she pointed to him with a gesture indicating that she was referring them to him, so that they might ask him about his story; or she pointed to them to listen to him for the answer to their rebuke of her, and they understood that from her gesture.

Since her gesture was equivalent to a reply in speech, their dialogue that followed the gesture is related by the phrase "they said," set apart without a conjunction.

The interrogative here is a denial. They denied that they should speak to one who is not of the sort that speaks, and they denied that she should refer them to speaking with him. That is: how could we expect an answer from him, or how could we put a question to him, since both circumstances call for speech.

The addition of the verb of being (kāna) in ﴿one who is in the cradle﴾ serves to show the firm establishment of his being in the cradle, in contrast with the one they were directed to converse with. This is an exaggeration on their part in denial, and an expression of wonder at her making light of them. Thus the verb kāna is redundant for emphasis, and for this reason it came in the past form, since the redundant kāna is generally in the past form.

His saying ﴿in the cradle﴾ is a predicate of the relative pronoun.

"Ṣabiyyan" (a young child) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the relative pronoun.

Al-mahd (the cradle): the bed of the infant and what is prepared for placing it.

[Page 98]

﴿He said, "Indeed, I am a servant of Allah. He has given me the Scripture (al-Kitab) and made me a prophet (nabiyy)."﴾ ﴿"And He has made me blessed wherever I am, and has enjoined upon me prayer and zakah (almsgiving) for as long as I live."﴾ ﴿"And [He has made me] dutiful toward my mother, and He has not made me a tyrant, wretched."﴾ ﴿"And peace is upon me the day I was born, the day I die, and the day I am raised alive."﴾

This speech of Jesus is among the things that the Gospels of the Christians have omitted, because they concealed the account of its reaching his people after his birth. This concealment is something to be wondered at. It also indicates that the Gospels were written in circumstances that were not preserved, so Allah the Exalted made His Prophet (ﷺ) aware of it.

The beginning with the attribute of servanthood to Allah was placed by Allah on the tongue of Jesus, because Allah knew that a people would say that he is the son of Allah.

The expression of the giving of the Scripture in the past tense is meant to indicate that Allah had decreed its giving to him, that is, He had decreed that He would give me the Scripture.

The Scripture (al-kitab): it is the sharia (sacred law) which by its nature is to be written so that no alteration may occur in it. Thus the application of the term "Scripture" to the sharia of Jesus is like its application to the Qur'an.

What is meant by the Scripture is the Injil (Gospel), which is what was written of the revelation with which Allah addressed Jesus.

It is also permissible that what is meant by the Scripture is the Tawrat (Torah), in which case the giving means the giving of knowledge of what is in the Torah, as in His saying, the Exalted, ﴿O Yahya, take the Scripture with strength﴾ [Maryam: 12]. In that case His saying "﴿and made me a prophet﴾" is an ascent through the ranks that Allah had granted him.

What is said about the expression of it in the past tense is like what is said about His saying "﴿has given me the Scripture﴾".

[Page 99]

Al-mubarak (the blessed): it is the one whose blessing accompanies his states in his deeds, his speech and the like, because al-mubarak is a passive participle from barrakahu, meaning he made him possessed of blessing, or from barraka fihi, meaning he made blessing accompany him.

Al-barakah (blessing): it is goodness and prosperity.

That is because Allah sent him with mercy to the Children of Israel, to make lawful for them some of what had been forbidden to them, and to call them to noble morals after their hearts had hardened and they had altered their religion. This is the greatest blessing that accompanied him. Among his blessings is that Allah made his settling in a place a cause of good for the people of that land, through its fertility, the guidance of its people, and their being granted success in goodness. For this reason, when the ignorant, the hard-hearted and the corrupt met him, they were transformed into righteous people, and their hearts were opened to faith and wisdom. For this reason you see that most of the Hawariyyun (disciples) were from the common unlettered people, fishermen and tax collectors, and they became callers to guidance, and their tongues overflowed with wisdom.

By this it becomes clear that his being blessed is more general than his being a prophet in a partial general sense, so in His saying "﴿and made me a prophet﴾" there was no sufficiency that would dispense with His saying "﴿and made me blessed﴾".

The generality in His saying "﴿wherever I am﴾" is a generality concerning places, that is, his blessing is not restricted to his being in the Sanctuary (al-Maqdis, the Temple) or in the assembly of the people of his town, but wherever he alights, blessing alights with him.

The wasiyyah (enjoinment): it is a firm command concerning a future action. That is, He decreed my enjoinment to prayer and zakah, meaning that He would command me with them as a firm and continuous command. So the use of the past tense form in "﴿enjoined upon me﴾" is like its use in His saying "﴿has given me the Scripture﴾".

Zakah: it is charity. What is meant is that he should pray and give zakah. This is a command specific to him, just as our Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to perform the night prayer. The indication of specificity is

[Page 100]

His saying "﴿as long as I live﴾", because it indicates the continuation of the duration of his life through the performance of prayer and charity, that is, that he should pray and give charity at times when he is able to do so, that is, other than times of calling (to the faith) or of necessity.

Thus the continuity derived from His saying "﴿as long as I live﴾" is a customary continuity intended to mean frequency. The intended meaning is not the prayer and charity obligatory upon his community, because the context of the speech concerns attributes by which Jesus, peace be upon him, was distinguished, and because he did not bring a legislation of prayer additional to what was prescribed in the Torah.

Al-barr, with a fatha on the ba', is a noun meaning "the dutiful one". It was mentioned just before. Allah the Exalted specially distinguished him with this among his people, because dutifulness to parents was weak among the Children of Israel at that time, and especially toward the mother, because she is made weak, since her excessive tenderness and hardship may embolden the child to be lax in dutifulness toward her.

Al-jabbar: the arrogant one, harsh toward people in his dealings with them. His saying in Surah Hud has already been mentioned: ﴿and they followed the command of every arrogant obstinate tyrant﴾ [Hud: 59].

Al-shaqiyy: the losing one, and the one whose states are turbid and painful for him, and it is the opposite of the happy one (al-sa'id). It was mentioned at His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Among them are the wretched and the happy﴾ [Hud: 105], at the end of Surah Hud.

The tyrant was described as wretched with regard to his outcome in the Hereafter, and perhaps also in this world.

His saying "﴿And peace is upon me the day I was born﴾" through to the end is an honouring of his dignity with Allah. He caused it to pass upon his tongue so that they would know that he was in a place of care from his Lord. The discussion of it has already been given in the verse about the mention of Yahya.

Peace has been introduced here, defined with the article al-, to indicate the genus, as an intensification of peace's attachment to him, to the extent that the entire genus of peace is upon him.

[Page 101]

This indicates his superiority over Yahya, since it was said concerning him, ﴿And peace is upon him the day he was born﴾ [Maryam: 15], and that is the difference between the definite form with the article of genus and the indefinite.

It is also permissible to make the article one of prior reference (al-'ahd), meaning "peace be to him", and this is a metaphor for Allah's honouring His servant by praising him in the highest assembly and by commanding that he be honoured.

Of this kind is the peace upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in His saying, the Exalted, ﴿O you who have believed, invoke blessings upon him and greet him with peace﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56], and what we were commanded in the tashahhud (the testimony recited in prayer), the words of the one reciting the tashahhud: "Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings."

It also indicates the preparation of an allusion against the Jews, since they reproached him and reviled him in the three states, saying: he was born of fornication, and they said he died crucified, and they said he will be gathered with the heretics and the disbelievers, because they claim that he disbelieved by means of rulings from the Torah.

As for the one you describe, he is not Jesus, because summoning a person with attributes other than his own is a distortion of his identity. When they ascribed to him attributes other than his true ones, they were placed in the position of those who do not know him. Therefore the demonstrative was brought so that the one described would be distinguished in the most complete way for those who wish to know him as he truly is. The intended distinction is the distinction of his true attributes from the false attributes they attached to him, not the distinction of his essence from other essences, since his essence was not present at the time the verse was revealed. That is, "This is the reality of Jesus, peace be upon him, and his true description."

The reciters (al-jumhūr) read ﴿قَوْلُ الحَقِّ﴾ (qawlu l-ḥaqqi, "the word of truth") with a nominative ending (raf'). Ibn 'Āmir, 'Āṣim and Ya'qūb read it with an accusative ending (naṣb). As for the nominative, it is a second predicate (khabar thānin) for the demonstrative, or a qualifier (ṣifah) for Jesus, or an apposition (badal) from him. As for the accusative, it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the demonstrative or from Jesus.

The meaning of ﴿قَوْلُ الحَقِّ﴾ is that those attributes you have heard are "the word of truth," that is, a statement that is the truth, and whatever contradicts them is falsehood. Or it means that Jesus, peace be upon him, is "the word of truth," that is, the thing spoken of as truth, namely the one formed from the word "Be," so he is. Here the verbal noun (maṣdar) is used in the sense of the passive participle, like "creation" (al-khalq) in His words ﴿This is the creation of Allah﴾ [Luqmān: 11].

Abū 'Alī al-Fārisī permitted that the accusative of ﴿قَوْلَ الحَقِّ﴾ be by the implicit verb "I affirm the word of truth" (uḥiqqu qawla l-ḥaqqi). That is, it is an emphatic verbal noun for the content of the sentence before it, governed obligatorily by a deleted verb. Its implied form is: "I affirm the word of truth." It is also permitted that ﴿قَوْلَ الحَقِّ﴾ be a verbal noun standing in for its verb, that is, "I say the word of truth." On these two readings it is an interjection.

It is also permitted that qawl be a verbal noun in the sense of the active participle (ism al-fā'il), serving as a qualifier for Jesus or as a circumstantial accusative from him. That is, "the speaker of truth, when he said ﴿Indeed, I am the servant of Allah, He has given me the Book﴾ [Maryam: 30] up to His words ﴿and the day I am raised alive﴾ [Maryam: 33]."

﴿الَّذِي فِيهِ يَمْتَرُونَ﴾ ("about which they dispute") is a second qualifier, or a second circumstantial accusative, or a second predicate for ﴿عِيسى ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾ (Jesus, son of Mary), according to what suits the aforementioned possibilities.

[p. 103]

Al-imtirā' means doubt. That is, "about which they doubt," meaning they hold a belief founded on doubt and error. If the relative pronoun refers to the statement, then the disputing about it is disputing its truthfulness. If it refers to Jesus, then the disputing about him is disputing his attributes, between those who exalt him and those who debase him.

The clause ﴿It is not for Allah to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 35] is either a confirmation of the meaning of servanthood, or an elaboration of the content of the clause ﴿about which they dispute﴾. In that case it stands in the position of a partial substitute (badal al-ba'ḍ) or an inclusive substitute (badal al-ishtimāl) from it. This is sufficient to refute the Christians' claim that Jesus is the son of Allah, because it is more important to refute, since it affirms Jesus' servanthood and declares Allah exalted above what does not befit the majesty of divinity, such as taking a son, or any trace of association. It is also because it is the claim that arises from excessive exaltation, so the attributes of praise mentioned for Jesus might strengthen their doubt about him. By contrast, the Jewish claim has been shown to be false by the enumeration of Jesus' good attributes.

The form ﴿It is not for Allah to take﴾ (mā kāna li-llāhi an yattakhidha) indicates the negation of a son from Him, exalted be He, in the most emphatic way. This is because the lam of denial (lām al-juḥūd) expresses the strongest emphasis of negation, and because a son is something that cannot coexist with the existence of what is negated from Him. Moreover, in His words "to take" (an yattakhidha) there is an indication that if He had a son, He would have created him and adopted him, and so he would be only one of His created beings. Therefore, affirming sonship for Him is an absurd statement.

The clause ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Maryam: 35] is an explanation of the clause ﴿It is not for Allah to take a son﴾. It refutes the doubt of the Christians, who considered the creation of a human being by the command of creation, without a customary cause, as proof that the one created is a son of Allah, exalted be He. The verse indicates that this reasoning would require that the origins of all existing things be sons of Allah. Even though that reasoning does not leave the submission to the command of creation.

﴿الَّذِي فِيهِ يَمْتَرُونَ﴾ ("about which they dispute") is a second qualifier, or a second circumstantial accusative, or a second predicate for ﴿عِيسى ابْنُ مَرْيَمَ﴾ (Jesus, son of Mary), according to what suits the aforementioned possibilities.

[p. 103]

Al-imtirā' means doubt. That is, "about which they doubt," meaning they hold a belief founded on doubt and error. If the relative pronoun refers to the statement, then the disputing about it is disputing its truthfulness. If it refers to Jesus, then the disputing about him is disputing his attributes, between those who exalt him and those who debase him.

The clause ﴿It is not for Allah to take a son﴾ [Maryam: 35] is either a confirmation of the meaning of servanthood, or an elaboration of the content of the clause ﴿about which they dispute﴾. In that case it stands in the position of a partial substitute (badal al-ba'ḍ) or an inclusive substitute (badal al-ishtimāl) from it. This is sufficient to refute the Christians' claim that Jesus is the son of Allah, because it is more important to refute, since it affirms Jesus' servanthood and declares Allah exalted above what does not befit the majesty of divinity, such as taking a son, or any trace of association. It is also because it is the claim that arises from excessive exaltation, so the attributes of praise mentioned for Jesus might strengthen their doubt about him. By contrast, the Jewish claim has been shown to be false by the enumeration of Jesus' good attributes.

The form ﴿It is not for Allah to take﴾ (mā kāna li-llāhi an yattakhidha) indicates the negation of a son from Him, exalted be He, in the most emphatic way. This is because the lam of denial (lām al-juḥūd) expresses the strongest emphasis of negation, and because a son is something that cannot coexist with the existence of what is negated from Him. Moreover, in His words "to take" (an yattakhidha) there is an indication that if He had a son, He would have created him and adopted him, and so he would be only one of His created beings. Therefore, affirming sonship for Him is an absurd statement.

The clause ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Maryam: 35] is an explanation of the clause ﴿It is not for Allah to take a son﴾. It refutes the doubt of the Christians, who considered the creation of a human being by the command of creation, without a customary cause, as proof that the one created is a son of Allah, exalted be He. The verse indicates that this reasoning would require that the origins of all existing things be sons of Allah. Even though that reasoning does not leave the submission to the command of creation.

[p. 104]

﴿And indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is the straight path.﴾

It is possible that this is a continuation of the speech that came from the tongue of ʿIsa, in confirmation of the innocence of his mother, and that what lies between them is an *iʿtiraḍ* (a parenthetical interjection), as was mentioned just before. The meaning is the generalization of Allah the Exalted's lordship (*rubūbiyyah*) over all creation.

Nafiʿ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Abu Jaʿfar, and Ruways from Yaʿqub read the hamza of *wa-anna* with a fatha. Al-Zamakhshari explained this as being on the assumption of the *lām al-taʿlīl* (the lam of causation, "because"). If it is from the speech of ʿIsa, then it is a cause for his words *fa-ʿbudūhu* ("so worship Him"), by way of an inversion of order for the sake of emphasizing the cause, since the cause establishes and confirms the effect. This follows the style of the Exalted's words: ﴿And indeed, the mosques are for Allah, so do not invoke anyone alongside Allah﴾ [al-Jinn: 18]. His words *fa-ʿbudūhu* would then be a consequence of His words ﴿Indeed, I am a servant of Allah﴾ [Maryam: 30], after he had appended what pertains to his own circumstances.

Since the complement of the *lām al-taʿlīl* contains the name of Allah, a pronoun referring to it is used afterward. The structure of the sentence is thus: "So worship Allah, because He is my Lord and your Lord."

It is also possible that it is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*) with His words ﴿with prayer and zakat﴾ [Maryam: 31]; that is, "and He has enjoined upon me that Allah is my Lord and your Lord." In this case the preposition has been elided, which is a regular practice with *anna*.

It is also possible that it is coordinated with *al-ḥaqq* in His words ﴿the word of truth﴾ [Maryam: 34], on the basis of making *qawl* carry the sense of *qāʾil* (speaker): that is, "the speaker of the truth, and the one who says that Allah is my Lord and your Lord." The hamza of *anna* may be read with either a fatha or a kasra after the root of *qawl*.

If it is among what the Prophet ﷺ was addressed with, that he should say it, then it is by way of an assumed verb of saying that has been omitted; or it is coordinated with Maryam in His words ﴿And mention in the Book Maryam﴾ [Maryam: 16], meaning: "Mention, O Muhammad, that Allah is my Lord"; and thus the consequence of *fa-ʿbudūhu* would follow His words ﴿It is not for Allah to take a son; glory be to Him﴾ [Maryam: 35] to the end of the passage.

[p. 105]

Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, and Rawh from Yaʿqub read the hamza of *inna* with a kasra. Its grammatical justification is clear under both possibilities.

The clause ﴿This is the straight path﴾ [Ali ʿImran: 51] is a *tadhyīl* (a concluding statement that generalizes the preceding sense) and a *fadhlakah* (a summary recapitulation) of what precedes it, across the various possible readings. The demonstrative refers to the content of what came before, under the various readings.

By "the straight path" is meant the correct belief. It is described by way of an intensive metaphor (*tashbīh balīgh*): correct belief is likened to the straight path in that it conveys one to guidance, just as the straight path conveys one to the intended destination with tranquility of mind. It is known that other than this is like the side-branches of a road: whoever travels them is cast by fears and perils, as in His words ﴿And that this is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow the other ways, lest they separate you from His way﴾ [al-Anʿam: 153].

﴿So the factions differed among themselves, and woe to those who disbelieved from the scene of a tremendous day.﴾

The fa' (فاء) here marks a consequence: the report that the differing occurred follows from the report that "this is a straight path." That is, the factions deviated from the straight path, and so they differed among themselves over the ways they took. In other words, "this is a straight path, whose followers do not differ in fundamental matters," but the factions took other ways that deviate from the straight path, so they did not agree on anything.

[Page 106]

His words ﴿among themselves﴾ are connected to "differed." Min (من) here is a particle of emphasis, meaning "they differed among themselves."

By "the factions" is meant the factions of the Christians, because the difference indicates that they had been in agreement, whereas the Jews did not agree with the Christians on anything of the religion. The Christians were united in monotheism during the lifetime of the Hawariyyun (disciples, the apostles of Jesus), and then differences arose among their followers. We have mentioned, in the commentary on His words, exalted is He, ﴿So believe in Allah and His messengers, and do not say "Three"﴾ [an-Nisa': 171], in Surat an-Nisa', that the disagreement resolved into three doctrines: the Malkaniyya (Melkites), also called the Jathaliqiyya (Catholics); the Ya'qubiyya (Jacobites); and the Nestoriyya (Nestorians). From these sects a number of other sects branched off, which al-Shahrastani mentioned, including the Alyaniyya, the Bilyarisiyya, the Miqdanusiyya, the Sibaliyya, the Butinusiyya, and the Buliyya, along with other sects. Among them is a sect that existed among the Arabs called the Rakusiyya, whose mention occurs in the hadith: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'Adi ibn Hatim: 'You are a Rakusi.'"

The scholars of language said: it is a Christianity mixed with the beliefs of the Sabians. After that there arose the sect of the I'tiradiyya, the Protestants, the followers of Luther. The most well-known sects today are the Malkaniyya (Catholics), the Ya'qubiyya (Orthodox), and the I'tiradiyya (Protestants). Since their disagreement has been confined to one source, which goes back to the divinity of Jesus, through delusion and misunderstanding regarding the meaning of the word "son" (ibn), which occurs in the Gospels as an attribute of the Messiah, although it has also been applied in them to his companions. The Torah also contains "You are the sons of Allah." In the Gospel of Matthew, the disciple, and the Gospel of John, the disciple, there are explicit statements that the Messiah is the son of a man and that Allah is his God and Lord. Thus their doctrines have been confined to disbelief in Allah. Therefore it is followed with His words, ﴿so woe to those who disbelieved from the scene of a tremendous day﴾, and His words ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ include these reported groups of Christians and include the polytheists and others.

The word mashhad (مَشْهَد) is capable of several meanings: it may be derived from mushahada (witnessing) or from shuhud (presence). Then it may be a mimi verbal noun with both meanings, or a noun of place for both, or a noun of time for both, meaning "a day in which that occurs and other things."

[Page 107]

Woe (al-wayl) applies to them in all of these possibilities. They have entered under the general term "those who disbelieved in Allah," meaning they denied His oneness, so they have certainly entered the category of polytheists; yet they are People of the Book, unlike the polytheists.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verse 38:

﴿How much they will hear and how much they will see on the day they come to Us! But the wrongdoers today are in clear error.﴾

﴿How much they will hear and how much they will see﴾ are two forms of exclamation (ta'ajjub), and it is an exclamation on the tongue of the Messenger and the believers. Or it is used for expressing wonder (al-ta'ajjub), and the two meanings are close. It is also used metaphorically (kinayah) for threatening them. Thus it is determined that the wonder is at the extent to which their condition has reached in evil, to the point that one marvels at their capacity to witness its sights and hear its horrors. The meaning: how much they will hear and how much they will see on that day, that is, how capable they will be of hearing and seeing what they hate. This is close to the meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿How patient they are over the Fire!﴾ [al-Baqarah: 175].

It is also permitted that ﴿Hear them and see﴾ is not used for wonder, but happens to come in the form of an exclamatory verb, while in its original sense it is an imperative addressed to an unspecified addressee: that he hear and see because of them. The object of hearing and seeing is omitted for the purpose of generality, so as to include everything that can be heard and seen. This is a metaphor for threat.

The pronoun referring to the absent ones returns to those who disbelieved, meaning: marvel at their condition on that day, from among the Christians and the idol-worshippers.

Page 108

The contrast (istidrak) conveyed by His saying ﴿But the wrongdoers today are in clear error﴾ refers to what the restriction by the time adverb in His saying ﴿on the day they come to Us﴾ implies, namely the anticipation of the evil of their condition on the Day of Resurrection, which suggests the assumption that they are now in ease of circumstance.

So it is conveyed that they are immersed in clear error, and that is among the evil of their condition, because of what follows from it of confusion of judgment and the obscuring of the situation for its possessor. This is the point (nukta) of restricting by the time adverb in His saying ﴿today, in clear error﴾.

The expression of them as (al-zalimun, "the wrongdoers") is an explicit noun in place of the pronoun. Its point is to single out the polytheists specifically, because the Qur'anic usage applies the term "wrongdoers" to idol-worshippers, and applies "wrong" (zulm) to the worship of idols. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, association [with Allah] is a great wrong﴾ [Luqman: 13].

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verse 39:**

﴿And warn them of the Day of Regret, when the matter will have been decided, while they are heedless and do not believe.﴾

He follows his warning of the punishment of the Hereafter, and his reproach for their wretched misguidance in this world, with a command to warn them, in order to be thorough in giving them every excuse.

The pronoun refers to the wrongdoers (al-zalimin), namely the polytheists of Makkah and others among the idol-worshippers, as shown by His words ﴿and they do not believe﴾ and ﴿and to Us they will be returned﴾ [Maryam: 40].

﴿The Day of Regret﴾ is in the accusative because it is an object that replaces the second object of ﴿warn them﴾, since the meaning is "warn them of the punishment of the Day of Regret."

*Al-hasrah* is intense remorse that leads to lamentation. By "the Day of Regret" is meant the Day of Reckoning. The day is attributed to regret because of the great amount of regret that takes place on it, as the wrongdoers lament what they neglected of the means of salvation. That day is thus, as it were, one particularly characterised by regret. It is a day of regret for them, even though it is a day of joy for the righteous.

On this reading, the *lam* in *al-hasrah* is the *lam* of mental (conceptual) definiteness (*lam al-'ahd al-dhihni*), which refers to a known but unspecified item. It is also permissible for the *lam* to be a substitute for the genitive complement (*mudaf ilayh*), meaning "the Day of the regret of the wrongdoers."

The meaning of ﴿when the matter will have been decided﴾ is that God's command to cast them into punishment has been carried out, so there is no one to reverse it.

It is also permissible that "the matter" means God's command for the Day of Resurrection to come, that is, when they are gathered.

*Idh* is a noun of time, in apposition to ﴿the Day of Regret﴾.

The clause ﴿while they are heedless﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to "the matter." It is a causal circumstantial clause (*hal sababiyyah*), since the implied sense is "when their matter has been decided."

*Al-ghaflah* is being distracted from something that ought to be known.

On the first possibility, the meaning of the circumstantial clause, in terms of the matter, is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for the swiftness with which the command to punish them is issued. That is, their matter is decided while they are in heedlessness, that is, in bewilderment. On the second possibility, it is a warning against the Day of Resurrection arriving upon them before they believe, as in His words ﴿It will not come upon you except suddenly﴾ [al-A'raf: 187]. This fits better with His words ﴿and they do not believe.﴾

The meaning of ﴿and they do not believe﴾ is the continuation of their unbelief until the decision of the matter arrives on the Day of Regret. The choice of the present-tense verb form here, rather than the active participle form, is because the present tense indicates the continuation of the action, moment by moment, in order to evoke that continuation in its wondrous length and firmness.

[p. 110]
﴿Indeed, it is We who inherit the earth and whoever is upon it, and to Us they will be returned.﴾

This is a *tadhyil* (a concluding generalization that closes a passage), following the Qur'an's usual practice of closing a topic with such a statement when it moves on to something else. The address is directed to the polytheists, in order to convey it to them.

The pronoun in *yurji'ūn* ("they will be returned") refers to "whoever is upon it" and also to what the pronoun of address in *wa-andhir-hum* ("and warn them") refers to.

The literal meaning of *al-irth* (inheritance) is the passing of a dead person's property to whoever remains after him. Here it is used metaphorically to mean the exclusive disposal of a thing without any partner. The earth was under the control of its inhabitants, both humans and animals, each according to what suits them. When humans and animals die, they go into the depths of the earth, and the earth passes out of their control, so no disposal of it remains except for its Creator. That disposal, which in outward appearance was shared, was only shared to the extent that Allah had granted them the right to dispose of it for a known term. Thus all things become under the sole disposal of Allah, and among this is His disposal through recompense.

The emphasis in the sentence ﴿Indeed, it is We who inherit the earth﴾ with the emphatic particle *inna* (*ḥarf al-tawkīd*, the particle of emphasis) is to remove doubt, because the polytheists deny recompense. So they deny that Allah inherits the earth and whoever is upon it in this sense.

As for the separating pronoun (*ḍamīr al-faṣl*) in His saying ﴿We inherit the earth﴾, it serves only to add emphasis and does not indicate exclusivity, since it does not serve to refute a contrary belief.

It has become clear to me that the separating pronoun is frequently used merely for emphasis when it follows another pronoun, such as His saying ﴿Indeed, I am Allah﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 14] in Surat Ṭā-Hā, and His saying ﴿and they, of the Hereafter, they are disbelievers﴾ [Yūsuf: 37] in Surat Yūsuf.

This concluding statement conveys, by way of warning to the polytheists, that they have no escape from being within the grip of the one Lord, whom they associated in worship with some of what is on the earth. It also conveys that their deities are not to be hoped in for benefit, since they are only among what Allah inherits. In this light, the placement of the phrase ﴿and to Us they will be returned﴾ is clear. The fronting (*taqdīm*) of "to Us" conveys restriction (*qaṣr*), meaning: they will return to no one other than Us. The implication of this fronting, with respect to the Muslims, is emphasis of concern, and with respect to the polytheists, it is restriction, as was previously explained regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, it is We who inherit the earth﴾.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verses 41–42:

﴿And mention in the Book Abraham. Indeed, he was a man of truth (siddiq), a prophet (nabi).﴾ ﴿When he said to his father, "O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees and cannot avail you at all?"﴾

It has already been established that among the most important themes this surah contains is the honouring of the earlier prophets and messengers. Since Abraham (peace be upon him) was the father of the prophets and the first to proclaim tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) in a lasting proclamation, through his building for it of the sanctuary of tawhid, which is the Ka'bah, the mention of Abraham was among the purposes of the surah. He is mentioned following the story of Jesus, because of the connection with the rebuttal of the polytheists at the end of that story, beginning from His saying, ﴿So woe to those who disbelieve, from the scene of a great Day﴾ [Maryam: 37] to His saying ﴿Indeed, We inherit the earth and whatever is upon it﴾ [Maryam: 40]. And since Abraham had brought the hanifiyyah (pure monotheistic faith) and the Arabs, who are the heirs of Abraham, opposed it with polytheism, placing his mention before the rest carries a sublime eloquence.

In this there is also consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding what he encountered from the polytheists of his people, since their situation resembles the situation of the people of Abraham.

The narration of the account of Abraham (peace be upon him) has proceeded in the style of the narration of the story of Maryam (peace be upon her), because of the importance of each, as has already been mentioned.

Page 112

The interpretation of ﴿And mention in the Book﴾ [Maryam: 16] has already been given at the beginning of the story of Maryam.

Al-siddiq, with the letter dal doubled, is an intensive form (sighat mubalaghah) of attribution, like the epithet "al-malik al-dalil" of Imru' al-Qays, and their saying: rajul missik, meaning miserly (shahih), and from it "ta'am hirrif" (spicy food). It is also said: dalil kharrit (a guide skilled in hidden paths), since he has expertise in the concealed routes through the deserts; it is derived from al-khart, which is the piercing of a thing, as if he pierces what is closed off with his sight.

It has already occurred in His saying ﴿Yusuf, O man of truth (siddiq)﴾ [Yusuf: 46]. Abraham is described as siddiq because of the extreme truthfulness of his carrying out what Allah Most High charged him with, not being turned away from it by anything that might be an excuse for the one charged, such as his hastening to attempt to slaughter his son when Allah commanded him to do so in the revelation of a dream. So truthfulness here means reaching the utmost limit of the attribute in the one described by it, as in the words of Ta'abbata Sharran:

"Indeed I am one who prepares my praise, directing it to the cousin of truthfulness, Shams ibn Malik."

The emphasis of this report by the particle of emphasis and by the insertion of the verb of being (kana) is for the sake of affirming it, adding to the praise of him.

The sentence "Indeed he was a siddiq, a nabi" stands in the position of giving the reason for the concern with mentioning him in the recitation. This sentence is interposed between the substituted noun and the substitute. For "idh" is a noun of time that stands as a substitute for Abraham, meaning: mention that particularly from the circumstances of Abraham, for it is the most important of what is mentioned about him, because it is the manifestation of his siddiqiyyah, when he addressed his father with that denunciation.

The nabi: it is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, from anba'ahu bi'l-khabar (he informed him of the news). What is meant here is that he is informed by Allah Most High through revelation. Most often the nabi is a messenger sent for conveying the message, and this is a legal (shar'i) meaning, so the nabi in it is a customary (conventional) reality. It has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah at His saying (﴿When they said to a prophet of theirs, "Send for us a king"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246]), which indicates that his saying to his father ﴿O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees﴾ was only from a revelation from Allah, to convey to his people the invalidity of idol worship.

Al-Jumhur read (nabi'an) with a doubled ya', the hamzah being replaced by ya' because of its heaviness and for harmony with the kasrah.

Nafi' alone read (nabi'an) with a hamzah at its end. With this, the Qur'anic closing rhyme stays on the letter alif, and similar such closing rhymes are numerous in the Qur'an's endings.

His saying ﴿When he said to his father﴾ etc. is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from Abraham. "Idh" is a noun of time stripped of the adverbial sense, since idh is, in verification, a fully declinable adverb. The meaning: mention Abraham at the time of his saying to his father, for that time is the most fitting of Abraham's times to be mentioned.

Abraham's father is Azar, whose mention has already been made in Surat al-An'am.

Abraham began his address to his father with calling him, although the presence makes calling unnecessary, intending to draw in his hearing and attention to receive what he is about to say to him.

The grandfather, the minister (al-Jadd al-Wazir), may Allah have mercy on him, said in what he dictated to me one night in the year 1318 AH:

Abraham knew that it is in the nature of ignorant people to belittle the young, however far his skill may reach, and especially fathers with their sons. So he turned to his father with his address using the description of fatherhood, as an allusion to his being sincere in giving him counsel. He presented to him the argument of the corruption of his worship, and the question about the cause of his worship and his mistaken action portrays it, alerting him to his error when he reflects upon his action. For if he heard that and tried to explain the reason for worshipping his idols, he would find no word to say for himself, and so he would perceive the foolishness of his opinion and the frivolity of his judgement, for if he worshipped a living, discerning being, there would be some kind of plausible doubt for him.

Page 114

He began with the argument grounded in the senses when he said to him ﴿Why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees﴾, so that is a sensory argument. Then he followed it with His saying ﴿and cannot avail you at all﴾. Then he moved on to repelling what troubles the father's mind of aversion to receiving guidance from his son, with his saying ﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge what has not come to you, so follow me; I will guide you to a straight path﴾ [Maryam: 43]. When he had fulfilled the right of that, he moved on to alerting him that what he was upon is a trace of the whisperings of Satan. Then he presented to him an argument suited to the obstinate in misguidance with his saying ﴿O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so you become a companion to Satan﴾ [Maryam: 45], meaning: Allah has conveyed the warning to you through my tongue; if you do not affirm it, then assume its occurrence, for your idols did not threaten you should you abandon their worship. This is like the poetry attributed to 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him):

"The astrologer and the physician both claim that bodies are not resurrected. I say: To you both:

If your saying is true, I am not a loser; but if my saying is true, then the loss is upon you both."

He said: In the repetition of the call "O my father" four times there is an emphasis required by the situation of bringing him down to acceptance of the admonition, since it is a situation of elaboration (ito'nab). This is compared with Luqman's repetition of his saying "O my son" three times. He said: Unlike Nuh's saying to his son ﴿O my son, board with us﴾ [Hud: 42], once only without repetition, because the narrowness of the situation calls for brevity, and this is among the ways of inimitability (i'jaz). The end of his speech, in approximately these words.

I say: The correct view is what he built upon, that the interrogative is used in its literal sense, as the author of the Kashshaf indicated, and it is figuratively used to express the negation of the cause asked about in His saying "why do you worship", so it is a metonymy for incapacity to produce what is asked about. It is thus an equivoque (tawriyah) in two meanings that the interrogative admits.

Page 115

"Abati": its origin is "abi" (my father); they dropped the ya' of the first person and compensated for it with a ta' by way of compensation, not by analogy, and this is specific to the words "ab" and "umm" in the vocative only. Perhaps it is a form that remains from ancient Arabic. Sibawayh held that the ta' becomes a ha' in pause, and al-Farra' disagreed with him, saying it remains a ta' in pause. The ta' is mostly kasrah, because it is a substitute for the ya', and the ya' is the daughter of kasrah; and when they gave it kasrah, they made the ya' fathah, and accordingly al-Jumhur read it.

Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read (ya abata) with fathah on the ta' without an alif after it, on the basis that they say (ya abata) with an alif after the ta', because when the ya' of the first person is addressed, its fathah and the lengthening of its fathah are permitted. So he read it on the consideration of dropping the alif for lightness and retaining the fathah.
