The interpretation of ﴿And mention in the Book﴾ [Maryam: 16] has already been given at the beginning of the story of Maryam.

Al-siddiq, with the letter dal doubled, is an intensive form (sighat mubalaghah) of attribution, like the epithet "al-malik al-dalil" of Imru' al-Qays, and their saying: rajul missik, meaning miserly (shahih), and from it "ta'am hirrif" (spicy food). It is also said: dalil kharrit (a guide skilled in hidden paths), since he has expertise in the concealed routes through the deserts; it is derived from al-khart, which is the piercing of a thing, as if he pierces what is closed off with his sight.

It has already occurred in His saying ﴿Yusuf, O man of truth (siddiq)﴾ [Yusuf: 46]. Abraham is described as siddiq because of the extreme truthfulness of his carrying out what Allah Most High charged him with, not being turned away from it by anything that might be an excuse for the one charged, such as his hastening to attempt to slaughter his son when Allah commanded him to do so in the revelation of a dream. So truthfulness here means reaching the utmost limit of the attribute in the one described by it, as in the words of Ta'abbata Sharran:

"Indeed I am one who prepares my praise, directing it to the cousin of truthfulness, Shams ibn Malik."

The emphasis of this report by the particle of emphasis and by the insertion of the verb of being (kana) is for the sake of affirming it, adding to the praise of him.

The sentence "Indeed he was a siddiq, a nabi" stands in the position of giving the reason for the concern with mentioning him in the recitation. This sentence is interposed between the substituted noun and the substitute. For "idh" is a noun of time that stands as a substitute for Abraham, meaning: mention that particularly from the circumstances of Abraham, for it is the most important of what is mentioned about him, because it is the manifestation of his siddiqiyyah, when he addressed his father with that denunciation.

The nabi: it is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, from anba'ahu bi'l-khabar (he informed him of the news). What is meant here is that he is informed by Allah Most High through revelation. Most often the nabi is a messenger sent for conveying the message, and this is a legal (shar'i) meaning, so the nabi in it is a customary (conventional) reality. It has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah at His saying (﴿When they said to a prophet of theirs, "Send for us a king"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 246]), which indicates that his saying to his father ﴿O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees﴾ was only from a revelation from Allah, to convey to his people the invalidity of idol worship.

Al-Jumhur read (nabi'an) with a doubled ya', the hamzah being replaced by ya' because of its heaviness and for harmony with the kasrah.

Nafi' alone read (nabi'an) with a hamzah at its end. With this, the Qur'anic closing rhyme stays on the letter alif, and similar such closing rhymes are numerous in the Qur'an's endings.

His saying ﴿When he said to his father﴾ etc. is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from Abraham. "Idh" is a noun of time stripped of the adverbial sense, since idh is, in verification, a fully declinable adverb. The meaning: mention Abraham at the time of his saying to his father, for that time is the most fitting of Abraham's times to be mentioned.

Abraham's father is Azar, whose mention has already been made in Surat al-An'am.

Abraham began his address to his father with calling him, although the presence makes calling unnecessary, intending to draw in his hearing and attention to receive what he is about to say to him.

The grandfather, the minister (al-Jadd al-Wazir), may Allah have mercy on him, said in what he dictated to me one night in the year 1318 AH:

Abraham knew that it is in the nature of ignorant people to belittle the young, however far his skill may reach, and especially fathers with their sons. So he turned to his father with his address using the description of fatherhood, as an allusion to his being sincere in giving him counsel. He presented to him the argument of the corruption of his worship, and the question about the cause of his worship and his mistaken action portrays it, alerting him to his error when he reflects upon his action. For if he heard that and tried to explain the reason for worshipping his idols, he would find no word to say for himself, and so he would perceive the foolishness of his opinion and the frivolity of his judgement, for if he worshipped a living, discerning being, there would be some kind of plausible doubt for him.

Page 114

He began with the argument grounded in the senses when he said to him ﴿Why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees﴾, so that is a sensory argument. Then he followed it with His saying ﴿and cannot avail you at all﴾. Then he moved on to repelling what troubles the father's mind of aversion to receiving guidance from his son, with his saying ﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge what has not come to you, so follow me; I will guide you to a straight path﴾ [Maryam: 43]. When he had fulfilled the right of that, he moved on to alerting him that what he was upon is a trace of the whisperings of Satan. Then he presented to him an argument suited to the obstinate in misguidance with his saying ﴿O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so you become a companion to Satan﴾ [Maryam: 45], meaning: Allah has conveyed the warning to you through my tongue; if you do not affirm it, then assume its occurrence, for your idols did not threaten you should you abandon their worship. This is like the poetry attributed to 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him):

"The astrologer and the physician both claim that bodies are not resurrected. I say: To you both:

If your saying is true, I am not a loser; but if my saying is true, then the loss is upon you both."

He said: In the repetition of the call "O my father" four times there is an emphasis required by the situation of bringing him down to acceptance of the admonition, since it is a situation of elaboration (ito'nab). This is compared with Luqman's repetition of his saying "O my son" three times. He said: Unlike Nuh's saying to his son ﴿O my son, board with us﴾ [Hud: 42], once only without repetition, because the narrowness of the situation calls for brevity, and this is among the ways of inimitability (i'jaz). The end of his speech, in approximately these words.

I say: The correct view is what he built upon, that the interrogative is used in its literal sense, as the author of the Kashshaf indicated, and it is figuratively used to express the negation of the cause asked about in His saying "why do you worship", so it is a metonymy for incapacity to produce what is asked about. It is thus an equivoque (tawriyah) in two meanings that the interrogative admits.

Page 115

"Abati": its origin is "abi" (my father); they dropped the ya' of the first person and compensated for it with a ta' by way of compensation, not by analogy, and this is specific to the words "ab" and "umm" in the vocative only. Perhaps it is a form that remains from ancient Arabic. Sibawayh held that the ta' becomes a ha' in pause, and al-Farra' disagreed with him, saying it remains a ta' in pause. The ta' is mostly kasrah, because it is a substitute for the ya', and the ya' is the daughter of kasrah; and when they gave it kasrah, they made the ya' fathah, and accordingly al-Jumhur read it.

Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read (ya abata) with fathah on the ta' without an alif after it, on the basis that they say (ya abata) with an alif after the ta', because when the ya' of the first person is addressed, its fathah and the lengthening of its fathah are permitted. So he read it on the consideration of dropping the alif for lightness and retaining the fathah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verse 43:

﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you, so follow me; I will guide you to a path, balanced and sound.﴾

The repetition of his address with the title of fatherhood is an emphasis to draw the mind's attention and to make the advice sincere, which is derived from the first address. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "Then he followed up with his call to the truth, gently and kindly. He did not call his father ignorant in an extreme way, nor did he describe himself as having superior knowledge; rather he said: 'Indeed, with me is a portion of knowledge that is not with you, and that is the knowledge of pointing to the balanced path. So do not be disdainful. Suppose that you and I are on a journey and I have knowledge of guidance that you lack; then follow me, and I will save you from going astray and wandering.'" End of quote. That is because his father regarded himself as possessing great knowledge, since he was the chief of his people's religion. Ibrahim intended the knowledge of revelation and prophethood.

The branching of his command that he be followed upon informing him of the knowledge he has is evidence that the principle that the knowledgeable person is worthy of being followed is fixed in the instinct of minds. Humankind has always sought out the sources of knowledge and learning to obtain what benefits and to guard against what harms. God the Exalted said: ﴿Ask the people of remembrance if you do not know﴾ [al-Nahl: 43].

In His saying ﴿I will guide you to a path, balanced﴾ there is a metaphor in the implicit form (istiʿarah makniyyah): Ibrahim is likened to a guide on the road who is perceptive of the mountain passes, and the attribution of "balanced path" to the path is the indicator of the comparison. It is also an explicit metaphor (istiʿarah musarrahah), in that the belief that leads to the truth and salvation is likened to the straight road that reaches the intended destination.

And "O my father" has already been discussed earlier, in a similar instance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verse 44:

﴿O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed, Satan has ever been, toward the Most Merciful, disobedient.﴾

The repetition of the address (nida') serves to reinforce what the first and second addresses conveyed. By "the worship of Satan" is meant the worship of idols. He expressed it as the worship of Satan to make clear its corruption and misguidance, for the attribution of misguidance and corruption to Satan is firmly established in human souls. However, those who follow him do not perceive their own state, and they follow his whisperings under the veil of deception, like their saying: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers following a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 23]. So there is concision (ijaz) in the speech, for its meaning is: "Do not worship the idols, for taking them is from the enticement of Satan to those who took them and set them up for the people, and worshipping them is from the whisperings of Satan to those who established the practices of their worship, and from his whisperings to the people who obeyed them in worshipping them. Whoever worships idols has worshipped Satan, and that is sufficient as manifest misguidance."

This is like His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And they invoke none but a rebellious Satan﴾ [al-Nisa': 117]. It has been discussed in Surat al-Nisa'. In this there is an instilling of aversion toward the worship of idols, because deep within human souls there is hatred of Satan and caution against his plotting.

Page 117
The clause ﴿Indeed, Satan has ever been disobedient toward the Most Merciful﴾ is a justification (ta'lil) for the prohibition against worshipping him and worshipping the traces of his whispering, by the fact that he is exceedingly disobedient to the Lord of vast mercy. Mentioning the description "'asiyyan," which is among the intensive forms (sigha al-mubalagha) of disobedience, together with the verb "kana" (has been), is to indicate that he never departs from disobedience to his Lord and that he is firmly established in it. Therefore he certainly commands only what contradicts mercy, that is, what leads to vengeance. For this reason the attribute "al-Rahman" was chosen from among the attributes of God, the Exalted, as a warning that worshipping idols brings about God's anger and thus leads to deprivation of His mercy. Whoever is in this state is deserving of not being followed.

The explicit mention of the name Satan in place of a pronoun, where one would have said "he has been disobedient toward the Most Merciful," serves to clarify the attribution of the predicate to its subject, and to intensify the aversion from Satan, since explicitly naming him alerts one to shun him, and so that the clause stands as an admonition in its own right. The discussion of "ya abati" has been given shortly before.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verse 45:

﴿O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so you would become a companion to Satan.﴾

Indeed, when he had established that his worship of idols was a following of the command of Satan, the disobedient one toward the Most Merciful, he moved on to anticipate his being deprived of Allah's mercy, that a punishment from Allah would befall him. So he warned him of the outcome of becoming one of the allies of Satan, concerning whom people do not differ in censuring them and in the evil of their end, although they become entangled with them out of misguidance through the final state of their affairs.

And to indicate that the root of the descent of punishment upon the one on whom it descends is deprivation from mercy in that state, he expressed the Majestic Name by the attribute "al-Rahman" (the Most Merciful), to point out that the descent of punishment upon one whose nature is to show mercy happens only because of the enormity of his crime, to the degree that the one whose nature is vast mercy deprives him of his mercy.

And al-Waliyy (the ally): the companion and the follower, and whoever shares their state and their affair is one; so he used "wilayah" (allegiance/alliance) as a metonymy for being joined together in the final destiny.

And the expression by "khawf" (fear), which indicates probability rather than certainty, is a matter of courtesy toward Allah the Exalted, by not affirming a matter concerning what falls within Allah's disposal, and to preserve hope in the soul of his father, so that he would consider escaping that punishment by desisting from worshipping idols. And the meaning of ﴿so you would become a companion to Satan﴾ is that you would be in following Satan in the punishment. The discussion of "Ya abati" (O my father) has already been mentioned shortly before.

[p. 119]

The clause *qāla* (he said) is detached (*fuṣilat*) because it occurs within a dialogue, as was explained earlier in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿They said: "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], in Surat al-Baqarah. The interrogative *istifhām* here expresses denial (*inkār*), a denial of Ibrahim's aversion to worshipping their idols. The addition of "the gods" (*al-ālihah*) to the pronoun of the speaker is an addition of allegiance and affiliation (*idafat wilayah wa intisab*) to the one added, for the purpose of honouring the one to whom it is added. In his reply, the son's call (to his father) came with the utmost harshness and arrogance, in contrast to what was in Ibrahim's speech of gentleness and tenderness. This indicates that he was hard-hearted, slow to understand, and extremely rigid in disbelief.

The phrase ﴿Are you turning away from my gods, O Ibrahim?﴾ is a nominal sentence (*jumlah ismiyyah*) composed of a subject (*mubtada'*, the inchoative) and an agent (*fā'il*) that stands in place of the predicate (*khabar*), according to the terminology of the grammarians, in keeping with the rules of verbal construction. However, when they regarded the noun that occurs second after the descriptive word (*wasf*) as an agent standing in place of the predicate, they attributed to that noun the status of the predicated element (*musnad ilayh*), and the descriptive word that is the subject took the status of the predicate (*musnad*). Because of this, the resort to this kind of arrangement, in the view of eloquent speakers (*bulaghā'*), is required by the situation, which calls for a nominal sentence to indicate the stability of the predicated element, and calls for emphasis on the descriptive word rather than the noun, for a purpose that makes it important. Thus the eloquent speaker resorts to placing the descriptive word first and the noun second. When the descriptive word has come to act as its verb would act, it became necessary for the grammarians to consider the descriptive word a subject, because the subject has precedence among nouns, while also considering it as requiring an agent; they made its agent stand in place of the predicate, so the structure came to have two aspects. The verified view is that it has the force of a fronted predicate and a delayed subject. For this reason al-Zamakhshari, in *al-Kashshaf*, considered this purpose and said: "The predicate has been placed before the subject in His words ﴿Are you turning away from my gods?﴾ because it was more important to them, and it is what he cares about most." (End of quotation.)

How excellent he is, though his pearl has been lost among most of those who look upon it. The arrangement of this verse indicates that the father of Ibrahim was denouncing Ibrahim for allowing aversion to their gods to take hold of himself, and was concerned with the matter of aversion to the gods, because it was a cause for astonishment. The vocative in His words *yā Ibrāhīm* ("O Ibrahim") completes the sentence of denial and astonishment, because the one at whose action one is astonished, though present, is addressed with the intention of alerting him to the evil of his action, as if he were absent and unaware of his action. So the speaker treats him as one absent, and calls him in order to return his right guidance to him. Therefore it is appropriate to pause at His words *yā Ibrāhīm*.

The clause ﴿If you do not desist, I will surely stone you﴾ is a new sentence (*mustaʾnafah*). The *lām* is an introductory particle of an oath (*muwaṭṭi'ah lil-qasam*), emphasising that he would stone him if he did not desist from his disbelief in their gods.

(Page 120)

*al-Rajm* is pelting with stones, and it is a well-known metonymy (*kināyah mashhūrah*) for killing by that pelting. The father's attribution of that act to himself admits of the literal sense, either because it was among their customs that a father has authority over the punishment of his son, or because he was a judge among his people. It also admits of the rational metonymy (*al-majāz al-ʿaqlī*), since perhaps he was a leader in their religion, so his people would stone Ibrahim on the basis of his judgment that he had departed from their religion.

The clause ﴿and leave me alone for a long time﴾ is conjoined (*ʿatf*) to the clause ﴿If you do not desist, I will surely stone you﴾. This is because he threatened him with a deferred punishment if he did not give up his disbelief in their gods, and with an immediate punishment, which is his expelling him from his company and cutting off conversation with him.

*al-Hajr* is cutting off conversation and cutting off companionship. The father ordered his son to abandon him rather than telling him that he himself would abandon him, in order to indicate that this abandonment means expulsion and dismissal, as a way of conveying contempt for him.

*Malīyyan* means "for a long time." It is on the pattern *faʿīl*, and no unaugmented verb or verbal noun is known for it. So *malīyyan* is derived from a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) that is no longer in use, and it is a *faʿīl* in the sense of *fāʿil*, because one says *amlā lahu* ("he gave him respite") when he lengthened the period for him, using the augmenting *hamzah* of transitivity. Thus *malīyyan* is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun in the accusative as an absolute object (*mafʿūl muṭlaq*), meaning "a long abandonment." It also derives from *al-mulāwah* (a long period), which refers to a lengthy stretch of time, and this root indicates abundance of a thing. It may also be accusative as an adjective of an omitted adverb of time, meaning "a long time." Based on the fact that *al-malā* (with the final vowel short) is predominantly used for time, mentioning it dispenses with mentioning the modified noun, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And We bore him upon one of planks and nails﴾ [al-Qamar: 13], meaning a vessel having planks.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verses 47–48:

Page 121

﴿He said, "Peace be upon you! I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord. Indeed, He has ever been gracious to me."﴾ ﴿"And I will leave you and what you invoke other than Allah, and I will invoke my Lord. Perhaps I will not be in invocation to my Lord unhappy."﴾

"Peace be upon you" is a farewell and a word of disengagement. He opened with it before the statement that followed, as an indication that the abandonment for the sake of Allah, the Exalted, and His good pleasure does not distress him. Part of Ibrahim's forbearance was that his parting from his father was tempered with kindness in his dealings with him at the last moment.

Al-Salam (peace) here means al-salamah (safety). "ʿAlā" (upon) is used for the figurative sense of elevation, which is establishment. This is a word of greeting and honour, and it was mentioned earlier at the words of the Exalted, ﴿And peace be upon him the day he was born﴾ [Maryam: 15]. He showed his eagerness for his father's guidance by saying, ﴿I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord﴾, meaning I will ask Him to forgive you this disbelief, by Allah guiding him to monotheism so that He forgives him the past association (shirk), since Ibrahim had not received a prohibition from Allah against seeking forgiveness for a polytheist. This is the apparent meaning of the words of the Exalted, ﴿And the request of forgiveness of Ibrahim for his father was only due to a promise he had made to him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 114]. His seeking forgiveness for him is what is related in the words of the Exalted, ﴿and forgive my father, for indeed he was of those who are astray﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 86]. The clause "I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord" is a resumed (independent) sentence, and the sign of the future together with the present-tense verb indicates that he will repeat the seeking of forgiveness in the future. The clause ﴿Indeed, He has ever been gracious to me﴾ is a justification for what the promise of seeking forgiveness contains of hope for forgiveness, in response to Ibrahim's supplication that Allah grant his father success in monotheism and rejection of association.

Page 122

Al-hafiyy: one who is exceedingly kind and gentle. It was discussed earlier in Surah al-A'raf at the words of the Exalted, ﴿They ask you as if you were well-informed about it﴾ [al-A'raf: 187].

The clause "And I will leave you" is conjoined to the clause "I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord." That is, the seeking of forgiveness occurs in the future, while my leaving you occurs now, since the present tense is often used for the present. Ibrahim expressed his resolve to leave them, and that he would not hesitate in this nor grieve over it when it is for the sake of Allah, the Exalted. This is what is related in the words of the Exalted, ﴿And he said, "Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me"﴾ [al-Saffat: 99]. He had indeed departed from the land of the Kaldanis, resolved to join al-Sham, according to the command of Allah, the Exalted.

Ibrahim saw that his abandoning of his father would not suffice, since the rest of the people held his father's opinion, so he decided to abandon them all; for this reason he said to him, "and I will leave you."

The pronoun of the plural addressees refers to Ibrahim and his people, treating them as though they were present in that gathering, since his father is one of them and their matter is one; or this statement was made in the presence of a group of them.

The idols were conjoined to the pronoun of the people, to indicate his hostility toward those idols, declaring the change of the evil.

He expressed the idols by way of the relative construction in the words ﴿and what you invoke other than Allah﴾, to hint at the reason for the construction of the predicate and the cause of his leaving them and their idols: that those idols are worshipped other than Allah and that the people worship them; therefore this is the reason for his leaving them and their idols.

Al-du'a' (invocation) means worship, because it entails invoking the one worshipped.

He added to the declaration of leaving their idols the declaration that he invokes Allah, as a precaution against their supposing that he intended merely to abandon worshipping their idols, so perhaps

Page 123

they would be content with his refraining from them; therefore he made clear to them that, on the contrary, he invokes Allah, whom they do not worship.

Allah is referred to by the description of lordship, attached to the pronoun of his own self, to indicate his singling out from among them in worshipping Allah, the Exalted; He is his Lord alone among them. So the idafah here conveys the meaning of relative restriction, together with the pride in Allah's lordship over him and the honouring of himself by that. The clause ﴿perhaps I will not be in invocation to my Lord unhappy﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of "and I invoke," meaning hoping that I will not be in invocation to my Lord unhappy. Its meaning was discussed earlier at the words of the Exalted, ﴿And I have never been, in my invocation to You, my Lord, unhappy﴾ [Maryam: 4] in this surah. In his declaring this hope in their midst there is an implicit reproach that they are unhappy through the invocation of their gods.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verses 49–50:

﴿So when he had withdrawn from them and from what they worshipped besides Allah, We gave him Isaac and Jacob, and We made each of them a prophet﴾ ﴿And We gave them of Our mercy, and We granted them a tongue of truthfulness, exalted﴾.

The mention of his withdrawing from them has been omitted, after the mention of his resolve to do so, for brevity in speech, because it is known that one such as him does not resolve upon a matter without carrying out his resolve, and because it suffices to mention what followed from it, namely that his resolve became an event that had already occurred, and its recompense from his Lord was already realized. For when he withdrew from his father and his people and felt lonely through that separation, Allah granted him offspring with whom he could find companionship: He gave him Isaac his son, and Jacob, his son's son, and made both of them prophets. And consider this a great honour for him in the sight of his Lord.

Allah's recompense to Abraham was not limited to granting him Isaac and Jacob, since there is nothing in the text that requires restriction, for he had also been granted Ishmael, and his granting of him appeared before the appearance of the granting of Isaac. All of this came after he had withdrawn from his people.

The reason the verse mentions Isaac and Jacob without mentioning Ishmael, saying "We gave him Ishmael and Isaac and Jacob," is that when Abraham withdrew from his people, he left with his wife Sarah, his cousin. She too had withdrawn from her people, out of pleasure toward her Lord and her husband. So Allah mentioned the gift that encompassed both Abraham and his wife, namely that He granted them Isaac and, after him, Jacob. And because this gift was a compensation for Abraham for parting from his father and his people, it was a gift of those who would keep company with Abraham and be a comfort to him, and they are Isaac and Jacob. As for Ishmael, Allah willed that he be far from Abraham in Mecca, so that he would be the neighbour of the House of Allah. Indeed, that neighbourhood is greater than the neighbourhood of Isaac and Jacob, their father.

Ishmael was mentioned separately, specifically, after this, and similar to it is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And remember Our servants Abraham, Isaac and Jacob﴾ [Sad: 45], then He said ﴿And remember Ishmael﴾ [Sad: 48] in Surat Sad. In the verses of al-Saffat He said ﴿And he said: Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [al-Saffat: 99] ﴿My Lord, grant me [a son] of the righteous﴾ [al-Saffat: 100] ﴿So We gave him good tidings of a forbearing boy﴾ [al-Saffat: 101], up to His saying (﴿And We gave him good tidings of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾ [al-Saffat: 112]). So Ishmael was mentioned there following His saying ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [al-Saffat: 99], since he is the one intended by the forbearing boy.

What is meant by the gift here is the decreeing of what was already in eternity with Allah, for the increase of Isaac and Jacob came some time after Abraham's departure, after he had settled in the land of Canaan and after he had passed through Egypt and returned from it. Likewise the increase of Ishmael came some time after his departure and after he had passed through Egypt, as is recorded in the hadith and in the Torah. Or it may be that the granting of Isaac and Jacob is narrated in the past tense relative to the time of the Qur'an's revelation, as an indication that this was his recompense for his sincerity.

The point in mentioning Jacob is that Abraham saw him as a grandson and was delighted by him, for Jacob was born fifteen years before Abraham's death, and that from Jacob arose a great nation.

The particle (lamma) is a particle of existence for existence, meaning it requires the existence of its response because of the existence of its condition. It may be that there is an interval between them, and then it indicates mere causality without specifying a time, as is the case here.

The pronoun in (lahum) refers to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, peace be upon them. The (min) in His saying ﴿And from their offspring is one who does good﴾ [al-Saffat: 113] is either a particle of partiality, a qualifier of an omitted noun indicated by "We granted," meaning "granted from Our mercy." Or it is a noun meaning "some" by interpretation, as was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿And among the people are those who say: We believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8] in Surat al-Baqarah. Although the grammarians did not establish for the word min a noun usage as they established it for the words kaf, 'an and 'ala, some instances of its usage require it, as al-Taftazani stated in his gloss on the Kashshaf, and 'Abd al-Hakim affirmed it. On this basis, min is in the accusative position as the object of the verb "We granted," meaning "We granted them some of Our mercy," and this is prophethood, since it is a mercy to them and to those to whom they were sent.

The description of "lisan" with "sidq" (truthfulness) is a description by a verbal noun.

The connection between the mention of Abraham and Jacob led to the mention of Moses at this point, because he was the most honoured prophet among the descendants of Isaac and Jacob. The discussion of the phrase *wadhkur* ("and mention") and of *innahu kana* ("indeed he was") is the same as the discussion of their counterparts in the mention of Abraham, except that the clause here is not parenthetical (*mu'tarida*) but is simply a resumption (*istcombining: isti'nāf*, a new independent sentence).

The majority of readers (*al-Jumhur*) read *mukhlisan* with a kasra on the *lam*, from *akhlasa* (intransitive), when sincerity is his attribute. Sincerity (*al-ikhlas*) in a matter means performing it without being mixed with negligence, laxity or leniency. It is derived from *al-khulus*, which means purity and the absence of mixture. What is meant here is sincerity in what is his task, which is the messengership, as indicated by the context.

Ḥamzah, ʿĀṣim, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read it with a fatḥa on the *lam*, from *akhlasahu*, meaning that He chose him.

[p. 128]

Moses is singled out with the title *al-mukhlis* on both readings, because this is his distinguishing quality. He was sincere in calling to God, so he made light of the greatest tyrant, Pharaoh, and debated with him as an equal debates an equal, as God related of him in His saying in Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ: ﴿He said: Did we not raise you among us as a child, and you remained among us for years of your life?﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 18] ﴿And you did your deed that you did, and you were of the ungrateful﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 19], up to His saying ﴿He said: Even if I bring you something clear?﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 29]. Likewise is what God related of him in His saying ﴿He said: My Lord, because of what You have blessed me with, I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 17]. Thus sincerity in discharging the trust of God, may He be exalted, was his distinction.

Also, because God chose him to speak with directly before He sent the angel with revelation to him, he was sincere (*mukhlaṣan*) in that respect, that is, chosen (*muṣṭafan*), because that is his distinction. God, may He be exalted, said ﴿And I have made you for Myself﴾ [Ṭāhā: 41]. The description of Moses combines that he is a messenger and a prophet. *Nabiyyan* is coordinated with *rasūlan*, even though *al-rasūl*, in the technical sense (*al-maʿnā al-sharʿī*), is more specific than *al-nabī*. This is because the messenger is one sent with revelation from God to convey it to the people, so every messenger is necessarily a prophet. As for the prophet, he is one who is informed (*al-munabbaʾ*) by revelation from God, even if he is not commanded to convey it. If he is not commanded to convey, he is a prophet but not a messenger. So the combination of the two here is for emphasis of the attribute, indicating that his messengership reached a strong level. Thus his saying *nabiyyan* is an emphasis of the attribute *rasūlan*.

The variant readings concerning the word *nabiyyan* were mentioned earlier when discussing Abraham.

The clause *wa-nādaynāhu* is coordinated with the clause *innahu kāna mukhlaṣan*, so it is, like it, a new sentence.

*Al-nidāʾ* is speech indicating a request for attention. Its original meaning is raising the voice to make a distant person hear, and then it is applied, by metonymy (*majāz mursal*), to requesting someone's attention. From it comes ﴿When it is called for prayer on the day of Friday﴾ [al-Jumuʿah: 9]. It is derived from *al-nadā*, with a fatḥa on the *nūn* and short vowel, meaning the carrying distance of a sound. Its verb is only heard in the form *mufāʿalah*, not because an action occurs from two sides, but because the *mufāʿalah* form expresses intensity (*al-mubālagha*). This was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿The likeness of one who calls to what hears nothing except a call and a cry﴾ [al-Baqarah: 171] in Sūrat al-Baqarah, and at His saying ﴿Our Lord, indeed we heard a caller calling to faith﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 193] in Āl ʿImrān. This *nidāʾ* is the speech directed to him from God, may He be exalted. God, may He be exalted, said ﴿I have chosen you above the people by My messages and by My speech﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 144] in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf. Its nature has been investigated there, and at His saying ﴿until he hears the speech of God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 6] in Sūrat Barāʾah.

*Al-Ṭūr* is the mountain lying between the lands of al-Shām and Egypt, and it is said that it is called Ṭūr Sīnāʾ. Its *jānib* (side) is its lower region. Describing it as *al-Ayman* (the right) is because it is the one on the right of someone facing the rising of the sun, since the direction of the sun is the direction by which people fix the regions.

*Al-taqrīb* (bringing near) originally means placing something in a place of nearness, and it is the opposite of distance. Here the figurative nearness is meant, which is revelation. So His saying *najiyyan* is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun of *Mūsā*, and it is a circumstantial clause emphasising the meaning of bringing near.

*Najiyy* is a *faʿīl* in the sense of a *mafʿūl* (passive), from *al-munājāh*, which is secret conversation. The speech which God did not address to anyone like it, nor disclosed to anyone, is likened to secret conversation. The pattern *faʿīl* in the sense of *mafʿūl* comes from a verb with an added letter by dropping the letter of augmentation, like *jalīs* (companion), *nadīm* (boon-companion) and *raḍīʿ* (nursling).

God, may He be exalted, said ﴿I have chosen you above the people by My messages and by My speech﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 144] in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf. Its nature has been investigated there, and at His saying ﴿until he hears the speech of God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 6] in Sūrat Barāʾah.

*Al-Ṭūr* is the mountain lying between the lands of al-Shām and Egypt, and it is said that it is called Ṭūr Sīnāʾ. Its *jānib* (side) is its lower region. Describing it as *al-Ayman* (the right) is because it is the one on the right of someone facing the rising of the sun, since the direction of the sun is the direction by which people fix the regions.

*Al-taqrīb* (bringing near) originally means placing something in a place of nearness, and it is the opposite of distance. Here the figurative nearness is meant, which is revelation. So His saying *najiyyan* is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun of *Mūsā*, and it is a circumstantial clause emphasising the meaning of bringing near.

*Najiyy* is a *faʿīl* in the sense of a *mafʿūl* (passive), from *al-munājāh*, which is secret conversation. The speech which God did not address to anyone like it, nor disclosed to anyone, is likened to secret conversation. The pattern *faʿīl* in the sense of *mafʿūl* comes from a verb with an added letter by dropping the letter of augmentation, like *jalīs* (companion), *nadīm* (boon-companion) and *raḍīʿ* (nursling).

As for the meaning of God granting him his brother: God strengthened him with him and helped him with him, since He made him a prophet and commanded him to accompany him in the call, because there was an impediment in Moses' tongue, while Aaron was eloquent of tongue. So he would speak on Moses' behalf with what he wished to convey, and he would be entrusted with the affairs of the community. That grant was made a mercy from God because God showed mercy to Moses when He made easy for him a brother of eloquent tongue, and completed him by praise, so that he would know what Moses meant by what he conveyed from God, may He be exalted. Aaron is not described as a messenger, since God did not send him, but He made him a conveyor on behalf of Moses. As for His saying (﴿So say: indeed we are two messengers of your Lord﴾ [Ṭāhā: 47]), it is by the figure of *taghlīb* (predominance of one term over another).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verses 54–55:

﴿And mention in the Book Isma'il. Indeed, he was true to his promise, and he was a messenger and a prophet.﴾ ﴿He used to enjoin his family to pray and to give zakat, and he was pleasing to his Lord.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verses 56–57:

﴿And mention in the Book Idris. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a prophet.﴾ ﴿And We raised him to a high station.﴾

Idris (إدْرِيسُ): a name made a proper name for the grandfather of Nuh (Noah), who is called Enoch (أخْنُوخ) in the Torah. Nuh is the son of Lamak, son of Matushalah, son of Enoch. Perhaps his name among the genealogists of the Arabs is Idris, or the Qur'an named him thus, as a name derived from study (al-dars), because of what will come shortly. His name among the Greeks is Hermes (هَرْمَسُ), and it is claimed that he is called thus among the ancient Egyptians as well. The correct view is that his name among the Egyptians is Tut, or Tuhuti, or Tuhuti, these being dialectal pronunciations of his name.

Ibn al-'Ibri mentioned in his history that Idris was called among the ancient Greeks Trismegistus (طُرَيْسَمَجِيسَطِيسَ). Its meaning in their language is "thrice-great in teaching," because he described God with three essential attributes, which are existence, wisdom, and life. End of quotation.

Page 131
The closeness of the first letters of this name to the letters of Idris is not hidden. Perhaps the Arabs shortened the name because of its length, so they confined themselves to its first part with a modification.

Idris was a prophet. In the fifth chapter of the Book of Genesis: "And Enoch walked with God."

It has been said: he was the first to establish for mankind the building of cities, the foundations of knowledge, the foundations of education, and the first to establish writing, the science of calculation by the stars, the rules of the motion of the planets, and the composition of elements by fire, for which reason the science of alchemy (al-kīmiyā') was attributed to him; and he was the first to teach people sewing. Thus he was the origin of those who established sciences, civilization, and rational systems. The reason for his being named Idris in the Qur'an is that a name was derived for him from study (dars), a form suitable for foreign proper names; for this reason he was denied declension (ṣarf), although his letters derive from an Arabic root, just as Iblis was denied declension, and just as Talut (Saul) was denied declension.

The disagreement of the readers (qurrā') concerning the word (نَبِيئًا) was mentioned earlier, at the mention of Ibrahim.

As for His saying (﴿And We raised him to a high station﴾): the majority of the exegetes say it is a metaphorical elevation. What is meant is elevation of rank, because of the knowledge he was given, by which he surpassed those before him. This was transmitted from al-Hasan, and Abu Muslim al-Isfahani held it. A group said: it is a literal elevation to the heavens. In the fifth chapter of the Book of Genesis: "And Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him." According to this view, his elevation is like the elevation of 'Isa (peace be upon him). The more evident view is that this took place after the taking of his soul and the turning of his body into spirit (rawhanah).

It is related of him that he remained thirteen years without sleeping or eating until he became spiritual, and then he was raised. As for the hadith of the Night Journey, there is no proof in it for this view, because it mentions several other prophets who were found in the heavens. It occurs in the hadith of Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah concerning the Night Journey of the Prophet

Page 132
- ﷺ - to the heavens, that "he found Idris in the heaven, and when he greeted him he said: 'Welcome, the righteous brother and the righteous prophet.'" From this it is taken that Idris was not a progenitor of the Prophet (ﷺ), since he did not say "the righteous son." But there is no proof in that, for he may have said it considering the brotherhood of monotheism and preferred it over the bond of kinship, and that was part of his wisdom. Moreover, it is possible that this was an error by the narrator, for that phrase is not established in the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah in Sahih al-Bukhari. Al-Bukhari, in the chapters on the prophets, definitively stated that Idris was the grandfather of Nuh or the grandfather of his father. This indicates that he did not see in his saying "welcome, the righteous brother" anything that precludes him being a forefather of the Prophet (ﷺ).

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verse 58:**

﴿Those are the ones on whom Allah bestowed favour from among the prophets, of the descendants of Adam, and of those whom We carried with Noah, and of the descendants of Abraham and Israel, and of those whom We guided and chose. When the verses of the Most Merciful were recited to them, they fell down in prostration and weeping.﴾

The sentence is a resumptive sentence (istinaf ibtida'i, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic). The demonstrative *ulā'ika* ("those") refers back to those mentioned from His words ﴿The mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zakariyya﴾ [Maryam: 2] up to this point. Using the demonstrative rather than a pronoun serves to draw attention to the fact that those being pointed to deserve what is mentioned after the demonstrative, because of the qualities mentioned along with them. That is, they were worthy of Allah's blessing upon them, of being among those guided and chosen, and of deserving their love for Allah, the Exalted, and their exaltation of Him.

Page 133

What is mentioned after the demonstrative is the substance of His words *"Allah bestowed favour upon them"* and His words ﴿and of those whom We guided and chose﴾. This is the best reward for the deeds they had done before, and for what was given to them of the distinctions of prophethood, truthfulness (*al-siddiqiyya*), and the like. Although these are blessings, guidance and choosing, this verse has added to them by attributing these gifts to Allah, the Exalted, as an honouring of them. That honouring is itself the reward for them, since nothing is greater for the one being rewarded than the honouring of him.

The majority of readers (*al-Jumhur*) read *min al-nabiyyīn* with two *yā'*s after the single letter *bā'*. Nafi' alone read it with a *hamza* after the *bā'*.

The clause ﴿when the verses of the Most Merciful were recited to them﴾ is a resumptive clause showing their thankfulness for the blessings of Allah upon them, and their drawing near to Him through humility before Him, by prostrating when His verses are recited and by weeping.
The weeping meant here is that which arises from the soul being moved by a mixture of reverence and fear.

*Sujjadan* is the plural of *sājid* (prostrating), and *bukiyyan* is the plural of *bākin* (weeping). The first is on the pattern *fu''al*, like *'udhdhal*. The second has the pattern *fu'ūl*, the plural of *fā'il*, like *qawmun qu'ūd* ("a people sitting"). This pattern occurs because its verb is *bakā yabkī*, so its root form was *bukūy*. When the *wāw* and the *yā'* came together and one of them was preceded by a sukun, the *wāw* was changed into a *yā'* and merged into the *yā'*, and the middle radical was given a vowel suited to the *yā'*. This pattern is attested (*samā'ī*, i.e. established by usage) in the plural of *fā'il* and similar forms.

This verse is one of the places of prostration in the Qur'an that are reported from the Prophet (ﷺ), following those prophets in prostrating when reciting the Qur'an. They prostrated often when reciting the verses of Allah that were revealed to them, and we prostrate, following them, when reciting the verses that have been revealed to us. He praised their prostration, intending that we imitate them as far as we are able, while we are engaged in mentioning their conduct. The Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated at this verse and established this practice for his community.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verses 59–63:

﴿So there succeeded them a generation who neglected the prayer and followed their desires; so they will meet with error.﴾ ﴿Except for one who repents, believes, and does righteousness; those will enter Paradise and will not be wronged at all.﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, which the Most Merciful has promised His servants in the unseen. Indeed, His promise is ever to be fulfilled.﴾ ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk, but only "Peace." And they will have their provision therein morning and evening.﴾ ﴿That is the Paradise which We cause to inherit from Our servants whoever was fearing (of Allah).﴾

This is a consequence of the praise of them: a reflection and a censure directed at a group of their descendants who did not follow the righteous example of their forefathers, and they are the ones meant by "al-khalf" (the later generation).

Al-khalf, with a sukun on the lam, means the bad offspring, and with a fatha on the lam, the good offspring. It was discussed earlier at His saying (﴿So there succeeded them a generation who inherited the Scripture﴾ [al-A'raf: 169]) in Surat al-A'raf. Here it includes all the nations that went astray, because they trace their lineage back to Idris, the grandfather of Nuh, since they are of the descendants of Nuh; and they also trace back to Ibrahim, so some of them are linked to him through the offspring of Isma'il, and they are the Arabs, and some of them are linked to him through the offspring of Ya'qub, and they are the Children of Israel.

Page 135
The phrase "min ba'dihim" (after them) encompasses many generations and eras; it is not a restrictive condition, since a successor (khalaf) can only come after its origin, but it was mentioned to evoke the passing away of the righteous.

Al-id'a' (neglect) is a metaphor for negligence, by likening it to the neglect of a precious possession. They neglected the worship of Allah and followed their desires, so they did not oppose what their souls inclined towards, even if it was corruption. His saying (﴿Indeed, We do not allow to be lost the reward of one who does good work﴾ [al-Kahf: 30]) in Surat al-Kahf has already been mentioned.

As for al-salat (the prayer), it is the worship of Allah alone.

These two descriptions comprehend the various kinds of disbelief and wickedness. Associating partners with Allah is a neglect of the prayer, because it is a turning away from submission to Allah the Exalted; thus the polytheists completely neglected the prayer, as He the Exalted said (﴿They said, "We were not of those who prayed"﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 43]). And association is following desires, because the polytheists followed the worship of idols merely out of desire, without any evidence; and these are the ones intended here. Those other than the polytheists, such as the Jews and Christians, neglected prayers and followed desires they had invented, and all of this is encompassed by the name "al-ghayy."

Al-ghayy: error. It is also applied to evil, just as its opposite, al-rushd (right guidance), is applied to good, as in His saying (﴿Is it evil that is intended for those on earth, or does their Lord intend for them right guidance?﴾ [al-Jinn: 10]) and His saying (﴿Say, "I possess not for you any harm or right guidance."﴾ [al-Jinn: 21]). So it is permissible that the meaning is: "they will meet the recompense of their error," like His saying (﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ [al-Furqan: 68]) regarding the recompense of sins. Al-ghayy was mentioned at His saying (﴿And their brothers extend them in error﴾ [al-A'raf: 202]) and His saying (﴿And if they see the way of error, they will take it as a way﴾ [al-A'raf: 146]), both in Surat al-A'raf. The indication of this is its contrast with their opposites in His saying (﴿those will enter Paradise﴾).

Page 136
The particle "sawfa" (will) indicates that their encountering error will recur in future times, as an intensification of their threat and a warning to them against persisting in that.

His saying (﴿those will enter Paradise﴾): the demonstrative was used regarding them to honour them and to alert them, to encourage them to repent from disbelief. The present tense, which indicates the present state, was used to show that they will not be delayed in the recompense. Al-Jannah (Paradise) is a proper name for the abode of reward and bliss. In it there are many gardens, as reported in the hadith: "Is it one Paradise? Indeed, it is many gardens." The word "zulm" (wronging) here means diminution, injustice, and delay, as in His saying (﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short therefrom in anything﴾ [al-Kahf: 33]) in Surat al-Kahf.

"Shay'an" (anything) is a noun meaning an entity or existent thing, and the intended meaning is not the verbal noun of wronging. Mentioning "shay'an" in the context of negation indicates the negation of every individual instance of diminution, injustice, and delay, so the negation of strong diminution is known by implication, to repel what might stir in their souls of brokenness after faith, under the assumption that prior disbelief lowers the quality of their final destination.

"Jannat" is a substitute for "al-Jannah." It is given in the plural form of "Jannat" although the substituted noun is singular, because it includes many gardens, as you know; and it is a substitute of full correspondence (badal mutabiq), not a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal).

"'Adn": permanence and abiding, i.e., gardens of eternal abode. Describing them with (﴿which the Most Merciful has promised His servants﴾) increases their honour and beautification. In this there is an incorporation (idmaj) of good tidings to the believers who came before, within the promise to those called to faith.

"Al-ghayb" (the unseen) is a verbal noun of "ghaba" (to be absent), so everything absent from observation is unseen. It was discussed at His saying (﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3]) at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

Page 137
The "ba'" in "bil-ghayb" is for time (zarfiyyah), i.e., He promised them these in times absent from them, that is, in eternity when He created it for them. He the Exalted said (﴿prepared for the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133]). In this is an indication that although it is hidden from them in this world, it is already prepared for them.

The clause (﴿Indeed, His promise is ever to be fulfilled﴾) is a justification for the clause (﴿which the Most Merciful has promised His servants in the unseen﴾) regarding "those will enter Paradise," as a promise from Allah that is certain to occur. This is a confirmation of the good tidings.

"Al-wa'd" (the promise) here is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle. It follows the pattern of "kasa," so Allah promised the righteous believers the gardens of 'Adn, and the gardens are promised to them by their Lord.

"Ma'tiyy" (that which is come to): that to which another comes. The verb "ityan" (coming) has been used metaphorically for the attainment of the awaited desired thing, likening one who obtains a thing after striving for it to one who walks to a place until he arrives at it, and likening the obtained thing to the intended place. So in His saying (ma'tiyyan) there is an allegorical image (tamthiliyyah), of which only one of the two configurations is mentioned, and it necessarily implies the other, since what is come to must have someone who comes.

The clause (﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk﴾) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from "His servants." "Al-laghw" is superfluous speech and what has no benefit in it. Its negation is a kinaya (metonymy) for the absence of even the slightest disturbances in Paradise, as He the Exalted said (﴿You will not hear therein any idle talk﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 11]), and a kinaya for making the recompense of the believers in Paradise the opposite of what they encountered in this world of harm and idle talk from the polytheists.

His saying "illa salaman" (except "peace") is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), and it is a metaphor from emphasizing a thing by means of something resembling its opposite, like the saying of al-Nabighah:

Page 138

"And there is no fault in them, except that their swords have notches from the clashing of battalions."
That is, rather, they will hear "salam" (peace). He the Exalted said (﴿And their greeting therein is "Peace"﴾ [Yunus: 10]) and said (﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk or sinful speech, except the saying "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25–26]).

"Rizq" (provision) is food. The nominal sentence was used to indicate the stability and continuity of that, so it conveys continuous recurrence, which is more specific than the recurrence conveyed by the present-tense verb and more abundant. The fronting of the adverbial phrase is for concern with their affair, and the attachment of "rizq" to the pronoun "hum" is for added exclusivity.

"Al-bukrah" is the first half of the day, and "al-'ashiyy" is the last half; combining them is a kinaya for the entirety of time, i.e., their provision is unlimited and unrestricted, but whenever they wish. For this reason, the night was not mentioned.

The clause (﴿That is the Paradise﴾) is an independent initiatory sentence. The demonstrative is for added distinction, as an honouring of its status, and the relative clause with its complement was attached to it as a description, to honour the righteous and to indicate that they are the people of Paradise, as He the Exalted said (﴿prepared for the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133]).

"Nurith" means "we make an heir," i.e., we give the inheritance. The true sense of inheritance is the transfer of a relative's property to his relative after his death, because he is the most entitled of people to his property; so it is a transfer conditioned by a state. It is here used metaphorically for a reward stored up for its recipient, likening it to the inherited property that eventually passes to its heir.

The majority read "nurith" with a sukun on the waw after a damma and a light ra'. Ruways from Ya'qub read "nuwarrith" with a fatha on the waw and a shadda on the ra', from the doubled form "warratha."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verses 59–63:
