The majority read "nurith" with a sukun on the waw after a damma and a light ra'. Ruways from Ya'qub read "nuwarrith" with a fatha on the waw and a shadda on the ra', from the doubled form "warratha."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verses 59–63:

﴿So there succeeded them a generation who neglected the prayer and followed their desires; so they will meet with error.﴾ ﴿Except for one who repents, believes, and does righteousness; those will enter Paradise and will not be wronged at all.﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, which the Most Merciful has promised His servants in the unseen. Indeed, His promise is ever to be fulfilled.﴾ ﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk, but only "Peace." And they will have their provision therein morning and evening.﴾ ﴿That is the Paradise which We cause to inherit from Our servants whoever was fearing (of Allah).﴾

This is a consequence of the praise of them: a reflection and a censure directed at a group of their descendants who did not follow the righteous example of their forefathers, and they are the ones meant by "al-khalf" (the later generation).

Al-khalf, with a sukun on the lam, means the bad offspring, and with a fatha on the lam, the good offspring. It was discussed earlier at His saying (﴿So there succeeded them a generation who inherited the Scripture﴾ [al-A'raf: 169]) in Surat al-A'raf. Here it includes all the nations that went astray, because they trace their lineage back to Idris, the grandfather of Nuh, since they are of the descendants of Nuh; and they also trace back to Ibrahim, so some of them are linked to him through the offspring of Isma'il, and they are the Arabs, and some of them are linked to him through the offspring of Ya'qub, and they are the Children of Israel.

Page 135
The phrase "min ba'dihim" (after them) encompasses many generations and eras; it is not a restrictive condition, since a successor (khalaf) can only come after its origin, but it was mentioned to evoke the passing away of the righteous.

Al-id'a' (neglect) is a metaphor for negligence, by likening it to the neglect of a precious possession. They neglected the worship of Allah and followed their desires, so they did not oppose what their souls inclined towards, even if it was corruption. His saying (﴿Indeed, We do not allow to be lost the reward of one who does good work﴾ [al-Kahf: 30]) in Surat al-Kahf has already been mentioned.

As for al-salat (the prayer), it is the worship of Allah alone.

These two descriptions comprehend the various kinds of disbelief and wickedness. Associating partners with Allah is a neglect of the prayer, because it is a turning away from submission to Allah the Exalted; thus the polytheists completely neglected the prayer, as He the Exalted said (﴿They said, "We were not of those who prayed"﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 43]). And association is following desires, because the polytheists followed the worship of idols merely out of desire, without any evidence; and these are the ones intended here. Those other than the polytheists, such as the Jews and Christians, neglected prayers and followed desires they had invented, and all of this is encompassed by the name "al-ghayy."

Al-ghayy: error. It is also applied to evil, just as its opposite, al-rushd (right guidance), is applied to good, as in His saying (﴿Is it evil that is intended for those on earth, or does their Lord intend for them right guidance?﴾ [al-Jinn: 10]) and His saying (﴿Say, "I possess not for you any harm or right guidance."﴾ [al-Jinn: 21]). So it is permissible that the meaning is: "they will meet the recompense of their error," like His saying (﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ [al-Furqan: 68]) regarding the recompense of sins. Al-ghayy was mentioned at His saying (﴿And their brothers extend them in error﴾ [al-A'raf: 202]) and His saying (﴿And if they see the way of error, they will take it as a way﴾ [al-A'raf: 146]), both in Surat al-A'raf. The indication of this is its contrast with their opposites in His saying (﴿those will enter Paradise﴾).

Page 136
The particle "sawfa" (will) indicates that their encountering error will recur in future times, as an intensification of their threat and a warning to them against persisting in that.

His saying (﴿those will enter Paradise﴾): the demonstrative was used regarding them to honour them and to alert them, to encourage them to repent from disbelief. The present tense, which indicates the present state, was used to show that they will not be delayed in the recompense. Al-Jannah (Paradise) is a proper name for the abode of reward and bliss. In it there are many gardens, as reported in the hadith: "Is it one Paradise? Indeed, it is many gardens." The word "zulm" (wronging) here means diminution, injustice, and delay, as in His saying (﴿Each of the two gardens brought forth its produce and did not fall short therefrom in anything﴾ [al-Kahf: 33]) in Surat al-Kahf.

"Shay'an" (anything) is a noun meaning an entity or existent thing, and the intended meaning is not the verbal noun of wronging. Mentioning "shay'an" in the context of negation indicates the negation of every individual instance of diminution, injustice, and delay, so the negation of strong diminution is known by implication, to repel what might stir in their souls of brokenness after faith, under the assumption that prior disbelief lowers the quality of their final destination.

"Jannat" is a substitute for "al-Jannah." It is given in the plural form of "Jannat" although the substituted noun is singular, because it includes many gardens, as you know; and it is a substitute of full correspondence (badal mutabiq), not a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal).

"'Adn": permanence and abiding, i.e., gardens of eternal abode. Describing them with (﴿which the Most Merciful has promised His servants﴾) increases their honour and beautification. In this there is an incorporation (idmaj) of good tidings to the believers who came before, within the promise to those called to faith.

"Al-ghayb" (the unseen) is a verbal noun of "ghaba" (to be absent), so everything absent from observation is unseen. It was discussed at His saying (﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3]) at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

Page 137
The "ba'" in "bil-ghayb" is for time (zarfiyyah), i.e., He promised them these in times absent from them, that is, in eternity when He created it for them. He the Exalted said (﴿prepared for the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133]). In this is an indication that although it is hidden from them in this world, it is already prepared for them.

The clause (﴿Indeed, His promise is ever to be fulfilled﴾) is a justification for the clause (﴿which the Most Merciful has promised His servants in the unseen﴾) regarding "those will enter Paradise," as a promise from Allah that is certain to occur. This is a confirmation of the good tidings.

"Al-wa'd" (the promise) here is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle. It follows the pattern of "kasa," so Allah promised the righteous believers the gardens of 'Adn, and the gardens are promised to them by their Lord.

"Ma'tiyy" (that which is come to): that to which another comes. The verb "ityan" (coming) has been used metaphorically for the attainment of the awaited desired thing, likening one who obtains a thing after striving for it to one who walks to a place until he arrives at it, and likening the obtained thing to the intended place. So in His saying (ma'tiyyan) there is an allegorical image (tamthiliyyah), of which only one of the two configurations is mentioned, and it necessarily implies the other, since what is come to must have someone who comes.

The clause (﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk﴾) is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from "His servants." "Al-laghw" is superfluous speech and what has no benefit in it. Its negation is a kinaya (metonymy) for the absence of even the slightest disturbances in Paradise, as He the Exalted said (﴿You will not hear therein any idle talk﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 11]), and a kinaya for making the recompense of the believers in Paradise the opposite of what they encountered in this world of harm and idle talk from the polytheists.

His saying "illa salaman" (except "peace") is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), and it is a metaphor from emphasizing a thing by means of something resembling its opposite, like the saying of al-Nabighah:

Page 138

"And there is no fault in them, except that their swords have notches from the clashing of battalions."
That is, rather, they will hear "salam" (peace). He the Exalted said (﴿And their greeting therein is "Peace"﴾ [Yunus: 10]) and said (﴿They will not hear therein any idle talk or sinful speech, except the saying "Peace, peace"﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25–26]).

"Rizq" (provision) is food. The nominal sentence was used to indicate the stability and continuity of that, so it conveys continuous recurrence, which is more specific than the recurrence conveyed by the present-tense verb and more abundant. The fronting of the adverbial phrase is for concern with their affair, and the attachment of "rizq" to the pronoun "hum" is for added exclusivity.

"Al-bukrah" is the first half of the day, and "al-'ashiyy" is the last half; combining them is a kinaya for the entirety of time, i.e., their provision is unlimited and unrestricted, but whenever they wish. For this reason, the night was not mentioned.

The clause (﴿That is the Paradise﴾) is an independent initiatory sentence. The demonstrative is for added distinction, as an honouring of its status, and the relative clause with its complement was attached to it as a description, to honour the righteous and to indicate that they are the people of Paradise, as He the Exalted said (﴿prepared for the righteous﴾ [Al 'Imran: 133]).

"Nurith" means "we make an heir," i.e., we give the inheritance. The true sense of inheritance is the transfer of a relative's property to his relative after his death, because he is the most entitled of people to his property; so it is a transfer conditioned by a state. It is here used metaphorically for a reward stored up for its recipient, likening it to the inherited property that eventually passes to its heir.

The majority read "nurith" with a sukun on the waw after a damma and a light ra'. Ruways from Ya'qub read "nuwarrith" with a fatha on the waw and a shadda on the ra', from the doubled form "warratha."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verse 64:

Page 139
﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord. To Him belongs what is before us and what is behind us and what is between that. And your Lord is never forgetful.﴾ (

The placement of this verse here is unusual. The majority of exegetes said: the occasion of its revelation was that Jibril, peace be upon him, delayed for some days in descending to the Prophet ﷺ, and the Prophet wished that Jibril's visits to him would be more frequent than they were, so he said to Jibril: "Why do you not visit us more often than you do?" Then this was revealed: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ up to the end of the verse, that is, up to His saying "forgetful." This was narrated by al-Bukhari and al-Tirmidhi from Ibn 'Abbas. Its apparent meaning is that it is a narration, and it is the most authentic of what has been related regarding its occasion of revelation and the most fitting to its placement here. No attention should be paid to other statements regarding its occasion of revelation.

The meaning is: God commanded Jibril, peace be upon him, to say this statement in reply to him. So the composition is the composition of the Qur'an, with the implied reading: "And say: we do not descend except by the command of your Lord," that is, say, O Jibril. Thus this was an address to Jibril so that he would convey it to the Prophet ﷺ as Qur'an. The wa' (and) here conjoins the omitted verb of saying to the preceding speech, as a conjunction of one narrative upon another with a change of addressee, and God commanded His Messenger to recite it here, and because it was revealed to be part of the Qur'an.

There is no doubt that the Prophet ﷺ said that to Jibril, peace be upon him, at the conclusion of the stories of the prophets in this surah, so the verse was affixed at the point which the revelation of the Qur'an had reached. The pronoun refers to Jibril and the angels: God informed His Prophet, through the tongue of Jibril, that the descent of the angels occurs only by the command of God Most High, and they have no choice

Page 140
in descending and in meeting the messengers. God Most High said: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command﴾ [al-Anbiya': 27]. "Natanazzalu" is a synonym of "nanzilu," and the root meaning of tanazzul is to make an effort to descend. This was applied to the descent of the angels from the heaven to the earth because it is a rare descent and a departure from their world, so it is as if it were effortful. God Most High said: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein﴾ [al-Qadr: 4].
The lam in "lahu" indicates ownership, namely ownership of disposal.

By "what is before us" is meant what is in front of us; by "what is behind us," what is behind us; and by "what is between that," what was on their right and on their left, since what is on the right and on the left is between the front and the back. The intent is the encompassing of all directions. Since that is described as belonging to God, it is necessary that it means the created beings that are in those directions. So the statement is a metonymy by the relation of location (majaz mursal bi-'alaqat al-hulul), like ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. It thus encompasses all created beings and entails the generality of their states and dispositions, such as the descent with revelation. It also entails the generality of times: the future, the past, and the present, and "what is before us and what is behind us and what is between that" has been interpreted as referring to these. The clause ﴿And your Lord is never forgetful﴾, according to this interpretation, is part of the speech dictated to Jibril as a reply to the Prophet ﷺ. "Nasiyyan" is an intensive form from "nasiya," meaning one who forgets much or intensely. 

Forgetting is heedlessness regarding the timing of things at their appointed times. Some have interpreted it here as "one who abandons," that is, your Lord never abandons you.

According to this, the intensiveness is directed toward

Page 141
the length of the duration of forgetting. And if it is interpreted as meaning intense forgetting, then the intensiveness must be directed toward the aspect of the negation of forgetfulness with respect to God, that is, the establishment of the negation of forgetting, like the intensiveness in His saying ﴿and your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46]. Here it is a kinaya (allusion) for the comprehensiveness of God's knowledge, that is, our descent is by God's command in accordance with His knowledge and wisdom in that matter; we do not descend except by His command, and He does not command us to descend except when His knowledge and wisdom require that He command us to do so.

Abu Muslim and the author of al-Kashshaf allowed that this verse is part of the continuation of the report of the speech of the people of Paradise, with the implied verb "yaqulun" (they say) as a circumstantial clause (hal) from His saying "for whoever was righteous," that is: "And we do not descend in this Paradise except by the command of your Lord," etc. This is a good interpretation. According to this, the second-person address in "by the command of your Lord" is the address of every speaker to his interlocutor. This permission is based on the view that what was related from Ibn 'Abbas is an opinion of his regarding the interpretation of the verse, and following it is not mandatory.

According to this, the clause ﴿And your Lord is never forgetful﴾ is a statement from God Most High to His Messenger, as a concluding remark (tadhyil) to what precedes it; or it is from the speech of the people of Paradise, meaning: "And our Lord was never heedless of granting what He promised us."

صفحة ١٤٢

This is a resumptive sentence from the speech of Allah, Exalted, as its phrase "so worship Him" and what follows require. It serves as an appended conclusion to the speech that Gabriel was taught, which contains that the angels do not act except by the permission of their Lord, and that all their states are in His grip. This indicates the comprehensiveness of His, Exalted, control over all created beings. Then He based on this the command to the Messenger, peace be upon him, to worship Him, so the address has shifted to him.

"Lord of the heavens" is in the nominative as a predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), which is obligatorily omitted in the context in which someone is described with descriptions and then one wishes to single him out with another predicate. This omission is what al-Sakkaki (al-Sakkaki, the rhetorician) called the omission that follows usage, as in the verse of al-Sawli, or Ibn al-Zubayr (the z vowelled with a fatha and the b with a kasra):

"I will thank Amr if his death is delayed, for favours he did not bestow upon me, though they were great."

"A youth whose wealth is not withheld from his friend, nor does he display complaint when the sandal slips."

"The heavens" (al-samawat) means the higher worlds. "The earth" means the lower world. "What is between them" means the atmospheres and horizons. These three encompass all created beings.

The address in "so worship Him," "and be steadfast," and "do you know" is to the Prophet (ﷺ). The branching of the command to worship Him upon this is clearly appropriate, and from it arises a transition to emphasizing monotheism (tawhid) and denouncing association of partners (shirk).

Al-ištibar (اصطبار, steadfastness) means intense patience in the face of a difficult matter, since the form ifti'al (افتعال) comes to indicate the intensity of the action. The usual construction would be to govern ishtibar with the preposition "upon" (ʿala), as Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And enjoin your family to prayer and be steadfast in it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 132]. However, here it is governed by "for" (li-), because it is implicitly made to include the meaning of firmness, i.e., "be firm in worship," since worship has many levels involving striving against the self. Some of these may overcome some souls, so one is able to be steadfast in some acts of worship and not others. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said about the night prayer ('isha'): "It is the heaviest prayer upon the hypocrites." Therefore, when Allah commanded His Messenger to be steadfast in all worship, and it contains many kinds requiring firmness of resolve, the one who performs worship was treated as one who contends against his own self, so the verb was governed by "for," as one says: "Stand firm against your enemies."

The sentence ﴿Do you know any namesake for Him?﴾ stands in the position of a reason (ta'lil) for the command to worship Him and to be steadfast in it. The word samiyy (سَمِيّ, namesake) here is best taken to mean "one who equals" (al-musami), i.e., one who is equal to Him in all His affairs. Ibn 'Abbas explained it as "equal," derived from musamah (equality of height or rank), so it is fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active), but it is taken from the causative form (al-mazid), as in the verse of 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib:

"From Rayhana, the one who calls, the one who hears" (i.e., the one who makes hear).

Just as Allah, Exalted, is called al-Hakim (the Wise), i.e., the one who makes matters firm, so samiyy here means one who is equal in attributes, such that equality in attributes is like equality in rank.

The interrogative is a denial (inkari): there is no equal to Allah, Exalted, i.e., there is no one who rivals Him, i.e., who resembles Him, existing.

It is also said that samiyy means one who shares the same name, as in His words concerning Yahya: ﴿We have not made for him before any namesake﴾ [Maryam: 7]. The meaning would be: you do not know anyone with the same name "Allah," for the polytheists did not name any of their idols "Allah" with the definite article, but they say of each one of them "a god" (ilah). The absence of naming other existing exalted beings by His name is a metonymy for people's acknowledgment that there is no equal to Him in the attribute of creating, because the polytheists did not dare to claim creative power for their gods. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [Luqman: 25]. With this, the sentence is a reason for the command to single Him out in worship on this interpretation as well.

صفحة ١٤٣

The absence of knowledge of His namesake is a metonymy for the non-existence of any namesake for Him, because knowledge entails the existence of the known. When His equal is absent, there is no one other than Him who deserves worship.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verses 66–67:

﴿And man says, "When I have died, shall I then be brought forth alive?"﴾ ﴿Does man not remember that We created him before, when he was nothing?﴾

When his saying (﴿So worship Him and be patient in His worship﴾ [Maryam: 65]) included the refutation of the belief in associating partners with Him, it was fitting to move on to refuting one of the consequences of polytheism, namely the denial by the polytheists that resurrection after death will occur, so that the two roots of disbelief are completely undone. The conjunction waw therefore joins one narrative to another, and the use of the present tense verb "says" (yaqulu) is to bring to mind the state of this speech, in order to express wonder at its speaker, a wonder of denial.

By "man" (al-insan) is meant a group of people, as indicated by His saying after it, ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them﴾ [Maryam: 68]. Thus it refers to those whose saying this was, and they were the majority of those addressed by the Qur'an at the time of its first revelation. It is also possible that a qualifier has been omitted, i.e., "the disbelieving man," as the qualifier is omitted in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿who seizes every ship by force﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], meaning every sound ship. So this is like His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Does man think that We will not assemble his bones? Yes, [We are] Able to put together even his fingertips﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 3–4]. Likewise is the application of "people" (al-nas) to specifically the polytheists among them in many verses, such as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O people, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21], up to His saying ﴿then bring a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23]; that address is to the polytheists. It has also been said that the definiteness of "man" is for a specific known person. It is said that the speaker of this was Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and it is said: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah.

The interrogation in ﴿When I have died, shall I then be brought forth alive?﴾ is a denial of the certainty of the occurrence of resurrection. Therefore the sentence on which the denial is imposed is introduced with the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida'), which indicates the emphasis of the sentence in which it occurs; that is, he says: what you have affirmed of my being brought back to life in the future will not happen. The complement of "akhruju" (I will be brought forth) is omitted, i.e., "I will be brought forth from the grave." The lam of initiation has entered in His saying ﴿shall I surely be brought forth alive?﴾ upon the imperfect future tense, by the clear presence of the future particle (sawfa), and this is evidence for the view of Ibn Malik that the lam of initiation enters upon the imperfect verb intended for the future and does not restrict it to the present. It appears that, with the clear indicator present, there should be no dispute about its not restricting the imperfect to the present, even though al-Zamakhshari insisted on prohibiting it, and interpreted what is here as the lam being an added emphatic particle and not the lam of initiation, and he interpreted His saying ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied﴾ [al-Duha: 5] similarly by positing an omitted subject, i.e., "and indeed you, your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied," so that the lam does not enter upon the imperfect. All of that is artificial and there is no necessity for it.

The clause ﴿Does man not remember?﴾ is conjoined to the clause "man says," i.e., he says that, and among the rebuke against him is that he does not remember that We created him before his existence.

The interrogation is a denial and an expression of wonder at the heedlessness of the man who denies resurrection regarding his first creation.

The majority read ﴿a-wa-lā yadhkuru﴾ with a sukun on the dhal and a damma on the kaf, from dhikr (remembrance) with a damma on the dhal. Abu Ja'far read it with a fatha on the dhal and a shadda on the kaf, on the basis that its original form is yatadhakkaru, so the second ta' was changed to dhal because their articulation points are close.

Al-shay' (thing) is that which exists, i.e., We created him and he was not existing.

Qabl (before) is among the nouns that necessarily take an annexed complement. When the annexed complement is omitted and is regarded as an indefinite annexed complement, with no specific word previously mentioned for it, qabl is built on damma, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿To God belongs the command, before and after﴾ [al-Rum: 4]. The implied meaning is: We created him before every state he is in. The implied meaning in the verse of Surat al-Rum is: to God belongs the command before every event and after it. The meaning: a denial of the disbelievers who say this and do not remember the state of the first creation, for it is more wondrous to those who measure things by the customary norms, since bringing into existence from non-existence without a prior model is more wondrous and more conducive to disbelief than restoring existing things that had models. Yet their structures decayed and their compositions changed. This is an analogy based on what is witnessed, even though the Capable One regards both matters as equal.

The majority read ﴿a-wa-lā yadhkuru﴾ with a sukun on the dhal and a damma on the kaf, from dhikr (remembrance) with a damma on the dhal. Abu Ja'far read it with a fatha on the dhal and a shadda on the kaf, on the basis that its original form is yatadhakkaru, so the second ta' was changed to dhal because their articulation points are close.

Al-shay' (thing) is that which exists, i.e., We created him and he was not existing.

Qabl (before) is among the nouns that necessarily take an annexed complement. When the annexed complement is omitted and is regarded as an indefinite annexed complement, with no specific word previously mentioned for it, qabl is built on damma, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿To God belongs the command, before and after﴾ [al-Rum: 4]. The implied meaning is: We created him before every state he is in. The implied meaning in the verse of Surat al-Rum is: to God belongs the command before every event and after it. The meaning: a denial of the disbelievers who say this and do not remember the state of the first creation, for it is more wondrous to those who measure things by the customary norms, since bringing into existence from non-existence without a prior model is more wondrous and more conducive to disbelief than restoring existing things that had models. Yet their structures decayed and their compositions changed. This is an analogy based on what is witnessed, even though the Capable One regards both matters as equal.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verses 68–70:

﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them and the devils, then We will surely bring them around Hell, on their knees.﴾ ﴿Then We will surely draw out from every faction whichever of them is most insolent toward the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿Then indeed We know best those most deserving of burning therein.﴾

The fa' (فَ) is a consequential particle following the sentence (﴿Does not man remember that We created him before, while he was nothing?﴾ [Maryam: 67]), in view of the threat it contains. The waw of oath (واوُ القَسَمِ) serves to confirm the warning. The oath by "your Lord," with the Lord made an annex to the pronoun of the addressee, who is the Prophet (ﷺ), is an incidental expression (idmaj) for honoring his rank. The pronoun in "We will surely gather them" refers to "man," which is meant as a genus that conveys customary totality (al-istighraq al-'urfi), as was previously explained; that is, "We will surely gather the polytheists."

Conjoining "the devils" to the pronoun of the polytheists serves the purpose of belittling them, by stating that they will be gathered together with the basest and most corrupt kind, and it also alludes to the fact that the devils are the cause of their misguidance, which necessitates this state for them. So He gathers them with the devils as a warning to them that their destiny is the destiny of the devils, a destiny certain to all people. Therefore He conjoins to it the sentence (﴿Then We will surely bring them around Hell, on their knees﴾), with the pronoun referring to all of them. This is another preparation for drawing near to the punishment; it is a warning upon a warning and a gradual casting of terror into their hearts. Thus the particle thumma (ثُمَّ) indicates sequence of rank (al-tartib al-rutbi), not temporal delay, since delay is not the intended meaning; rather, the intention is that they are transferred from a state of punishment to a more severe one.

Juthiyyan (جُثِيًّا) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun of "We will surely bring them." Juthiyy is the plural of jāth (جَاثٍ), and its pattern is fu'ūl, like qā'id/qu'ūd and jālis/julūs; this is a pattern transmitted from usage (samā'ī) for the plural of fā'il. Its parallel was previously mentioned (﴿They fell down prostrating and weeping﴾ [Maryam: 58]). The original form of juthiyy is juthuww with two waws, because its verb is from the waw root: one says jathā yajthū when he kneels on his knees, which is the posture of the humble and abased. Then, when two waws came together in juthuww, they were found burdensome after a damma on the tha', so it was lightened by removing the previous cause of heaviness, namely the damma, and it was replaced by a kasra on the tha'. When the tha' took a kasra, it became necessary to change the following waw into a ya' for harmony, so the waw and the ya' came together, one of them preceded by a sukun, so the other waw was changed into a ya' and both were assimilated, becoming juthiyy. This kneeling is not the kneeling of people in the gathering described in His saying (﴿And you will see every nation kneeling. Every nation will be called to its record﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 28]); that is a kneeling of submission to God, whereas this kneeling around Hell is a kneeling of humiliation.

The statement regarding the conjoined sentence (﴿Then We will surely draw out from every faction﴾) is like the statement regarding the sentence "Then We will surely bring them," and this is another state of terror, more severe than the two before it, namely a state in which they are separated for being cast into the ranks of Hellfire according to the degrees of their extremism in disbelief.

Al-naz' (النَّزْعُ) is taking out something from something else, and from it comes naz' al-ma' min al-bi'r (drawing water from the well).

Al-shi'ah (الشِّيعَةُ) is the group that supports someone, i.e., follows him, so they are of one opinion. It was previously mentioned in His saying (﴿And We certainly sent before you among the sects of the former peoples﴾ [al-Hijr: 10]) in Surat al-Hijr. What is meant here is the factions of the people of disbelief, i.e., from every faction among them, i.e., from among those whom We have brought around Hell.

Al-'utiyy (العُتِيُّ) is disobedience and arrogance. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) on the pattern fu'ūl, like khurūj and julūs, and the waw was changed into a ya'. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ḥafs, and Khalaf read it with a kasra on the 'ayn, in imitation of the vowel of the tā', as was previously mentioned regarding juthiyyan.

The meaning: We will distinguish from every group that is gathered in a particular class of the religion of misguidance whoever is among that faction most disobedient to God and most arrogant toward Him. This is a threat to the great leaders of the polytheists, such as Abu Jahl, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and their counterparts.

Ayyu (أيُّ) is a relative pronoun meaning "whichever" (bi-ma'na ma wa-min). It is generally the case that the first part of its relative clause is omitted, and it is then built on damma. The original structure is: "whichever of them is more disobedient toward the Most Merciful." The mention of the attribute "the Most Merciful" here serves to make their insolence appear monstrous, because one who is greatly merciful toward creation is deserving of gratitude and kindness, not of disbelief and rebellion.

Since this drawing out and distinguishing is general, each group might claim that others are more disobedient; therefore God Most High informed that He knows who among them is most deserving of the burning of the Fire, since its levels differ in degree. Al-suliyy (الصُّلِيُّ) is the verbal noun of ṣalliya al-nār, like raḍiya, and it is a verbal noun transmitted by usage on the pattern fu'ūl. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ḥafs, and Khalaf read it with a kasra on the ṣād, in imitation of the vowel of the lām, as was previously mentioned regarding juthiyyan.

The two prepositional phrases (ḥarfā al-jarr) are connected to the comparative elatives (af'al al-tafḍil).

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa'l-Tanwīr) on Sūrat Maryam (19), verses 71–72:**

﴿Not one of you will there be but will pass over it [the Fire]. That is a decree from your Lord, inevitable.﴾ ﴿Then We will save those who feared Allah, and We will leave the wrongdoers therein on their knees.﴾

When [Allah] mentioned the drawing out of those who deserve the Fire more than the rest of the groups of disbelief, He followed it with [the statement] that all the groups of polytheism will enter the Fire. This is to repel the supposition that the drawing out of those who are "more severe against the Most Merciful in rebellion" (Maryam 19:69) is the furthest punishment those groups receive, by their thinking that their leaders will serve as a ransom for them from the Fire, or something similar. That is, that drawing out does not turn the rest of the factions away from the Fire, for Allah has made the Fire obligatory upon all of them. This sentence is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) between the statement ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them﴾ (Maryam 19:68) etc., and the statement ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them as clear evidence, those who disbelieved say﴾ (Maryam 19:73) etc.

The address in ﴿Not one of you﴾ is a shift (iltifāt, a change from the third person to the second person) from the absence in His saying ﴿We will surely gather them﴾ and ﴿We will surely bring them forth﴾ (Maryam 19:68). It moves from the third person to the second in a rising confrontation with the threat, so that there is no room for ambiguity about what is meant by the third-person pronoun, since the pronoun of address is more definite than the pronoun of absence. The expected form would be: "Not one of them will there be but will pass over it." It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that he used to read ﴿Not one of them﴾, and likewise ʿIkrima and a group [of readers] recited it so. The meaning is: there is not one among you, from among those who were drawn out from every faction and others, but will pass over Jahannam, by a decree that Allah has decided, so there is no changer of His words. That is, do not suppose that their intercession will benefit you, or that the might of your factions will protect you, or that you will shift the blame onto your chiefs and the great ones of your misguidance, or that they will be a ransom for you from the Fire.

This is similar to His saying: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the misguided﴾ (al-Ḥijr 15:42) ﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all﴾ (al-Ḥijr 15:43), that is, the misguided and others. The particle ʾinna here is for negation.

*Al-wurūd* (passing over/coming to): its literal sense is arriving at water in order to draw from it. It is used, as a common figurative extension, for arriving in general. But the use of *wurūd* for entering is not known, except as a figurative usage that is not well-known, so it requires an indicator (qarīna).

The sentence ﴿Then We will save those who feared Allah﴾ is an addition that escalates the threat, by stating that they [the wrongdoers] will remain in punishment eternally. Thus their passing over Hell is not limited to a fixed term. *Thumma* (then) indicates sequence in rank, to honour the rescue of those who feared Allah and to disfigure the state of those who remain in Hell on their knees. The meaning is: "And in addition to that, We will save those who feared Allah from passing over Hell." It does not mean "then He will save the righteous from among them," but rather that they have escaped passing over into the Fire. The mention of saving the righteous, that is the believers, is an interpolation (*idmāj*), bringing good news to the believers within the threat against the polytheists.

The sentence ﴿And We will leave the wrongdoers therein on their knees﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon the sentence ﴿Not one of you [there will be] but will pass over it﴾. The wrongdoers are the polytheists. The use of *alladhīna ẓalamū* (those who did wrong) is an explicit noun in place of the pronoun. The original would be: "And We will leave you, O wrongdoers." *Nadhar* means "to leave." It is an imperfect verb for which the Arabs had no past tense from its own root; they dispensed with the past of *nadhar* by using the past of *tarak* ("to leave"), as already explained at His saying ﴿Then leave them in their discourse, playing﴾ (al-Anʿām 6:91) in Sūrat al-Anʿām.

Therefore, the address in His saying ﴿Not one of you [there will be] but will pass over it﴾ is not to all people, believers and disbelievers, in the sense of beginning a new statement, such that it would imply that the believers pass over the Fire together with the disbelievers and then are saved from its punishment. This meaning is heavy and the context rejects it, since there is no connection between it and the preceding verses. Also, Allah's favour toward the believers with Paradise and honouring them with high stations is incompatible with driving them in one line with the polytheists. How could that be, when He began the discourse with His saying ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them and the devils﴾ (Maryam 19:68), and said ﴿On the Day We gather the righteous to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾ (Maryam 19:85) ﴿and drive the criminals to Hell as a thirsty herd﴾ (Maryam 19:86)? This is explicit in the difference of the gathering of the two groups. Thus the placement of this verse here is like the placement of His saying ﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all﴾ (al-Ḥijr 15:43) following His saying ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the misguided﴾ (al-Ḥijr 15:42). It should not be supposed that Hell is the promised place of the sincere servants of Allah, despite its earlier mention, because the context of praise rejects that.

[Page 151]

This verse is a point of difficulty and the subject of much dispute. All the exegetes agree that the righteous will not be touched by the Fire of Hell. They differed over the interpretation of the verse. Some took the pronoun in *minkum* (among you) to refer to all those addressed by the Qur'an, and this was narrated from some of the early generation (salaf). But the corruption of the meaning, and its contradiction to the wisdom of Allah and to the evidence indicating the safety of the believers that day from encountering even the slightest punishment, struck them, so they took various paths of interpretation. Some interpreted *wurūd* as mere passing by, without the believers being harmed. This is far removed from the usage, since *wurūd* is intended only to mean the attainment of what is contained in the place reached, as its origin is the arrival of a water-basin. In the verses of the Qur'an, it comes only to mean the destination into the Fire, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell; you will arrive at it﴾ (al-Anbiyāʾ 21:98) ﴿If these were gods, they would not have arrived at it﴾ (al-Anbiyāʾ 21:99), and His saying ﴿He will precede his people on the Day of Resurrection and lead them into the Fire; and wretched is the place they are led to﴾ (Hūd 11:98), and His saying ﴿And We will drive the criminals to Hell as a thirsty herd﴾ (Maryam 19:86). Moreover, bringing the believers to the Fire has no benefit, so it would be pointless, and what al-Fakhr [al-Rāzī] mentioned as benefits, which he called benefits, carries no weight.

[Page 152]

Others interpreted the arrival at Hell as passing over the *ṣirāṭ* (the bridge over Hell). They cited the reports about people passing over the *ṣirāṭ* at varying speeds of crossing. This is less remote than the previous interpretation.

Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr narrated, regarding these two interpretations, hadiths that do not go beyond the rank of weakness, from what Aḥmad narrated in his *Musnad* and al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī in *Nawādir al-Uṣūl*. The most authentic in this matter is what Abū ʿĪsā al-Tirmidhī narrated, saying: "People will come to the Fire, then they will depart from it according to their deeds," the hadith concerning the passing over the *ṣirāṭ*.

Some people put together, in support of this, the authentic hadith: "No Muslim loses three children and then enters the Fire, except for the *taḥillat al-qasam*" (the minimal fulfilment of an oath). They interpreted *taḥillat al-qasam* as what is in this verse, His saying ﴿Not one of you [there will be] but will pass over it﴾. This interpretation is false, because there is no oath in this verse that needs to be fulfilled. Rather, the meaning of the hadith is that whoever among the believers deserves punishment because of sins, if three of his children have died, they will be an expiation for him, so he will enter the Fire only briefly, resembling what is done to fulfil the minimal requirement of an oath, that is, to release oneself from it. **Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa'l-Tanwīr) on Sūrat Maryam (19), verses 71–72:**

﴿Not one of you will there be but will pass over it [the Fire]. That is a decree from your Lord, inevitable.﴾ ﴿Then We will save those who feared Allah, and We will leave the wrongdoers therein on their knees.﴾

When [Allah] mentioned the drawing out of those who deserve the Fire more than the rest of the groups of disbelief, He followed it with [the statement] that all the groups of polytheism will enter the Fire. This is to repel the supposition that the drawing out of those who are "more severe against the Most Merciful in rebellion" (Maryam 19:69) is the furthest punishment those groups receive, by their thinking that their leaders will serve as a ransom for them from the Fire, or something similar. That is, that drawing out does not turn the rest of the factions away from the Fire, for Allah has made the Fire obligatory upon all of them. This sentence is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) between the statement ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them﴾ (Maryam 19:68) etc., and the statement ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them as clear evidence, those who disbelieved say﴾ (Maryam 19:73) etc.

The address in ﴿Not one of you﴾ is a shift (iltifāt, a change from the third person to the second person) from the absence in His saying ﴿We will surely gather them﴾ and ﴿We will surely bring them forth﴾ (Maryam 19:68). It moves from the third person to the second in a rising confrontation with the threat, so that there is no room for ambiguity about what is meant by the third-person pronoun, since the pronoun of address is more definite than the pronoun of absence. The expected form would be: "Not one of them will there be but will pass over it." It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that he used to read ﴿Not one of them﴾, and likewise ʿIkrima and a group [of readers] recited it so. The meaning is: there is not one among you, from among those who were drawn out from every faction and others, but will pass over Jahannam, by a decree that Allah has decided, so there is no changer of His words. That is, do not suppose that their intercession will benefit you, or that the might of your factions will protect you, or that you will shift the blame onto your chiefs and the great ones of your misguidance, or that they will be a ransom for you from the Fire.

This is similar to His saying: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the misguided﴾ (al-Ḥijr 15:42) ﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all﴾ (al-Ḥijr 15:43), that is, the misguided and others. The particle ʾinna here is for negation.

*Al-wurūd* (passing over/coming to): its literal sense is arriving at water in order to draw from it. It is used, as a common figurative extension, for arriving in general. But the use of *wurūd* for entering is not known, except as a figurative usage that is not well-known, so it requires an indicator (qarīna).

The sentence ﴿Then We will save those who feared Allah﴾ is an addition that escalates the threat, by stating that they [the wrongdoers] will remain in punishment eternally. Thus their passing over Hell is not limited to a fixed term. *Thumma* (then) indicates sequence in rank, to honour the rescue of those who feared Allah and to disfigure the state of those who remain in Hell on their knees. The meaning is: "And in addition to that, We will save those who feared Allah from passing over Hell." It does not mean "then He will save the righteous from among them," but rather that they have escaped passing over into the Fire. The mention of saving the righteous, that is the believers, is an interpolation (*idmāj*), bringing good news to the believers within the threat against the polytheists.

The sentence ﴿And We will leave the wrongdoers therein on their knees﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon the sentence ﴿Not one of you [there will be] but will pass over it﴾. The wrongdoers are the polytheists. The use of *alladhīna ẓalamū* (those who did wrong) is an explicit noun in place of the pronoun. The original would be: "And We will leave you, O wrongdoers." *Nadhar* means "to leave." It is an imperfect verb for which the Arabs had no past tense from its own root; they dispensed with the past of *nadhar* by using the past of *tarak* ("to leave"), as already explained at His saying ﴿Then leave them in their discourse, playing﴾ (al-Anʿām 6:91) in Sūrat al-Anʿām.

Therefore, the address in His saying ﴿Not one of you [there will be] but will pass over it﴾ is not to all people, believers and disbelievers, in the sense of beginning a new statement, such that it would imply that the believers pass over the Fire together with the disbelievers and then are saved from its punishment. This meaning is heavy and the context rejects it, since there is no connection between it and the preceding verses. Also, Allah's favour toward the believers with Paradise and honouring them with high stations is incompatible with driving them in one line with the polytheists. How could that be, when He began the discourse with His saying ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them and the devils﴾ (Maryam 19:68), and said ﴿On the Day We gather the righteous to the Most Merciful as a delegation﴾ (Maryam 19:85) ﴿and drive the criminals to Hell as a thirsty herd﴾ (Maryam 19:86)? This is explicit in the difference of the gathering of the two groups. Thus the placement of this verse here is like the placement of His saying ﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all﴾ (al-Ḥijr 15:43) following His saying ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the misguided﴾ (al-Ḥijr 15:42). It should not be supposed that Hell is the promised place of the sincere servants of Allah, despite its earlier mention, because the context of praise rejects that.

[Page 151]

This verse is a point of difficulty and the subject of much dispute. All the exegetes agree that the righteous will not be touched by the Fire of Hell. They differed over the interpretation of the verse. Some took the pronoun in *minkum* (among you) to refer to all those addressed by the Qur'an, and this was narrated from some of the early generation (salaf). But the corruption of the meaning, and its contradiction to the wisdom of Allah and to the evidence indicating the safety of the believers that day from encountering even the slightest punishment, struck them, so they took various paths of interpretation. Some interpreted *wurūd* as mere passing by, without the believers being harmed. This is far removed from the usage, since *wurūd* is intended only to mean the attainment of what is contained in the place reached, as its origin is the arrival of a water-basin. In the verses of the Qur'an, it comes only to mean the destination into the Fire, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell; you will arrive at it﴾ (al-Anbiyāʾ 21:98) ﴿If these were gods, they would not have arrived at it﴾ (al-Anbiyāʾ 21:99), and His saying ﴿He will precede his people on the Day of Resurrection and lead them into the Fire; and wretched is the place they are led to﴾ (Hūd 11:98), and His saying ﴿And We will drive the criminals to Hell as a thirsty herd﴾ (Maryam 19:86). Moreover, bringing the believers to the Fire has no benefit, so it would be pointless, and what al-Fakhr [al-Rāzī] mentioned as benefits, which he called benefits, carries no weight.

[Page 152]

Others interpreted the arrival at Hell as passing over the *ṣirāṭ* (the bridge over Hell). They cited the reports about people passing over the *ṣirāṭ* at varying speeds of crossing. This is less remote than the previous interpretation.

The most authentic in this matter is what Abū ʿĪsā al-Tirmidhī narrated, saying: "People will come to the Fire, then they will depart from it according to their deeds," the hadith concerning the passing over the *ṣirāṭ*.

The commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 19, verses 73–74:

﴿When Our clear verses are recited to them, those who disbelieve say to those who believe: "Which of the two groups is better in station and finer in assembly?"﴾ ﴿How many generations have We destroyed before them, who were better in furnishings and in appearance?﴾

This is coordinated with His saying (﴿And man says: "When I am dead, shall I really be brought forth alive?"﴾ [Maryam: 66]). This is another kind of the deception of the polytheists through worldly life, and their attributing happiness to the conditions of a pleasant life in this world. The polytheists would look down on the believers and consider themselves happier than them.

The recitation (al-tilawa) means reading (al-qira'a). It has been discussed earlier at His saying (﴿And they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Sulayman﴾ [al-Baqara: 102]) in al-Baqara, and at His saying (﴿And when His verses are recited to them, it increases them in faith﴾ [al-Anfal: 2]) at the beginning of al-Anfal. The Prophet (ﷺ) would recite the Qur'an to the polytheists, and they would hear verses of reproach against them and warnings of an evil end, and verses of good tidings to the believers of a good outcome. The polytheists would deny this and say: "If there were any good for the believers, it would have been hastened for them. We are in blessing and are people of dominion, while the followers of Muhammad are common people. How could they surpass us, or even be equal to us? If we were with Allah as Muhammad says, He would have favoured the believers with comfort of living. Instead they are in a state of hardship and are not our equals. So if Muhammad were to distance them from his assembly, we would follow him."

Allah the Exalted says (﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance. You are not accountable for them in any way, nor are they accountable for you in any way, so that you would drive them away and thus be among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-An'am: 52]) ﴿And thus We tried some of them through others, so that they would say: "Are these the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us?" Is Allah not most knowing of the grateful?﴾ [al-An'am: 53].

[Page 154]

And He the Exalted says (﴿And those who disbelieve say to those who believe: "If it had been good, they would not have preceded us to it"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 11]). Because the polytheists used to reason by this corrupt analogy and deceive by it, their saying was made dependent on the time of the recitation of the verses of the Qur'an to them. So the meaning of "clear verses" (al-ayat al-bayyinat) is the verses of the Qur'an, and their being "clear" means that their proof against them is evident and full of convincing evidences. The lam in His saying (﴿to those who believe﴾) may be causal, meaning they said it for the sake of those who believe, i.e., regarding their situation, and in this case the statement is the polytheists' speech among themselves. It may also be connected to the verb "said" (qala), since it transitively governs its complement, and in this case their statement is an address from them to the believers. The interrogative (al-istifham) in their saying (﴿Which of the two groups﴾) is a rhetorical interrogative (istifham taqriri), i.e., one that seeks affirmation of a known matter.

Those other than Ibn Kathir read (maqaman) with a fatha on the mim, as a noun of place from qama, used figuratively (majazan) for status and rank, as in His saying (﴿And for one who fears the station of his Lord there are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46]). It is derived from standing (al-qiyam), which is used figuratively for prominence and power.

Ibn Kathir read it with a damma on the mim, from aqama in the sense of residing in a place, and it is used for dwelling in this world. The meaning is: better in life.

The clause (﴿How many generations have We destroyed before them﴾ [Maryam: 98]) is an address from Allah to His Messenger. Allah has destroyed the people of many generations who were more luxurious in enjoyment and more beautiful in appearance than the polytheists of the Arabs. This clause is therefore a parenthetical insertion between the narration of their saying and the instruction to the Prophet (ﷺ) about what to answer them. Its placement is a threat, and what follows it is the answer.

Al-athath is the household goods that are used for adornment. As for (ri'yan), the majority read it with a hamza after the ra', and after the hamza a ya', on the pattern fi'l in the sense of maf'ul, like dhibh, from the sight (al-ru'ya), i.e., better in what is seen, that is, in appearance and form.

[Page 155]

Qalun, on the authority of Nafi', and Ibn Dhakwan, on the authority of Ibn 'Amir, read (riyyan) with a shadda on the ya' and without a hamza. This is either because it is from the change of the hamza into a ya' and its assimilation into the other ya', or because it is from al-riyy, which means blessing and luxury, as in the saying "rayyan min al-na'im" (saturated with blessing). Its original root is al-riyy, the opposite of thirst, because riyy is used metaphorically for luxury, just as longing (al-talahhuf) is used metaphorically for suffering.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verses 75–76:

﴿Say, "Whoever is in error, the Most Merciful will extend for him an extension until, when they see what they are promised, either the punishment or the Hour, then they will know who is worse in position and weaker in soldiers."﴾ ﴿And Allah increases in guidance those who are guided; and the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in return.﴾.

This is a response to their saying (﴿Which of the two groups is better in position and finer in company?﴾ [Maryam: 73]). Allah taught His Messenger ﷺ how to expose their sophistry or their doubt. He informed them that what they enjoy of worldly blessing is merely a respite from Allah granted to them, because the refuge of the disbeliever is istidraj (gradual leading on). The criterion for distinguishing between the blessing that arises from Allah the Exalted's pleasure with His servant and the blessing that is istidraj for one who disbelieves in Him is to look at the state of the one who is in blessing, whether he is in a state of guidance or a state of error. Allah the Exalted said concerning the first group (﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer – We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely give them their reward according to the best of what they used to do.﴾ [An-Nahl: 97]). And He said concerning the others (﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children is us hastening to them in good things? Rather, they do not perceive.﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 54]).

Page 156
The meaning: whoever is immersed in error is deceived by Allah's granting him respite, so delusion mounts him, just as it mounted them when they said (﴿Which of the two groups is better in position and finer in company?﴾ [Maryam: 73]). The lam in His saying (﴿then let the Most Merciful extend for him an extension﴾) is the lam of command or supplication; it is used figuratively in the necessary meaning of command, namely affirmation, i.e., "then the Most Merciful will certainly extend for him an extension," meaning that this is certain to occur according to Allah's custom of granting respite to the astray, as an excuse for them, just as He said (﴿Did We not give you a life long enough that whoever would remember might remember therein?﴾ [Fatir: 37]). It is also an admonition to the Muslims not to be deceived by Allah's bestowing favour upon the astray, to the point that the believers would pray to Allah for it, out of their indifference to the long duration of the disbelievers' bliss. If the intent of "Say" is that the Prophet should say this to the disbelievers, then the lam of command is purely figurative for affirmation; and if the intent is that the Prophet should convey that Allah said this, then the lam of command is also figurative and metaphorical, in such a way that Allah the Exalted commands Himself to extend for them.

Al-madd: its literal meaning is letting out a rope and lengthening it. It is used figuratively for granting respite, as here, and for lengthening, as in the saying "May Allah extend your life" (madda Allahu fi 'umrik).

Madda (an absolute object) is an emphatic object of its verb, i.e., "let him extend the extension intensely," so that will certainly come to an end. Ḥattā indicates the endpoint of the extension and is initial (ibtida'iyya), i.e., the Most Merciful extends for him until they see what they are promised; that is, there is no escape for them from seeing the punishment they were threatened with, and the length of their time in blessing will not avert it from them.

So the endpoint is the content of the sentence that follows it, not a single word. The implied sense is: the Most Merciful extends for them until they see the punishment, then they will know who is happier and who is more wretched.

Page 157
The future particle (sa-) is for emphasis of their attaining knowledge at that time, and not to indicate the future, since the future has already been derived from the endpoint.
Immā is a particle of distribution (tafsil) for (﴿what they are promised﴾): what they were threatened with of punishment, either the punishment of this world or the punishment of the Hereafter, for each of them will not fail to see one of the two punishments or both.

The word "punishment" is in the accusative as the object of "they see." Immā here is not a conjunction; it is parenthetical between the governing verb and its object, as in the verse of Ta'abbaṭa Sharran:

"They are two paths: either captivity and obligation, or blood – and death is more fitting for the free man."
Here "captivity," "obligation," and "blood" are in the genitive (after immā).

His saying (﴿worse in position and weaker in soldiers﴾) is the counterpart of their saying (﴿better in position and finer in company﴾ [Maryam: 73]). Makān is synonymous with maqām, and junud means helpers, since nadī is meant as its people, as previously explained; thus "finer in company" is matched with "weaker in soldiers."

The clause (﴿And Allah increases in guidance those who are guided﴾) is conjoined to the clause (﴿whoever is in error, the Most Merciful will extend for him an extension﴾), because that clause contains respite leading to continued error; and continuation is increase. The meaning is by ihtibak (an implicit balancing): the Most Merciful extends for him an extension, so he increases in error; and He extends for those who are guided, so they increase in guidance.

The clause (﴿and the enduring good deeds are better﴾) is conjoined to the clause (﴿And Allah increases in guidance those who are guided﴾), and it is an ascent from the good news of their deliverance to the good news of the elevation of their ranks. That is, the enduring good deeds are better than the safety from punishment implied by His saying (﴿so they will know who is worse in position and weaker in soldiers﴾); that is, it will become clear that what the disbelievers enjoyed of blessing and might was less than what the Muslims had of hardship and weakness, when considered in terms of their outcomes. For the disbelievers' outcome is punishment, and the believers' outcome is safety from punishment, and beyond that, for the believers, is reward.

"The enduring good deeds" are two descriptors of an omitted noun known from context: the deeds whose bliss and good endure, and "the righteous" (ṣāliḥāt) are, for their doers, better with Allah than the blessing of deliverance from punishment. The reason for placing "enduring" before "righteous" has already been discussed in the commentary on its counterpart in the middle of Surat al-Kahf.

Al-maradd: the place of return. What is meant by it is the outcome of the matter.

And He said concerning the others (﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children is us hastening to them in good things? Rather, they do not perceive.﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 54]).

Page 156
The meaning: whoever is immersed in error is deceived by Allah's granting him respite, so delusion mounts him, just as it mounted them when they said (﴿Which of the two groups is better in position and finer in company?﴾ [Maryam: 73]). The lam in His saying (﴿then let the Most Merciful extend for him an extension﴾) is the lam of command or supplication; it is used figuratively in the necessary meaning of command, namely affirmation, i.e., "then the Most Merciful will certainly extend for him an extension," meaning that this is certain to occur according to Allah's custom of granting respite to the astray, as an excuse for them, just as He said (﴿Did We not give you a life long enough that whoever would remember might remember therein?﴾ [Fatir: 37]). It is also an admonition to the Muslims not to be deceived by Allah's bestowing favour upon the astray, to the point that the believers would pray to Allah for it, out of their indifference to the long duration of the disbelievers' bliss. If the intent of "Say" is that the Prophet should say this to the disbelievers, then the lam of command is purely figurative for affirmation; and if the intent is that the Prophet should convey that Allah said this, then the lam of command is also figurative and metaphorical, in such a way that Allah the Exalted commands Himself to extend for them.

Al-madd: its literal meaning is letting out a rope and lengthening it. It is used figuratively for granting respite, as here, and for lengthening, as in the saying "May Allah extend your life" (madda Allahu fi 'umrik).

Madda (an absolute object) is an emphatic object of its verb, i.e., "let him extend the extension intensely," so that will certainly come to an end. Ḥattā indicates the endpoint of the extension and is initial (ibtida'iyya), i.e., the Most Merciful extends for him until they see what they are promised; that is, there is no escape for them from seeing the punishment they were threatened with, and the length of their time in blessing will not avert it from them.

So the endpoint is the content of the sentence that follows it, not a single word. The implied sense is: the Most Merciful extends for them until they see the punishment, then they will know who is happier and who is more wretched.

Page 157
The future particle (sa-) is for emphasis of their attaining knowledge at that time, and not to indicate the future, since the future has already been derived from the endpoint.
Immā is a particle of distribution (tafsil) for (﴿what they are promised﴾): what they were threatened with of punishment, either the punishment of this world or the punishment of the Hereafter, for each of them will not fail to see one of the two punishments or both.

The word "punishment" is in the accusative as the object of "they see." Immā here is not a conjunction; it is parenthetical between the governing verb and its object, as in the verse of Ta'abbaṭa Sharran:

"They are two paths: either captivity and obligation, or blood – and death is more fitting for the free man."
Here "captivity," "obligation," and "blood" are in the genitive (after immā).

His saying (﴿worse in position and weaker in soldiers﴾) is the counterpart of their saying (﴿better in position and finer in company﴾ [Maryam: 73]). Makān is synonymous with maqām, and junud means helpers, since nadī is meant as its people, as previously explained; thus "finer in company" is matched with "weaker in soldiers."

The clause (﴿And Allah increases in guidance those who are guided﴾) is conjoined to the clause (﴿whoever is in error, the Most Merciful will extend for him an extension﴾), because that clause contains respite leading to continued error; and continuation is increase. The meaning is by ihtibak (an implicit balancing): the Most Merciful extends for him an extension, so he increases in error; and He extends for those who are guided, so they increase in guidance.

The clause (﴿and the enduring good deeds are better﴾) is conjoined to the clause (﴿And Allah increases in guidance those who are guided﴾), and it is an ascent from the good news of their deliverance to the good news of the elevation of their ranks. That is, the enduring good deeds are better than the safety from punishment implied by His saying (﴿so they will know who is worse in position and weaker in soldiers﴾); that is, it will become clear that what the disbelievers enjoyed of blessing and might was less than what the Muslims had of hardship and weakness, when considered in terms of their outcomes. For the disbelievers' outcome is punishment, and the believers' outcome is safety from punishment, and beyond that, for the believers, is reward.

"The enduring good deeds" are two descriptors of an omitted noun known from context: the deeds whose bliss and good endure, and "the righteous" (ṣāliḥāt) are, for their doers, better with Allah than the blessing of deliverance from punishment. The reason for placing "enduring" before "righteous" has already been discussed in the commentary on its counterpart in the middle of Surat al-Kahf.

Al-maradd: the place of return. What is meant by it is the outcome of the matter.

[Page 159]

This is a continuation of His saying, ﴿And man says, "When I am dead, shall I indeed be brought forth alive?"﴾ [Maryam 19:66], and of what is connected to it of digressions and subsidiary remarks. The point of connection is that the speaker of this statement was in the same delusion as that of his companions, namely the delusion of denying resurrection (al-Ba'th).

The verse alludes to the story of Khabbab ibn al-Aratt with al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi. In the Sahih it is reported that Khabbab used to make swords in Mecca. He made a sword for al-'As ibn Wa'il, and its price was a debt owed to him by al-'As. Khabbab had embraced Islam, so he came to demand his debt from al-'As. Al-'As ibn Wa'il said to him, "I will not pay you until you disbelieve in Muhammad." Khabbab, who had become angry, said, "I will not disbelieve in Muhammad until God causes you to die and then resurrects you." Al-'As said, "Will I be resurrected after death?" He said, "Yes." Al-'As said mockingly, "If that is so, then I will have wealth and children, and at that time I will pay you your debt." So this verse was revealed concerning that. Thus al-'As ibn Wa'il is the one meant by ﴿the one who disbelieved in Our signs﴾.

The interrogative in ﴿Have you seen﴾ (a'fa-ra'ayta) is used to express wonder at the disbelief of this disbeliever, and the verb "seeing" (al-ru'ya) is used metaphorically for knowledge of his strange story.

The story is treated as if it were something witnessed by the eye, because seeing is one of the strongest ways of knowing. He is referred to by a relative clause (al-mawsul) because of the matter of wonder contained in the clause, especially his saying ﴿I will surely be given wealth and children﴾.

The purpose of the interrogative is to draw the mind's attention to knowledge of this story, or to its recollection if the listener already knows it.

The address is to everyone who is fit to be addressed, so no specific individual is intended. It is also permissible that it is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ).

"The signs" (al-ayat) means the Qur'an, that is, he disbelieved in and denied what was revealed to him of the signs. Among them are the signs of resurrection.

"Walad" (child) is a collective noun (ism jam') for the singular walad. Thus the majority of readers recited it so. Hamza and al-Kisa'i, in this surah, in the four occurrences, recited it as "wulₓd" (with a damma on the waw and sukun on the lam), which is then the plural of walad, like asad and usd.

The clause ﴿Has he attained the unseen?﴾ (a-ittala'a al-ghayb) is a reply to his statement, according to the method of the wise style (al-uslub al-hakim), by taking his statement at the surface level of its wording, namely the promise of paying the debt from the wealth he will find when he is raised. Therefore the interrogative in ﴿Has he attained the unseen?﴾ is both denial and expression of wonder.

The verb "ittala'a" is of the pattern "iftaʿala" from "tala'a" (to rise), for intensification in the occurrence of the act of rising, which is ascending. For this reason the place of rising is called "matla'" (with light vowel) and "muttala'" (with doubled letter). For this reason the term "ittila'" (looking into or overseeing something) came to be applied, because the one who wishes to oversee a place hidden from him ascends to it from a height. The basic usage is that the verb "ittala'a" is intransitive and does not need a transitive particle, as He, may He be exalted, said ﴿He said, "Will you look down?"﴾ [al-Saffat 37:54] ﴿So he looked down and saw him in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Saffat 37:55]. When "ittala'a" is construed with the sense of "to ascend over" (ashrafa), it takes the preposition of elevation (ʿala), as in His saying ﴿If you had looked upon them, you would have turned away from them in flight﴾ [al-Kahf 18:18]. This was mentioned briefly in Surat al-Kahf.

Thus "al-ghayb" (the unseen) in this verse is in the accusative as a direct object, not by dropping the preposition, as some exegetes supposed.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "The choice of this word has a particular significance. It says: has he reached such a degree of greatness that he has ascended to knowledge of the unseen?" End of quotation.

Therefore "al-ghayb" is what is hidden from sight. The meaning is: Has he risen above the world of the unseen and seen wealth and children prepared for him when the Day of Resurrection comes? Or has he seen his wealth and his child going with him in the Hereafter? For when he said "then I will have wealth and children," he meant that his wealth and his children would return to him on that day. Or has he made a covenant with God that He will give him that, so that he became certain of its occurrence? For there is no way to know what has been prepared for him on the Day of Resurrection except through one of these two: either by unveiling and witnessing it, or by God informing him that He will give him it.

The object of "al-ʿahd" (covenant) is omitted, as the context indicates. Its estimated sense is: that He will give him wealth and children.

"ʿInda" (with) is a spatial adverb, and it is a metaphor by implicature (istiʿara bi'l-kināya), by likening the promise to a written document in which a pact and a contract between him and God is written, placed with God. This is because people, when they wanted to document what they agreed upon, wrote it in a document and placed it in a secure, well-known location, as the polytheists wrote the document of severance between themselves and the Banu Hashim and placed it in the Ka'ba. al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

"Fearing oppression and the bloody quarrel; and can whims undo what is in the writings?"

Perhaps, in his being followed by the words ﴿We will surely record what he says﴾, there is an allusion to this meaning, by way of observing the correspondence (muraʿat al-nazir). Here, among His names, "al-Rahman" (the Most Merciful) was chosen. This is because evoking its meaning is more fitting for fulfilling what He has covenanted concerning the supposed blessing of this disbeliever, and because mentioning this name is a rebuke to the polytheists who said ﴿And what is al-Rahman?﴾ [al-Furqan 25:60].

"Kalla" (By no means!) is a particle of deterrence and rebuke against the content of a preceding statement by the same speaker, or against a statement that is reported from another speaker or heard from him, as in His saying ﴿The companions of Musa said, "We are surely overtaken"﴾ [al-Shuʿara 26:61] ﴿He said, "By no means! Surely my Lord is with me"﴾ [al-Shuʿara 26:62]. Most often it comes after the end of the false statement it refutes, but it may precede the false statement for the sake of emphasizing the refutation and hastening it, and to arouse eagerness to hear the speech that follows it, as in His saying ﴿By no means! By the moon﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:32] ﴿and by the night when it departs﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:33] ﴿and by the morning when it brightens﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:34] ﴿Indeed it is one of the greatest matters﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:35], according to one of two interpretations. Because it contains the sense of nullification, it has the meaning of negation. It is the opposite of "ay" (yes) and "ajal" (indeed) and similar particles of affirmation, with the preceding speech as its implied referent.

The meaning is: what he has reported of his claim, and of his delusion, will not occur. Usually it is followed by a statement after it, for it is not known in the speech of the Arabs that a speaker says "kalla" in rejecting a statement and then falls silent.

Because it is a particle of deterrence, it conveys a complete meaning on which silence is fitting. For this reason it is permissible, according to the majority, to pause upon it. al-Mubarrad prohibited pausing upon it, on the basis that it must be followed by a statement. al-Farra' said: "Its positions are four. A position where it is good to pause upon it and to begin with it, as in this verse. A position where it is good to pause upon it but not good to begin with it, as in His saying ﴿I fear that they will kill me." He said: "By no means! Go, both of you"﴾ [al-Shuʿara 26:14–15]. A position where it is good to begin with it but not good to pause upon it, as in His saying ﴿By no means! Indeed it is a reminder﴾ [ʿAbasa 80:11]. A position where neither of the two is good, as in His saying ﴿Then by no means! You will come to know﴾ [al-Takathur 102:4]."

al-Farra's statement shows that the disagreement between the majority and al-Mubarrad is verbal, because pausing is more general than complete silence.

The particle of future (sa-) in His saying ﴿We will surely record﴾ is for affirming that this will certainly happen, as in His saying ﴿He said, "I will surely ask forgiveness for you from my Lord"﴾ [Yusuf 12:98].

"Al-madd" (extension) in "al-ʿadhab" (the punishment) means increase of it, as in His saying ﴿Let the Most Merciful extend for him an extension﴾ [Maryam 19:75].

The phrase "mā yaqūlu" (what he says) in both places is a brevity, because if his statement were quoted it would be long. This is like His saying ﴿Say: "Messengers before me have certainly come to you with clear proofs and with what you have spoken of"﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:183]; that is, and with an offering that fire consumes. That is, what he said of impiety and mockery of Islam, and what he said of wealth and children. That is: We will record his recompense and destroy him, and We will inherit what he named of wealth and children, that is, We will inherit the very substances of what he named, since it is not conceivable that his speech and his words should be inherited from him. So "mā yaqūlu" is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the pronoun of the accusative in "narithuhu" (We will inherit him), since the estimated sense is: We will inherit his child and his wealth.

"Al-irth" (inheritance) is used metaphorically for seizing and taking away, or it is a metonymy for its concomitant, which is destruction. Its purpose is to remind him of death, or to threaten him with the imminence of his destruction.

The meaning of inheriting his children is that they will become Muslims and enter the party of God. For al-'As was the father of ʿAmr, the great Companion, and of Hisham, the Companion martyred on the day of Ajnadayn. So here is good news for the Prophet (ﷺ), and a blow and grief for al-'As ibn Wa'il.

"Fard" (alone) is the one who has nothing with him by which he becomes a number, indicating that he will be gathered as a disbeliever alone, apart from his child, and with no wealth. "Fardan" is a circumstantial accusative (hal).
