Hamza and al-Kisa'i, in this surah, in the four occurrences, recited it as "wulₓd" (with a damma on the waw and sukun on the lam), which is then the plural of walad, like asad and usd.

The clause ﴿Has he attained the unseen?﴾ (a-ittala'a al-ghayb) is a reply to his statement, according to the method of the wise style (al-uslub al-hakim), by taking his statement at the surface level of its wording, namely the promise of paying the debt from the wealth he will find when he is raised. Therefore the interrogative in ﴿Has he attained the unseen?﴾ is both denial and expression of wonder.

The verb "ittala'a" is of the pattern "iftaʿala" from "tala'a" (to rise), for intensification in the occurrence of the act of rising, which is ascending. For this reason the place of rising is called "matla'" (with light vowel) and "muttala'" (with doubled letter). For this reason the term "ittila'" (looking into or overseeing something) came to be applied, because the one who wishes to oversee a place hidden from him ascends to it from a height. The basic usage is that the verb "ittala'a" is intransitive and does not need a transitive particle, as He, may He be exalted, said ﴿He said, "Will you look down?"﴾ [al-Saffat 37:54] ﴿So he looked down and saw him in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Saffat 37:55]. When "ittala'a" is construed with the sense of "to ascend over" (ashrafa), it takes the preposition of elevation (ʿala), as in His saying ﴿If you had looked upon them, you would have turned away from them in flight﴾ [al-Kahf 18:18]. This was mentioned briefly in Surat al-Kahf.

Thus "al-ghayb" (the unseen) in this verse is in the accusative as a direct object, not by dropping the preposition, as some exegetes supposed.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "The choice of this word has a particular significance. It says: has he reached such a degree of greatness that he has ascended to knowledge of the unseen?" End of quotation.

Therefore "al-ghayb" is what is hidden from sight. The meaning is: Has he risen above the world of the unseen and seen wealth and children prepared for him when the Day of Resurrection comes? Or has he seen his wealth and his child going with him in the Hereafter? For when he said "then I will have wealth and children," he meant that his wealth and his children would return to him on that day. Or has he made a covenant with God that He will give him that, so that he became certain of its occurrence? For there is no way to know what has been prepared for him on the Day of Resurrection except through one of these two: either by unveiling and witnessing it, or by God informing him that He will give him it.

The object of "al-ʿahd" (covenant) is omitted, as the context indicates. Its estimated sense is: that He will give him wealth and children.

"ʿInda" (with) is a spatial adverb, and it is a metaphor by implicature (istiʿara bi'l-kināya), by likening the promise to a written document in which a pact and a contract between him and God is written, placed with God. This is because people, when they wanted to document what they agreed upon, wrote it in a document and placed it in a secure, well-known location, as the polytheists wrote the document of severance between themselves and the Banu Hashim and placed it in the Ka'ba. al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

"Fearing oppression and the bloody quarrel; and can whims undo what is in the writings?"

Perhaps, in his being followed by the words ﴿We will surely record what he says﴾, there is an allusion to this meaning, by way of observing the correspondence (muraʿat al-nazir). Here, among His names, "al-Rahman" (the Most Merciful) was chosen. This is because evoking its meaning is more fitting for fulfilling what He has covenanted concerning the supposed blessing of this disbeliever, and because mentioning this name is a rebuke to the polytheists who said ﴿And what is al-Rahman?﴾ [al-Furqan 25:60].

"Kalla" (By no means!) is a particle of deterrence and rebuke against the content of a preceding statement by the same speaker, or against a statement that is reported from another speaker or heard from him, as in His saying ﴿The companions of Musa said, "We are surely overtaken"﴾ [al-Shuʿara 26:61] ﴿He said, "By no means! Surely my Lord is with me"﴾ [al-Shuʿara 26:62]. Most often it comes after the end of the false statement it refutes, but it may precede the false statement for the sake of emphasizing the refutation and hastening it, and to arouse eagerness to hear the speech that follows it, as in His saying ﴿By no means! By the moon﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:32] ﴿and by the night when it departs﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:33] ﴿and by the morning when it brightens﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:34] ﴿Indeed it is one of the greatest matters﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:35], according to one of two interpretations. Because it contains the sense of nullification, it has the meaning of negation. It is the opposite of "ay" (yes) and "ajal" (indeed) and similar particles of affirmation, with the preceding speech as its implied referent.

The meaning is: what he has reported of his claim, and of his delusion, will not occur. Usually it is followed by a statement after it, for it is not known in the speech of the Arabs that a speaker says "kalla" in rejecting a statement and then falls silent.

Because it is a particle of deterrence, it conveys a complete meaning on which silence is fitting. For this reason it is permissible, according to the majority, to pause upon it. al-Mubarrad prohibited pausing upon it, on the basis that it must be followed by a statement. al-Farra' said: "Its positions are four. A position where it is good to pause upon it and to begin with it, as in this verse. A position where it is good to pause upon it but not good to begin with it, as in His saying ﴿I fear that they will kill me." He said: "By no means! Go, both of you"﴾ [al-Shuʿara 26:14–15]. A position where it is good to begin with it but not good to pause upon it, as in His saying ﴿By no means! Indeed it is a reminder﴾ [ʿAbasa 80:11]. A position where neither of the two is good, as in His saying ﴿Then by no means! You will come to know﴾ [al-Takathur 102:4]."

al-Farra's statement shows that the disagreement between the majority and al-Mubarrad is verbal, because pausing is more general than complete silence.

The particle of future (sa-) in His saying ﴿We will surely record﴾ is for affirming that this will certainly happen, as in His saying ﴿He said, "I will surely ask forgiveness for you from my Lord"﴾ [Yusuf 12:98].

"Al-madd" (extension) in "al-ʿadhab" (the punishment) means increase of it, as in His saying ﴿Let the Most Merciful extend for him an extension﴾ [Maryam 19:75].

The phrase "mā yaqūlu" (what he says) in both places is a brevity, because if his statement were quoted it would be long. This is like His saying ﴿Say: "Messengers before me have certainly come to you with clear proofs and with what you have spoken of"﴾ [Al ʿImran 3:183]; that is, and with an offering that fire consumes. That is, what he said of impiety and mockery of Islam, and what he said of wealth and children. That is: We will record his recompense and destroy him, and We will inherit what he named of wealth and children, that is, We will inherit the very substances of what he named, since it is not conceivable that his speech and his words should be inherited from him. So "mā yaqūlu" is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the pronoun of the accusative in "narithuhu" (We will inherit him), since the estimated sense is: We will inherit his child and his wealth.

"Al-irth" (inheritance) is used metaphorically for seizing and taking away, or it is a metonymy for its concomitant, which is destruction. Its purpose is to remind him of death, or to threaten him with the imminence of his destruction.

The meaning of inheriting his children is that they will become Muslims and enter the party of God. For al-'As was the father of ʿAmr, the great Companion, and of Hisham, the Companion martyred on the day of Ajnadayn. So here is good news for the Prophet (ﷺ), and a blow and grief for al-'As ibn Wa'il.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verses 81–82:

﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah, that they might be for them a source of might.﴾ ﴿No! They will deny their worship, and they will be opposed to them.﴾

It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the sentence ﴿And man says, "When I have died, shall I indeed be brought forth alive?"﴾ [Maryam: 66]. The pronoun in "they have taken" refers to those who associated partners with Allah, because the speech has proceeded concerning some of them. And al-ittikhādh (taking, adopting) means making a person take a thing for himself, so the taking here is made to denote belief and worship. In the verb al-ittikhādh there is an indication that their belief regarding those gods is something agreed upon and fabricated, which Allah did not command, as He, exalted is He, said concerning Ibrahim (﴿He said, "Do you worship what you carve?"﴾ [al-Saffat: 95]). And in His saying (﴿besides Allah﴾) there is an indication that the truth requires that they take Allah as their God, for by that the correct belief is established from the beginning of creation, and sound reason points to it.

The meaning of (﴿that they might be for them a source of might﴾) is that they might be ones who grant them might (muʿizzīn), i.e., supporters. He thus describes the gods with the verbal noun (ʿizz) to portray the belief of the polytheists about their gods, that they are the very essence of might; that mere affiliation to them confers might upon them.

Page 164

He applied to the gods the pronoun of the rational being, because the polytheists who took them imagined them to be intelligent, governing beings. The two pronouns in His saying (﴿they will deny … and they will be﴾) may refer to the gods, i.e., the gods will disavow the polytheists' worship of them, and so denial and rejection are expressed by kufr (disbelief); and the gods will be humiliation, the opposite of might. The more apparent view is that the pronoun of (﴿they will deny﴾) refers to the polytheists, i.e., the polytheists will reject the worship of the gods, which then corresponds to His saying (﴿and they have taken gods besides Allah﴾). In this there is complete antithesis, i.e., after they took the effort to make them gods for themselves, they will disavow their worship. The use of the verb (﴿they will deny﴾) favours this reading, because kufr is common in intellectual disavowal of belief, not in disavowal in general; and that the pronoun of "they will be" refers to the gods, and in it there is a scattering of pronouns. There is no harm in this, since the context returns each to what suits it, as in the saying of ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas:

"We returned, and had we not, their host would have surrounded the Muslims and seized what they had gathered."

i.e., the host of the polytheists seized what the Muslims had gathered of the spoils.

It is also permissible that both pronouns (they will deny and they will be) refer to the polytheists, and that "inna" is the particle of the future indicating an imminent occurrence; i.e., the polytheists will disavow the worship of idols, enter Islam, and be opposed to the idols, demolishing their shrines and cursing them. This is then a glad tiding to the Prophet (ﷺ) that his religion will prevail over the religion of disbelief. In this antithesis there is double tibaq (antithesis).

And because it has the meaning of a verbal noun, when it is used as a description it retains one form and does not agree with the thing it describes.

[Page 165]

﴿Have you not considered that We sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with a strong incitement?﴾ ﴿So do not hasten against them. We are only counting for them a count.﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (*istinaf bayani*, a sentence that answers an implied question) responding to a question that stirs in the soul of the Messenger (ﷺ) concerning the disbelievers' persistence in misguidance, both collectively and individually, and the evil outcome that this drew upon them. It begins from God's words, ﴿And man says, "When I have died, shall I really be brought forth alive?"﴾ (Maryam 19:66), and includes the mention of God's granting them respite in this world and what He has prepared for them of punishment in the Hereafter. It is interposed between the clause ﴿And they have taken besides God gods﴾ (Maryam 19:81) and the clause ﴿The Day We will gather the righteous﴾ (Maryam 19:85). It also serves as a concluding summary (*tadhyil*) of those verses and an affirmation of their content, since it draws out their state, and it contains consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) regarding their being granted respite and the delay of their punishment.

The interrogative in ﴿Have you not considered﴾ is exclamatory (*ta'jibi*). Its like is common in Arabic speech, where they use interrogation to negate an action. What is intended is the occurrence of its opposite, urging the addressee to be concerned with bringing it about; that is, "how is it that you have not seen this?" The sending of the devils upon the disbelievers, because its effects are so evident, is treated as a thing seen and witnessed, so the wonder is directed at its sight by the words "have you not seen that."

*Al-azz* means the agitating and the inner provoking, derived from *aziz al-qidr*, the bubbling of a cooking pot when its boiling intensifies. The agitation of their belief, the contradiction of their statements, and the fabrication of their lies are likened to boiling, with its rising, falling, crackling and subsiding. Thus it is a metaphor (*isti'arah*), and its affirmation by the verbal noun (*ta'kid bil-masdar*) is a supporting elaboration (*tarshih*). The sending of the devils upon them means their being subjugated by them and their failing to benefit from the prophetic guidance that rescues from their snares, and this is due to their disbelief and their turning away from listening to the admonitions of revelation.

To point to this meaning, the speech shifted from the pronoun to the explicit noun in the phrase ﴿upon the disbelievers﴾. The clause ﴿inciting them﴾ was made a restrictive circumstantial state (*hal muqayyad*) of the sending, because the devils are sent upon all people, but God protects the believers from the plots of the devils in proportion to the strength of their faith and the soundness of their deeds. ﴿Have you not considered that We sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with a strong incitement?﴾ ﴿So do not hasten against them. We are only counting for them a count.﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (*istinaf bayani*, a sentence that answers an implied question) responding to a question that stirs in the soul of the Messenger (ﷺ) concerning the disbelievers' persistence in misguidance, both collectively and individually, and the evil outcome that this drew upon them. It begins from God's words, ﴿And man says, "When I have died, shall I really be brought forth alive?"﴾ (Maryam 19:66), and includes the mention of God's granting them respite in this world and what He has prepared for them of punishment in the Hereafter. It is interposed between the clause ﴿And they have taken besides God gods﴾ (Maryam 19:81) and the clause ﴿The Day We will gather the righteous﴾ (Maryam 19:85). It also serves as a concluding summary (*tadhyil*) of those verses and an affirmation of their content, since it draws out their state, and it contains consolation for the Messenger (ﷺ) regarding their being granted respite and the delay of their punishment.

The interrogative in ﴿Have you not considered﴾ is exclamatory (*ta'jibi*). Its like is common in Arabic speech, where they use interrogation to negate an action. What is intended is the occurrence of its opposite, urging the addressee to be concerned with bringing it about; that is, "how is it that you have not seen this?" The sending of the devils upon the disbelievers, because its effects are so evident, is treated as a thing seen and witnessed, so the wonder is directed at its sight by the words "have you not seen that."

*Al-azz* means the agitating and the inner provoking, derived from *aziz al-qidr*, the bubbling of a cooking pot when its boiling intensifies. The agitation of their belief, the contradiction of their statements, and the fabrication of their lies are likened to boiling, with its rising, falling, crackling and subsiding. Thus it is a metaphor (*isti'arah*), and its affirmation by the verbal noun (*ta'kid bil-masdar*) is a supporting elaboration (*tarshih*). The sending of the devils upon them means their being subjugated by them and their failing to benefit from the prophetic guidance that rescues from their snares, and this is due to their disbelief and their turning away from listening to the admonitions of revelation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verses 85–87:

﴿On the Day We shall gather the God-fearing to the Most Merciful as a delegation,﴾ ﴿and drive the criminals to Hell like thirsty cattle driven to water.﴾ ﴿They will have no power of intercession, except for one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful.﴾

This completes the establishment of the weakness of the usefulness of their gods to them, following His saying: ﴿and they will become opponents to them﴾ [Maryam: 82]. So the clause ﴿they will have no power of intercession﴾ is the beginning of the speech, and it explains the clause ﴿and they will become opponents to them﴾ [Maryam: 82]. The time-phrase and what is added to it is an incidental insertion (idmaj), by which the honour of the believers and the humiliation of the disbelievers are made clear. Implicit in it is an additional clarification of the clause ﴿and they will become opponents to them﴾ [Maryam: 82], namely that they were the cause of their being driven to Hell as thirsty cattle and of their opposition to the state of the believers in that great scene. Thus the time-phrase is connected to ﴿they will have no power﴾.

The pronoun in ﴿they have no power﴾ refers to the gods. The meaning: they are not able to benefit those whom they took as gods, so that they might be a source of might for them.

Al-hashr (gathering) is the general act of assembling, and it occurs in good as here, and in bad as in His saying: ﴿Gather those who did wrong, and their spouses, and what they used to worship﴾ [al-Saffat: 22] ﴿besides God, and guide them to the path of the Blazing Fire﴾ [al-Saffat: 23]. For this reason, the verb "We shall gather" was followed by the qualifier "as a delegation" (wafdan), that is, gathering of delegations to kings, since delegations are honoured. The Arabs had delegations to their kings and noble men at certain times, and notables among the Arabs had annual delegations (wifadat) to their kings and masters. Every tribe had a delegation, and there is a proverb: "The wretched one is the delegate of the Baraajim." The Arabs followed this custom, so they sent delegations to the Prophet ﷺ because he was the most noble of masters. The year of the delegations was the ninth year of the Hijra, following the conquest of Makkah, when Islam spread among the lands of the Arabs. Mentioning the attribute "the Most Merciful" here is clearly appropriate to the delegation.

Al-sawq (driving) is making cattle move ahead of their herders, who place them in front of them so that they fear their rebuke and whips and do not escape from them. So al-sawq is the movement of fear and caution. His saying "wirdan" is a circumstantial state (hal) intended for comparison, which is why it came as an unchanging noun, since the meaning of comparison makes it like a derived noun. Al-warid, with a kasra on the waw, originally means going to water, and the animals that arrive at water are called "wirdan," by an elision of the modified noun, meaning "possessors of arrival," just as the water to which people come is called "wirdan." He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And wretched is the watering-place to which they are brought﴾ [Hud: 98]. The exception in ﴿except for one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), meaning: but the one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful will possess intercession on that day, that is, the one whom God has promised that he will intercede, and they are the prophets and the angels.

The meaning of "they have no power" (la yamlikun) is "they are not able," since al-milk is applied to capability and ability. It has already been mentioned at His saying: ﴿Say: Do you worship besides God what possesses neither harm nor benefit for you?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 76] in Surat al-'Uqud.

[p. 170]

It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the sentence "﴿And man says, 'When I have died...'﴾" [Maryam: 66], or on the sentence "﴿And they have taken besides Allah gods...﴾" [Maryam: 81], completing the report of their statements. The statement is that Allah has a son, which is the saying of the polytheists: the angels are the daughters of Allah. This was discussed in Surat al-Nahl and elsewhere. The explicit meaning of the speech is a refutation of the polytheists, and its implication (kināya, metonymy) is an indirect allusion (taʿrīḍ) to the Christians, who resembled the polytheists in attributing a son to Allah. Thus it completes the refutation in His saying, exalted is He, just before: "﴿It is not for Allah to take a son; glory be to Him﴾" [Maryam: 35], and so on. The pronoun refers to the polytheists, so it is understood from this that the purpose of reporting their statement is not merely to inform about them or to teach their religion, but to make their statement appear monstrous and reprehensible. They only said this to support their worship of the angels and jinn and their belief that these would intercede for them.

The mention of "al-Raḥmān" here is a report of their statement in meaning, for they do not mention the name al-Raḥmān and do not acknowledge it; they denied it, as Allah related about them: "﴿And when it is said to them, 'Prostrate to the Most Merciful,' they say, 'And what is the Most Merciful?'﴾" [al-Furqan: 60]. They only say "Allah has taken a son," as related of them in many verses, including the verse of Surat al-Kahf. So the mention of al-Raḥmān here is the placing of a synonym in the position of its synonym (waḍʿ al-murādif fī mawḍiʿ murādifihi). The mention of the name al-Raḥmān is intended to enrage them by mentioning a name they denied. It also contains an allusion to the incoherence of their statement, since the attribute al-Raḥmān contradicts taking a son, as will come in His saying: "﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾."

The address in "﴿You have certainly brought﴾" is to those who said, "The Most Merciful has taken a son." It is a shift of address (iltifāt) for the purpose of conveying the reproach to them in a very explicit manner, in which the meaning is not ambiguous, as was mentioned previously in His saying: "﴿And there is none of you but will approach it﴾" [Maryam: 71]. So it is not good to estimate it as "Say, you have certainly brought." The sentence "﴿You have certainly brought a terrible thing﴾" is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāf) explaining the condemnation and reproach required by the sentence "﴿And they said, 'The Most Merciful has taken a son'﴾."

Nāfiʿ and al-Kisāʾī read "yakādu" (with the letter yāʾ), disregarding the feminine marker, since this is permissible in usage when the verb does not have a connected feminine pronoun as its subject. The rest of the readers read "takādu" (with the letter tāʾ), which is the other mode.

Al-tafaṭṭur means splitting open (al-inshiqāq). Combining it with "﴿and the earth is split open﴾" is a variation in the use of synonyms, to avoid the heaviness of repeating the same word. Al-khurūr means falling down (al-suqūṭ).

The "min" in His saying "minhu" (from it) is causal (lil-taʿlīl), and the pronoun governed by "min" refers either to "shayʾan idda" (a monstrous thing) or to the statement understood from "﴿They said, 'Allah has taken a son'﴾."

The discourse proceeds with exaggeration in depicting the horror of this statement, to the point that it reaches great inanimate things and changes their very existence.

Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, and al-Kisāʾī read "yatafaṭṭarna" with a yāʾ followed by a tāʾ. Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, Abū Jaʿfar, Yaʿqūb, Khalaf, and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim read it with a yāʾ followed by a nūn, from infiṭār. Both forms are the intransitive (muṭāwaʿa) of faṭara, either in its geminated form (faṭṭara) or its simple form (faṭara). The difference between the two patterns in usage is hardly definable. The attempt to distinguish between them, as in al-Kashshāf and al-Shāfiya, does not hold generally.

Allah says: "﴿And the day the sky is split open with clouds﴾" [al-Furqan: 25], and "﴿When the sky is split open﴾" [al-Infitar: 1]. In this verse the readings "yatafaṭṭarūna" and "yanfaṭirūna" are also reported. The principle is that the two readings agree in eloquence.

Al-hadd is the demolition of a building. "Haddan" is in the position of an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq) to specify the type of khurūr, i.e., the falling of demolition, which is that they fall in fragments and pieces.

"﴿That they attribute to the Most Merciful a son﴾" is connected to each of "yatafaṭṭarna," "tanshaqqu," and "takhirru." It is formed by deleting the preposition lām before the masdariyya particle "an," which is a regular deletion. Its purpose is to emphasize what was conveyed by "minhu," and to add a clarification of what the pronoun in "minhu" refers to, out of concern for making it clear.

The meaning of "daʿaw" is "attributed" (nasabū), as in His saying: "﴿Call them by their fathers﴾" [al-Ahzab: 5]. From it one says "iddaʿā ilā Banī Fulān," meaning he claimed kinship with them, i.e., he claimed lineage. Bashāma ibn Ḥazn al-Nahshalī said:

"We, the sons of Nahshal, do not claim a father other than ourselves,
nor does he buy us with sons."

The sentence "﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾" is coordinated with the sentence "﴿And they said, 'The Most Merciful has taken a son'﴾."

[p. 172]
The meaning of "yanbaghī" is "it is attainable" (yatatawwā) or "it is permissible" (yajūz). The original root of the verb (ibtighāʾ) is that it is the intransitive (muṭāwaʿa) of the verb baghā, which means "sought." The meaning of its intransitive form is to be affected by what is sought from it, i.e., to respond to the request.

Al-Ṭībī reported from al-Zamakhsharī that he said, in the book of Sībawayh: "Every verb that involves effort (ʿilāj) has its intransitive form come in the infiʿāl pattern, such as ṣarafa, ṭalaba, and ʿalima; and what does not involve effort, such as ʿadima and faqada, does not allow an intransitive infiʿāl form at all." End of quotation.

So it becomes clear that the basic meaning of yanbaghī is "responds to the request." Since the request varies in meaning according to what is requested, the meaning of yanbaghī varies according to context, so it is used with the meanings: "is attainable," "is possible," "is suitable," and "is fitting." Most of these usages originated as metonymy and became so well known that they now stand in place of the direct statement.

The meaning in this verse is: "It is not permissible for the Most Merciful to take a son." This is based on the principle that if the impossible were sought, it would not be attainable, since it is impossible and power does not relate to it. This is not because Allah is incapable of it. Compare His saying: "﴿They said, 'Glory be to You; it was not for us to take any protectors besides You'﴾" [al-Furqan: 18], which conveys the meaning: it is not feasible for us, or we are not empowered to take guardians other than You. Compare "﴿Nor is it possible for the sun to overtake the moon﴾" [Ya-Sin: 40], which conveys the meaning: they are not able to. Compare "﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him﴾" [Ya-Sin: 69], which conveys the meaning: it is not becoming to him. Compare "﴿And grant me a kingdom that is not befitting for anyone after me﴾" [Sad: 35], which conveys the meaning: its request would not be granted to whoever asks for it.

The meaning of "yanbaghī" is "it is attainable" (yatatawwā) or "it is permissible" (yajūz). The original root of the verb (ibtighāʾ) is that it is the intransitive (muṭāwaʿa) of the verb baghā, which means "sought." The meaning in this verse is: "It is not permissible for the Most Merciful to take a son." This is based on the principle that if the impossible were sought, it would not be attainable, since it is impossible and power does not relate to it. This is not because Allah is incapable of it. Its mention at "﴿except one who comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾" is an argument for the need of all existent things for Him and their acknowledgment of His ownership of them.

Compare "﴿Nor is it possible for the sun to overtake the moon﴾" [Ya-Sin: 40], which conveys the meaning: they are not able to. Compare "﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him﴾" [Ya-Sin: 69], which conveys the meaning: it is not becoming to him. Compare "﴿And grant me a kingdom that is not befitting for anyone after me﴾" [Sad: 35], which conveys the meaning: its request would not be granted to whoever asks for it.

There is a difference between your saying "yanbaghī laka an lā tafʿala hādhā" (it is fitting for you not to do this) and "lā yanbaghī laka an taf'ala kadhā" (it is not fitting for you to do such and such). What is meant here: it is not permissible, given the majesty of Allah, that He take a son, because all existent things other than His Essence, may He be exalted, must be equal in being created by Him and in being servants to Him. That contradicts sonship, because the sonship of God is part of divinity. This is one of the two interpretations of His saying: "﴿Say, 'If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers'﴾" [al-Zukhruf: 81], i.e., if He had a son, I would have worshipped him before you.

The meaning of "﴿āti al-Raḥmān ʿabdan﴾" (coming to the Most Merciful as a servant) is the figurative coming, which is acknowledgment and confession, like the expression "bāʾa bikadhā" (he returned with such and such), whose original meaning is "returned" but which is used with the meaning "confessed." "ʿAbdan" is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning: acknowledging to Allah His divinity, not independent of Him in anything, while being in the state of a servant. It is also permissible to make "ātī al-Raḥmān" mean "arriving at Him after death," so that the meaning is that he lives as a servant and is gathered as a servant, such that no claim of sonship mixes with him, in this world or in the Hereafter.

The repetition of the name al-Raḥmān four times in this verse is an allusion that the attribute al-Raḥmān, which is established for Allah and whose reality the polytheists do not deny even though they deny the word, contradicts the claim that He has a son. This is because al-Raḥmān indicates the generality and abundance of mercy, meaning that it encompasses every existent that is in need of Allah's mercy. This is not truly established except by realizing servanthood in the existent. For if some existents were a son of Allah, that son would be independent of His mercy, because by sonship he would be equal to Him in divinity, which requires absolute independence. And because taking a son requires the adopter's kindness and mercy toward him, and that contradicts God being the bestower of every mercy.

Thus the mention of this attribute at "﴿And they said, 'The Most Merciful has taken a son'﴾" and at "﴿that they attribute to the Most Merciful a son﴾" records their foolishness. Its mention at "﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son﴾" is an allusion to the evidence for the unsuitability of Allah taking a son. Its mention at "﴿except one who comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾" is an argument for the need of all existent things for Him and their acknowledgment of His ownership of them.

[p. 174]
The sentence "﴿He has enumerated them and counted them with an exact count﴾" is a conjunction on the sentence "﴿You have certainly brought a terrible thing﴾." It is a fresh initiatory sentence to threaten those who make this statement. The plural pronouns refer to what the pronoun in "﴿And they said...﴾" referred to, and what follows it. It does not refer to "﴿whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾." The meaning is that Allah certainly knows everyone who said that and has counted them, so none of them escapes from His punishment.

The meaning of "﴿And all of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone﴾" is the nullification of the reason for which they said "Allah has taken a son." They claimed that the taking of a son by Allah entails their worship of the angels and jinn, so that these would be their intercessors with Allah. So Allah cut off their hope in that by saying that each one comes on the Day of Resurrection individually, with no one to help him, as in His saying in the previous verse: "﴿And they will come to Us alone﴾" [Maryam: 80].

In this there is an allusion that they will come to what they dislike of punishment and humiliation in the way that an unarmed person comes to one who is able to take revenge.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verse 96:**

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, the Most Merciful will endow for them affection.﴾

The connection of the verses to one another in meaning requires that this verse describes the state of the believers on the Day of Resurrection, in contrast to the state of the polytheists. Their coming (to the Lord) will therefore not be a state of solitude, but a state in which some of them find companionship with others.

When the verse before it was concluded by stating that the polytheists will come on the Day of Resurrection alone (﴿fardan﴾), this implied that they will come to a situation in which one who is entangled in it would wish for someone to repel it from him and support him. The implication of this is that they are under divine wrath. Following this, (the verse) mentions the state of the righteous believers, that they are the opposite of the state of the polytheists, and that on that day they will be in a station of affection and honour. The meaning is: the Most Merciful will make for them friends (*awidda'*) from among the angels, as He, the Exalted, said (﴿We are your allies in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾ [Fussilat: 31]), and He will place affection between their souls, as He, the Exalted, said (﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾ [al-A'raf: 43]). The choice of the verbal noun (*al-masdar*, i.e. *wudd*, affection) is so that it encompasses several objects connected to affection.

It has also been explained that the making of affection means that God will place love for them in the hearts of the people of goodness. This was related by al-Tirmidhi from Qutaybah ibn Sa'id, from al-Darawardi. However, this addition is not (reported) from anyone who narrated the hadith other than Qutaybah ibn Sa'id, nor from Qutaybah ibn Sa'id in any narration other than that of al-Tirmidhi. Therefore, this addition is an *idraj* (an insertion into the text of a hadith by a narrator, not part of the original report) by Qutaybah, in al-Tirmidhi's version specifically.

It has also been explained that God will place love for them from Himself, the Exalted. In this case, the "making" (*ja'l*) here is like the "casting" in His saying, the Exalted (﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39]). This is the most apparent of the interpretations of *wudd*. Among the scholars of tafsir, groups have offered various opinions on it, varying in acceptability.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 19, verse 97:

﴿So We have only made it easy in your tongue that you may give good tidings thereby to the God-fearing and warn thereby a people given to contention.﴾ .

This is an indication that the surah is ending. The nature of bringing a comprehensive statement after the varied branches of discourse is that it signals the speaker is about to fold up his carpet (tadhyil, "appendage"). This is the nature of the concluding appendages and closings (al-khawatim), which are what signal the end of speech. Since the surah contained lessons, narratives, glad tidings and warnings, here it comes with a mention of the Qur'an and an explanation of some of the wisdoms in its revelation.

It is permissible to take the fa' (fa') as fasihah (an eloquent fa', indicating an implied statement), which points to an assumed statement that the mentioned words indicate, as if it were said: "Convey what has been sent down to you, even if the polytheists dislike what it contains of nullifying their religion and warning them of the evil outcome; for We did not send it down to you except for giving glad tidings and warning." 

And do not be concerned with the rage or resentment that arises from that. This is because the polytheists used to say to the Prophet ﷺ: "If you would refrain from reviling our gods and our fathers and deriding our opinions, we would follow you."

It is also permissible that the fa' is for deduction (al-tafri') from the threat against the disbelievers in His saying (﴿Indeed, He has enumerated them and counted them with a [complete] counting﴾ [Maryam: 94] ﴿And all of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection, alone﴾ [Maryam: 95]), and the promise to the believers in His saying (﴿Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds - the Most Merciful will bring about for them affection﴾ [Maryam: 96]). The deduced element is the content of "that you may give good tidings thereby" etc., and "warn thereby" etc., meaning: that is the effect of turning away from what you were sent with of warning, and the effect of turning toward what you were sent with of glad tidings, from what We have made easy in your tongue, for We did not send it down to you except for that.

The pronoun of absence refers to the Qur'an by indication of the context, like His saying (﴿until it [the sun] disappeared behind the veil﴾ [Sad: 32]). By this it is known that "making easy" means facilitating the recitation of the Qur'an. This is an incidental (idmaj) praise of the Qur'an, that it is made easy for recitation, like His saying, exalted is He (﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember?﴾ [al-Qamar: 17]).

Al-lisan (tongue) means language, i.e., in your language, which is Arabic, like His saying (﴿And indeed, it is the revelation of the Lord of the worlds. The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down, upon your heart, that you may be of the warners, in a clear Arabic language﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 192–195]); for the revelation of the Qur'an in the best and most eloquent of languages is among the causes of its superiority over other books and of the ease of memorizing it, which was not made easy for the like of it in other books.

The ba' (in bihi/bilisanika) is causal (sababiyyah) or accompanying (musahabah).

He described the disbelievers with "a people given to contention" (qawman luddan), as a reproach to them, that they are people who go to excess in dispute and obstinacy, i.e., people determined upon their falsehood. Luddan is the plural of alad, and it is the strongest in ladad, which is refusal to acknowledge the truth. In the authentic hadith: "The most hateful of men to Allah is the alad khasim (the most contentious disputant)."

Among the blameworthy traits that polytheism brought upon the Arabs, which they mixed with the good qualities of their character, is that they sometimes praised one another for ladad. Someone said in lamenting another:

Indeed, beneath the stones are resolve and determination, and a most contentious disputant, shut tight against reason.

The contrast between "the God-fearing" and "a people given to contention" is fitting, because taqwa is compliance and obedience, while shirk is disobedience and ladad.

In it there is an allusion that their disbelief stems from obstinacy, while they know that what Muhammad ﷺ brought is the truth, as He, exalted is He, said (﴿So indeed, they do not deny you, but it is the wrongdoers who reject the signs of Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 33]).

The application of the word "qawm" to them is to indicate that ladad is their characteristic, the quality from which their being a people was formed, as was mentioned in His saying, exalted is He (﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who reason﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164]) in Surat al-Baqarah, and His saying, exalted is He (﴿And signs and warnings do not avail a people who do not believe﴾ [Yunus: 101]) in Surat Yunus.

[p. 178]

When they were described as stubborn and obstinate, the passage was followed by a veiled threat against them for this, by reminding them of the nations that God uprooted because of their tyranny and their obstinacy, so that these nations would serve them as a measure and an example. The sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿So We have made it easy only in your tongue﴾ [Maryam: 97], in view of what it contains of good news for the believers and warning for the opponents, since the veiled threat against them is a warning to them and also good news to the believers that their relief from their harm is near.

[p. 178 continued]
"Kam" (how many) is khabariyya (used to state a fact), expressing a large number. Al-qarn means a nation and a generation. It is also used for the period of time in which a nation lives, and it is commonly estimated at one hundred years. The "min" is bayaniyya (explanatory), and what follows it is the tamyiz (specifying noun) of "kam".

The interrogation in ﴿Do you perceive any of them﴾ is inkariyy (a denial). The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, following His words ﴿So We have made it easy only in your tongue﴾ [Maryam: 97]; that is, "Do you not perceive?", meaning you do not sense any of them. Al-ihsas is perception through the senses, meaning you do not see any of them.

Al-rikz is a faint sound; it is also said al-rizz. Both forms have been transmitted in the verse of Labid:

*"She sensed the faint sound of the companion, and it startled her from the far side of the unseen, while the companion was her sickness."*

This is a kinaya (metonymy) for their annihilation: the disappearance of the attributes of existence is used to express the disappearance of their existence.

[p. 179]
In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.
Surat Ta-Ha

The surah is named after the two letters pronounced at its beginning, Ta-Ha.

The two letters are written in their written form, not as the names of the letters are pronounced by the reciter, following the orthography of the Mushaf, as was mentioned earlier in Surat al-A'raf. Likewise, its name appears in the books of Sunna in the hadith of the conversion of Umar ibn al-Khattab, as will come shortly.

In the tafsir of al-Qurtubi, on the authority of the Musnad of al-Darimi, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "God, blessed and exalted, recited Ta-Ha 'in two names' two thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth. When the angels heard the Qur'an they said: 'Blessed is the nation upon which this will descend'." The hadith continues.

Ibn Furak said: Its meaning is that God made His speech manifest and made it audible to whomever He wished among the angels. Thus this naming is related from the Prophet ﷺ.

He mentioned in al-Itqan, from al-Sakhawi, that it is also called "the Surah of the Interlocutor" (al-Kalim). In the same work, from al-Hudhali in his Kamil, that it is called "the Surah of Musa".

[p. 180]
It is Meccan in its entirety according to the majority opinion. Ibn 'Atiyya and many exegetes restricted themselves to this view.
In al-Itqan it is stated that an exception is made from it: the verse ﴿So be patient over what they say, and glorify the praise of your Lord before the rising of the sun and before its setting﴾ [Ta-Ha: 130], and so on.

In al-Itqan it is also favoured that the following is excepted from it: the words of the Most High ﴿And do not extend your eyes toward what We have given enjoyment to some pairs of them, the splendour of the life of this world﴾ [Ta-Ha: 131], and so on. This is because Abu Ya'la and al-Bazzar related from Abu Rafi' who said: "The Prophet ﷺ hosted a guest, so he sent me to a Jewish man to ask him to lend him flour until the new moon of Rajab. He said: 'No, except against a pledge.' I came to the Prophet and informed him. He said: 'As for me, by God, I am trustworthy in heaven and trustworthy on earth. I had not left his presence until the verse ﴿And do not extend your eyes toward what We have given enjoyment to some pairs of them, the splendour of the life of this world﴾ [Ta-Ha: 131] was revealed'." End of quotation.

In my view, if the hadith of Abu Rafi' is sound, then it is a case of confusing recitation with revelation. Perhaps the Prophet ﷺ recited it while remembering it, and Abu Rafi' thought it was being revealed at that very moment, though he had not heard it before; or the word "descent" was applied to recitation. There are many similar instances in the transmitted reports on occasions of revelation, as I have noted more than once.

This surah is the forty-fifth in the order of revelation. It was revealed after Surat Maryam and before Surat al-Waqi'a. It was revealed before the conversion of Umar ibn al-Khattab, according to what al-Daraqutni related from Anas ibn Malik, and Ibn Ishaq in his Sira from him, who said: "Umar went out with a sword strapped on. It was said to him: 'Your brother-in-law and your sister have converted.' Umar came to them, and with them was Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, who was teaching them the surah 'Ta-Ha'. He said: 'Give me the book that you have, so I may read it.' His sister said to him: 'You are unclean, and none touches it except the purified. So get up and wash, or perform ablution.' Umar stood, performed ablution, took the book and read Ta-Ha. When he had read a portion of it, he said: 'How good and how noble is this speech!'" The story continues to its end.

Al-Fakhr mentioned, on the authority of some exegetes, that this surah is among the first to have been revealed in Mecca.

[p. 181]
Umar's conversion took place in the fifth year of the mission, shortly before the first emigration to Abyssinia. Thus this surah was revealed in the fifth year, or in the last part of the fourth year of the mission.

Its verses are counted, according to the count of the people of Medina and Mecca, as one hundred and thirty-four; according to the count of the people of Syria, one hundred and forty; according to the count of the people of Basra, one hundred and thirty-two; and according to the count of the people of Kufa, one hundred and thirty-five.

* * *
It contains the following purposes:
A challenge (tahaddi) to the Qur'an by mentioning the disjoined letters at its beginning, and an indication that it is a revelation from God to guide those who are receptive to guidance; most of the surah deals with this matter.

Reminding of the greatness of God, the Most High. And confirming the mission of Muhammad ﷺ by showing that it resembles the mission of the greatest messenger before him, whose renown had spread among the people. So he sets forth the example of the revelation of the Qur'an to Muhammad ﷺ by the speech of God to Musa, peace be upon him.

It expands on the upbringing of Musa, God's support for him, His victory over Pharaoh through proof and miracles, and His turning aside of Pharaoh's plot from him and from his followers.

The deliverance of Musa and his people, the drowning of Pharaoh, and the honours God bestowed upon the Children of Israel in their departure from the land of the Copts.

And the story of the Samiri and his making of the calf which the Children of Israel worshipped during Musa's absence, peace be upon him.

[p. 182]
All of this is a veiled indication that the outcome of the mission of Muhammad ﷺ will be like the outcome of the mission of Musa, peace be upon him: victory over his opponents. Therefore the discourse moves from this to a warning to those who turned away from the Qur'an and for whom its examples and admonitions were of no benefit.
It also establishes the evil recompense in the Hereafter for those who placed their leadership in the hand of Satan, and warns them of evil punishment in this world.

And it consoles the Prophet ﷺ regarding what they say, and strengthens him in his religion.

Interwoven with this is the affirmation of resurrection, and the awe-inspiring depiction of the Day of Judgment and the events and terrors that precede it.
